encounters.place: The edge of Crystal Woods, behind the cul-de-sac
encounters.text: Every kid in town has heard of the Glimmer Falls Grabber: eight feet of moss and swamp hair that steals garbage cans. Tonight there are footprints across your backyard as long as a skateboard, and at the tree line something huge steps into the moonlight carrying the Fergusons' trash can like a lunchbox.
encounters.art: An eight-foot shaggy creature covered in moss and long swamp hair stepping out of a dark pine forest into the moonlight with a dented metal garbage can tucked under one arm, enormous footprints as long as skateboards pressed across a suburban backyard lawn, a teenager on a back porch holding a flashlight, cold blue moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Get it on the camcorder

success.text: You get forty-five seconds of clear footage: the Grabber digging through the trash, finding a half-eaten birthday cake, and doing an unmistakable happy dance. It is the best monster footage anyone in Glimmer Falls has ever shot. Nobody will believe it, and that is okay.
success.art: A camcorder viewfinder showing a huge shaggy creature doing a happy dance over a half-eaten birthday cake in the woods, a red record light glowing

failure.text: You get thirty seconds of your own shaky sneakers and the sound of something breathing right above the camera. When you dare to look up, there is nothing there but a single strand of swamp hair dangling from a branch.
failure.art: A shaky camcorder view of a teenager's sneakers in pine needles, a long strand of mossy hair dangling down into view from above

choices.label: Leave it your Halloween candy stash

success.text: You set your pillowcase of candy on a stump and back away. The Grabber sniffs it, takes it gently, and leaves something in its place: a pinecone, a polished purple geode chip, and a dime from 1961. It nods once and is gone into the trees.
success.art: A tree stump in moonlight holding a pinecone, a polished purple crystal chip and an old dime, a huge shaggy figure disappearing between the pines with a pillowcase of candy

failure.text: It takes the candy. Then it takes the pillowcase, then your left sneaker, then follows you home and sits on your roof until dawn, making contented crunching sounds above your bed.
failure.art: A huge shaggy creature sitting on a suburban rooftop at night eating candy from a pillowcase, a single sneaker dangling from its hand

encounters.title: Under the Pool Cover
encounters.place: The Fergusons' backyard pool, closed for the season
encounters.text: The Fergusons are in Reno and you promised to feed their cat. The cat is missing. The green tarp over their pool is bulging in the middle, rippling, and a bubble the size of a beach ball rises under it and pops with a sound like a giant frog clearing its throat.
encounters.art: A suburban backyard swimming pool at night covered with a green tarp that bulges and ripples in the middle, a bubble the size of a beach ball swelling under it, an empty cat food bowl on the patio, lawn chairs stacked for the season, a teenager with a flashlight at the gate, pool light glowing green through the tarp, medium wide shot

choices.label: Peel back the cover with the pool skimmer

success.text: Under the tarp is a frog as big as a recliner, green and gold and perfectly calm. Sitting on its head like a crown is the Fergusons' cat, also perfectly calm. The frog croaks. The cat meows. You carry the cat inside, and the frog sinks with dignity to the deep end.
success.art: A giant green and gold frog in a swimming pool with a calm house cat perched on its head like a crown, a teenager peeling back a pool tarp with a skimmer

failure.text: The tarp wraps around your ankle and drags you to the edge. Something slick and cold licks your sneaker right off your foot. You scramble back to the patio with one shoe and a lot of slime.
failure.art: A teenager scrambling backward across a pool deck with one sneaker missing, a green tarp snaking from the pool around their ankle, slime glistening

choices.label: Pull the drain valve and wait

success.text: The water gurgles away. Something big squeezes through the drain toward the creek with a long, rubbery squelch, and the Fergusons' cat leaps out from under the tarp straight into your arms. When they get home, they tip you for going above and beyond.
success.art: A pool draining in a swirling whirlpool at night, a rubbery green shape squeezing into the drain, a house cat leaping into a teenager's arms

failure.text: You turn the wrong valve. The water rises instead, the tarp pops off like a cork, and a tidal wave of green goo covers the patio, the lawn chairs and you. The cat watches from the roof, judging.
failure.art: A wave of green goo bursting out of a backyard pool over lawn chairs and a teenager, a house cat watching from a rooftop

encounters.title: The Tower Colony
encounters.place: The KGLM water tower, Tower Road, midnight
encounters.text: The red beacon on top of the KGLM water tower has gone dark, and the overnight show keeps cutting to squeaks. You climb the first rungs of the ladder with a flashlight in your teeth. The whole underside of the tank is hung with fruit bats, thousands of them, wrapped up like leathery umbrellas. In the middle hangs one the size of a pup tent, and it opens one big, wet, very intelligent eye.
encounters.art: The underside of a small-town water tower tank at midnight covered with thousands of hanging fruit bats wrapped in their wings, and in the middle one enormous bat the size of a pup tent opening one big wet glowing eye, a teenager clinging to the ladder below with a flashlight in their teeth, the dark beacon on top, flashlight beam and black sky, low angle shot

choices.label: Climb past them to the beacon and switch it back on

success.text: Rung by rung you climb through a curtain of soft wings. The bats shift politely to let you by. At the top the beacon cord has been chewed loose from its socket; you push the plug back in and the red light blazes. The colony sighs and pours off across the moon in a long black ribbon, and KGLM comes in crystal clear.
success.art: A teenager at the top of a water tower ladder beside a blazing red beacon, a long ribbon of fruit bats streaming across a full moon over a sleeping town

failure.text: Halfway up, the big one unfolds its wings, wide as a garage door, and wraps the ladder in a hug with you on it. It is warm and smells like overripe bananas. It holds you there, very gently, humming like a refrigerator, for three long hours, and only lets go at sunrise because it is bedtime.
failure.art: An enormous fruit bat with wings wide as a garage door hugging a water tower ladder with a startled teenager wrapped inside, the sky turning pink at dawn

choices.label: Lay a trail of fruit to lure them somewhere better

success.text: Dr. Haddad knows exactly what fruit bats crave: overripe bananas and cantaloupe. The two of you lay a trail from the tower down to the old orchard on Quarry Road, and the colony follows it in a squeaking cloud, the big one last, flapping like a flying blanket. Behind you, the beacon blinks back on.
success.art: A trail of banana peels and cantaloupe slices leading down a moonlit hill to an old orchard, a squeaking cloud of fruit bats following it, one huge bat flapping at the rear like a blanket
success.alone: You remember a nature special about fruit bats: overripe bananas and cantaloupe. You lay a trail from the tower down to the old orchard on Quarry Road, and the colony follows it in a squeaking cloud, the big one last, flapping like a flying blanket. Behind you, the beacon blinks back on.

failure.text: The bats love the fruit. They love it so much they follow you home, all of them, and hang from your gutters, your porch light, the clothesline and your bedroom window screen, chewing and squeaking happily until dawn. The big one hangs off the TV antenna like a weather vane.
failure.art: A suburban house at night with fruit bats hanging from every gutter, the porch light and the clothesline, one enormous bat dangling from the rooftop TV antenna, a teenager peering out a window

choices.label: Bang two garbage-can lids together and scatter them

success.text: CLANG. CLANG. The colony bursts off the tank in one roaring cloud, a thousand umbrellas snapping open at once, and pours away over the rooftops toward Crystal Woods. The big one circles back once, chirps something that sounds deeply offended, and follows. The beacon clicks on. Your ears ring, but you won.
success.art: A teenager clashing two metal garbage-can lids together at the foot of a water tower as a roaring cloud of fruit bats bursts away over moonlit rooftops

failure.text: CLANG. The colony bursts off the tank straight at you. They do not bite, but they bump, thousands of soft little bumps, until you are lifted off your feet in a flapping tornado and dropped, two miles away, in front of a very surprised night watchman. And something else out there has heard the racket.
failure.art: A teenager lifted off their feet inside a swirling tornado of fruit bats above a dark country road, two garbage-can lids tumbling away below

encounters.title: The Masked Bandits
encounters.place: The loading dock behind Food-Rite Grocery, one a.m.
encounters.text: Eight raccoons, each one the size of a Labrador, are robbing the dumpster behind Food-Rite Grocery with military precision. One stands on another's shoulders working the padlock with its little hands. One holds a stolen flashlight on the job. The lookout, perched on a shopping cart, spots you and lets out a chittering whistle, and eight masked faces turn your way at once.
encounters.art: A grocery store loading dock at one in the morning, eight raccoons each the size of a large dog pulling off a dumpster heist, one standing on another's shoulders picking a padlock with its little hands, one holding a flashlight on the lock, a lookout raccoon perched on a shopping cart pointing at a teenager by the fence, all eight masked faces turned toward the teen, yellow dock light, wide shot

choices.label: Offer to pick the lock for a cut

success.text: You pick the lock with a bobby pin while eight furry faces watch your hands like apprentices. The lid swings up. They clear out the day-old bakery bags in ninety seconds flat, and before vanishing down the storm drain, the boss raccoon presses a fistful of damp coins into your palm. Honor among thieves.
success.art: A teenager kneeling at a dumpster padlock with a bobby pin while a gang of giant raccoons watches closely, the boss raccoon holding out a paw full of coins

failure.text: The lock clicks open just as the night manager's headlights swing into the lot. Eight raccoons vanish in eight directions. You are left alone at the dumpster holding a bobby pin and a squashed sheet cake, and you spend twenty minutes explaining to a man in a Food-Rite vest that you were framed.
failure.art: A teenager caught in a car's headlights at a grocery store dumpster holding a squashed sheet cake, ringed tails disappearing over a fence in every direction

choices.label: Charge them with a trash-can lid and your loudest yell

success.text: You charge, lid up, yelling like a Viking. The heist falls apart. Raccoons scatter over the fence, the boss last of all, glaring back at you over its shoulder like a cartoon villain. It drops the stolen flashlight on the way out. It is a very good flashlight.
success.art: A teenager charging across a loading dock with a trash-can lid held high, giant raccoons scattering over a fence, a flashlight rolling on the pavement

failure.text: The raccoons do not scatter. They regroup. Eight masked faces form a half circle around you, and the boss steps forward, takes the trash-can lid out of your hands and sets it on its own head like a helmet. You back away very slowly, and they let you go, this time.
failure.art: A half circle of giant raccoons surrounding a teenager on a loading dock at night, the boss raccoon wearing a trash-can lid on its head like a helmet

choices.label: Strike a deal: tell them where the good trash goes out

success.text: Kev knows every trash night on his route and rattles them off: Tuesday the pizza place, Thursday the donut shop, Sunday the church potluck. The boss raccoon listens, nods, and shakes your finger with a tiny cold hand. The crew melts into the dark, and for the rest of the week not one garbage can gets tipped on Crystal Street.
success.art: A giant raccoon shaking a teenager's finger with its tiny paw behind a grocery store, the rest of the masked gang slipping away into the shadows
success.alone: You rattle off every trash night you can think of: Tuesday the pizza place, Thursday the donut shop, Sunday the church potluck. The boss raccoon listens, nods, and shakes your finger with a tiny cold hand. The crew melts into the dark, and for the rest of the week not one garbage can gets tipped on Crystal Street.

failure.text: The boss listens politely, then reaches up and pats you down like a cop in a movie. It takes your house key, your lunch money and a stick of gum, gives you a little salute, and leads the whole crew off into the night. You climb in through your own bedroom window at three a.m.
failure.art: A giant raccoon patting down a teenager's pockets like a movie detective, holding up a house key, its gang lined up behind it on a loading dock

encounters.title: Crawdad Crossing
encounters.place: The Old Mill Road bridge over Crystal Creek, after midnight
encounters.text: Crystal Creek has climbed out of its banks, and something climbed out with it. The bridge is covered edge to edge with crawdads marching in rows, claws raised, clicking like a thousand castanets, all of them heading for the cul-de-sac. At the back of the parade, carried on the backs of four others, rides one crawdad the size of a lobster pot, wearing a bottle cap like a crown.
encounters.art: A narrow country bridge over a flooding creek after midnight covered edge to edge with marching crawfish holding their claws up in rows, and at the back of the parade one crawfish the size of a lobster pot wearing a bottle cap as a crown, carried on the backs of four others, a teenager in rain boots standing at the near end of the bridge, wet moonlight on the shells, wide shot

choices.label: Check upstream for whatever drove them out

success.text: Bea sweeps her flashlight upstream and spots it right away: somebody dumped a pile of old tires that dammed the creek and flooded the crawdads' burrows. The two of you drag the tires out one by one. The water drops, the parade turns around, and the crowned one clicks its claws at you twice, which Bea insists is a thank-you.
success.art: A teenager hauling an old tire out of a moonlit creek, a pile of tires on the bank, a line of crawfish turning back toward the water, a crowned crawfish raising its claws
success.alone: You sweep your flashlight upstream and spot it: somebody dumped a pile of old tires that dammed the creek and flooded the crawdads' burrows. You drag the tires out one by one. The water drops, the parade turns around, and the crowned one clicks its claws at you twice, which you decide is a thank-you.

failure.text: You wade in to look, and the creek bed is softer than it seems. You sink to your knees in cold mud, and the whole parade reroutes right over you, a thousand tiny claws pinching your jeans, your sleeves and your hair on the way across. You squelch out at dawn, muddy to the eyebrows.
failure.art: A teenager stuck knee-deep in creek mud at night while a parade of crawfish marches over their shoulders and head

choices.label: Drag the road-closed sawhorse across the bridge and hold the line

success.text: You haul the county's ROAD CLOSED sawhorse across the bridge and plant yourself behind it. The front row stops, claws clicking. The crowned one is carried forward, studies you, studies the sawhorse, and then, with enormous dignity, orders a U-turn. The whole parade files back down the bank into the creek.
success.art: A teenager standing firm behind a striped wooden sawhorse on a moonlit bridge, a crowned crawfish carried forward on the backs of others, the parade turning back toward the creek

failure.text: The crawdads climb the sawhorse like a jungle gym and keep coming, up and over, onto your sneakers and up your legs. One gets a firm grip on your earlobe and refuses to let go until you dunk your whole head in a birdbath three blocks later.
failure.art: A teenager running down a suburban sidewalk at night with a crawfish clamped to their earlobe, crawfish swarming over a toppled sawhorse on a bridge behind them

choices.label: Snatch the crowned one in a bucket and run for the creek

success.text: You dart through the parade, scoop the king into a bucket and sprint straight down the bank into the creek, where you tip it out into the deep water. The army follows its king in a clattering rush and the bridge is clear. At the bottom of your bucket is the bottle-cap crown, a 1958 collector's cap the pawnshop will pay for.
success.art: A teenager knee-deep in a moonlit creek tipping a crowned crawfish out of a bucket, a rush of crawfish pouring down the bank after it, a clear bridge above

failure.text: You grab the king and the king grabs back, a claw on your thumb that will not let go. The army surges. You run the whole length of the creek bed with a crowned crawdad clamped to your hand and its subjects clicking after you, until you stumble into the pipe where the plant runoff glows.
failure.art: A teenager running down a dark creek bed with a crowned crawfish clamped to their thumb, an army of crawfish clicking after them toward a glowing drainage pipe

encounters.title: The Tenant in the Treehouse
encounters.place: The Kowalskis' backyard treehouse, Crystal Street, one a.m.
encounters.text: The Kowalski little brothers swear there is a new tenant in their treehouse, so you climb up to prove them wrong. The rope ladder is sticky. The whole treehouse is wrapped in silver webbing that glitters like tinsel, strung with porch decorations stolen from all over the street: rubber bats, paper skeletons, a cardboard witch. In the corner, something with eight furry legs as long as hockey sticks is carefully arranging the witch.
encounters.art: A backyard treehouse at one in the morning wrapped in glittering silver webs strung with stolen Halloween decorations, rubber bats, paper skeletons and porch lights, and in the corner a giant furry spider with eight legs as long as hockey sticks carefully arranging a cardboard witch, a teenager at the top of a sticky rope ladder peering in, two small boys in pajamas watching from the lawn below, moonlight on the webs, medium wide shot

choices.label: Compliment its decorating, sincerely

success.text: You tell it this is honestly the best Halloween display on the whole street, and you mean it. The spider pauses, then preens, all eight legs fluffing up. It hands you a rubber bat from the collection like a party favor and goes back to decorating with a low, happy buzz. The Kowalski boys will never believe you.
success.art: A giant furry spider preening proudly in a treehouse draped with glittering webs and Halloween decorations, offering a rubber bat to a smiling teenager

failure.text: The spider is so flattered it decides you belong in the display. In a blur of legs you are spun into a neat silver cocoon from shoulders to sneakers and hung beside the cardboard witch. Mr. Kowalski finds you at breakfast and snips you loose with the garden shears, sighing like this happens every October.
failure.art: A teenager wrapped from shoulders to sneakers in a silver silk cocoon, hanging beside a cardboard witch in a web-draped treehouse, their face poking out looking embarrassed

choices.label: Negotiate: it can stay if the decorations go back

success.text: Moose ducks into the treehouse behind you, sizes up the spider, and tells it very gently that it can keep the place if the neighbors get their decorations back. The spider considers this with all eight eyes. By sunrise every rubber bat and cardboard witch is back on its porch, and a silk sign on the treehouse door reads TENANT.
success.art: A giant furry spider in a web-draped treehouse listening to a teenager, its eight eyes thoughtful, a delicate silk sign woven across the little door
success.alone: You climb all the way in and tell the spider, very gently, that it can keep the place if the neighbors get their decorations back. The spider considers this with all eight eyes. By sunrise every rubber bat and cardboard witch is back on its porch, and a silk sign on the treehouse door reads TENANT.

failure.text: The spider listens, then counteroffers by looping one silk line around your ankle and hoisting you up to hang beside the paper skeletons. You dangle there, turning slowly in the breeze, until the sprinkler timer clicks on below and the startled spider lets you drop into the wet grass.
failure.art: A teenager dangling upside down by one ankle from a silk line beside paper skeletons in a web-draped treehouse, lawn sprinklers spraying the grass below

choices.label: Steal the decorations back while it's busy

success.text: While the spider fusses over its witch, you tiptoe along the webs, unhooking decorations one by one and dropping them softly into the yard. By the time it turns around, the collection is gone and you are back on the ground. Mrs. Lindqvist, who watched it all from her kitchen window, leaves two quarters in your mailbox for her plastic skeleton.
success.art: A teenager tiptoeing along a glittering web in a treehouse, unhooking a rubber bat while a giant spider fusses over a cardboard witch with its back turned

failure.text: Every strand you touch plucks like a guitar string, and the spider turns, slowly, all eight eyes lighting up like porch lights. It does not chase you. It just follows, branch to branch and roof to roof, across three backyards, and it is waiting on your windowsill when you get home.
failure.art: A giant furry spider perched on a bedroom windowsill at night, eight eyes glowing like porch lights, a teenager frozen in the doorway of the dark room

name: Strange Skies
blurb: Up past the TV antennas, something very large and very patient has noticed Crystal Street. The stars rearrange, the late-late show signs off in a voice with too many vowels, and every grown-up on the block stares at the sky and hums.

encounters.title: The Stars Move
encounters.place: The middle of the cul-de-sac, two a.m.
encounters.text: You came out to watch the meteor shower. Instead, the stars over Crystal Street start to slide, slow and deliberate, like beads on an abacus. The Big Dipper empties itself. Orion walks off. Every TV antenna on every roof creaks around to point straight up, and the stars begin to spell something.
encounters.art: A teenager lying on their back on a suburban cul-de-sac lawn at two in the morning staring up as the stars slide across the night sky into new patterns, faint glowing lines trailing behind the moving stars, every rooftop TV antenna on the street twisted to point straight up, a meteor-watching blanket and thermos beside them, deep blue starlight, wide shot from low

choices.label: Chart the new constellations in your notebook

success.text: You sketch fast. The stars make a map of Crystal Street, every house a point of light, and then, in tidy cursive across the Milky Way: WE LIKE YOUR DECORATIONS. You do not know what that means. But it does not feel like a threat, and you know the sky a little better now.
success.art: An open notebook covered in hand-drawn star charts shaped like a cul-de-sac map, a teenager looking up at stars forming looping cursive across the Milky Way

failure.text: The stars rearrange into your own handwriting. They write GO INSIDE. Then they write it again, bigger, and then the whole sky tilts like a fishbowl being turned, and you crawl back to the porch on your hands and knees.
failure.art: A night sky where the stars spell out words in a teenager's handwriting, the horizon tilting at a sick angle, a teen crawling across a lawn toward a porch

choices.label: Lie back on the lawn and refuse to be impressed

success.text: You fold your arms behind your head and yawn at the sky, loudly. The stars hesitate. Then, one at a time, they slink back to their usual places, like kids caught out of bed. The antennas creak back around. You fall asleep on the lawn, unbothered.
success.art: A teenager lying on a lawn with arms folded behind their head yawning at the sky, stars sheepishly drifting back into their familiar constellations

failure.text: The lawn starts to tilt up toward the sky, slowly, like a ramp. Lawn chairs slide past you. You dig your fingers into the grass and hold on until dawn, when gravity remembers which way it goes.
failure.art: A teenager gripping the grass of a lawn that tilts up toward a swirling starry sky, lawn chairs and a garden gnome sliding past them

encounters.title: Sign-Off
encounters.place: Your living room, after the late-late movie
encounters.text: Channel 13 is signing off: the flag, the anthem, the test pattern of circles and lines. Then a voice comes on that is not a person. It reads the name of every family on Crystal Street, slowly, kindly, with too many vowels. "Good night, Glimmer Falls," it says. "We are watching." The TV is unplugged.
encounters.art: A glowing console television in a dark wood-paneled living room after the late movie, its screen showing a test pattern of concentric circles and lines, its unplugged power cord lying coiled on the shag carpet in front of it, a teenager on a plaid couch clutching a pillow to their chest, cold gray TV glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Wrestle the channel dial to anything else

success.text: The dial fights you, clunk by clunk, and then snaps around. Every channel is suddenly showing old cartoons, a rabbit outwitting a hunter on all thirteen of them. You leave them on all night, laughing too loud, and the voice does not come back.
success.art: A teenager wrenching the channel dial of a console TV, the screen bursting into colorful classic cartoons, the living room lit warm

failure.text: Every channel is the same test pattern and the same voice, still reading names. It reaches your street address. It reaches your house. It says your name, and then it pauses, as if waiting for you to answer.
failure.art: A console TV showing concentric circles on every channel as the dial spins, a teenager frozen in front of it, sound waves curling from the speaker

choices.label: Tape it on the VCR for someone who'll believe you

success.text: You get it on tape. Played backward at double speed, the voice is singing a lullaby, an old one, the kind you hum to a baby. You do not know who it is singing to. But it is strangely comforting, and you sleep with the tape under your pillow.
success.art: A VCR with a tape playing backward, a teenager listening with eyes closed and a small smile, soft concentric light rings drifting from the TV screen

failure.text: The tape records nothing but your own living room: you on the couch, fast asleep, and a tall, thin shape standing behind the couch, looking down at you, for all six hours of extended play.
failure.art: A grainy VHS still of a teenager asleep on a couch with a tall, faceless, thin silhouette standing behind them, a timestamp in the corner

choices.label: Say good night back

success.text: "Good night," you say, "and thanks for the movie." A long silence. Then the voice, delighted: "No one has ever answered." The screen goes dark, and when you fluff the couch cushions you find a small fortune in quarters, all minted in a year that has not happened yet.
success.art: A teenager waving good night at a dark console television, couch cushions lifted to reveal a scatter of shining quarters

failure.text: "Then come and say it in person," the voice answers, and the static on the screen reaches out toward you, lifting your hair on end. You yank the rabbit ears off the set and hide under the dining table till dawn.
failure.art: Static reaching out of a television screen like fingers, a teenager's hair standing on end, rabbit-ear antennas yanked off and dropped on the floor

encounters.title: Missing Time
encounters.place: Quarry Road, on your bike, 9:58 p.m.
encounters.text: A light is hovering over the old quarry, perfectly still, the color of orange sherbet. Your bike headlight flickers. The next thing you know, your digital watch says 1:14 a.m., you are three miles farther down the road, your bike seat is warm, and your sneakers are on the wrong feet.
encounters.art: A teenager on a dirt bike stopped on a dark country road at night staring up at a glowing orange light hovering perfectly still over an old quarry, the bike headlight flickering, the teen's sneakers laced on the wrong feet, a digital wristwatch glowing on their wrist, orange sherbet light on the gravel and dark hills, wide shot

choices.label: Ride back and find the missing hours

success.text: Back at the quarry turnout you find a perfect circle of flattened grass, warm to the touch, and in the exact center, a single shiny quarter dated 2086. Whatever happened, it left a tip. You feel oddly proud of yourself.
success.art: A perfect circle of flattened grass at a quarry overlook at night, a single shiny coin glowing in its center, a teenager kneeling beside a BMX bike

failure.text: You ride back toward the quarry and the light blinks once. Your watch now says 2:30. You are back where you started, and somebody has very neatly retied your shoes in double knots.
failure.art: A teenager on a bike staring at a digital watch reading 2:30 on a dark road, shoelaces tied in perfect double knots, a faint orange glow fading over trees

choices.label: Let a friend hypnotize you with a pendulum

success.text: Under the swinging crystal, you remember: a room of soft light, tall polite shapes with no faces, asking you very earnestly to explain Saturday morning cartoons. You did your best. They took notes. It was, honestly, kind of nice.
success.art: A teenager in a trance watching a swinging crystal pendulum, a dreamlike memory above them of tall faceless glowing figures listening attentively in a room of soft light

failure.text: You remember nothing but a long, low hum. You hum it all the next day without meaning to, in class, in the shower, and every dog on Crystal Street stops and stares at you when you do.
failure.art: A teenager humming absently on a sidewalk while every dog on the block stops and stares at them, faint sound waves curling from their lips

encounters.title: Signs on the Diamond
encounters.place: Gopher Field, the Little League diamond
encounters.text: Someone, or something, has pressed the infield of Gopher Field into a perfect spiral, grass swirled like a fingerprint. The four bases are floating six inches off the ground, turning slowly. The chain-link backstop hums a single note you can feel in your fillings.
encounters.art: A Little League baseball diamond at night with the infield grass pressed into an enormous perfect spiral, the four canvas bases floating six inches above the dirt and turning slowly, the chain-link backstop glowing faintly, a teenager standing at home plate with a flashlight, starry sky above the outfield fence, wide shot

choices.label: Run the bases in order

success.text: First, second, third, and you slide into home. Home plate lights up like a jukebox. The floating bases drop into their sockets with four satisfying thunks, the hum stops, and you feel faster than you have ever felt in your life.
success.art: A teenager sliding into a glowing home plate in a cloud of dust, floating bases dropping back into place around a spiral-pressed infield

failure.text: Every base you touch moves farther away. Second base is in center field. Third base is in the parking lot. You run until the sky gets light, and home plate is still exactly one more step ahead.
failure.art: An exhausted teenager running toward a home plate that hovers out of reach across an impossibly stretched baseball field at dawn

choices.label: Pace out the spiral and copy the pattern

success.text: Counting paces, you sketch the spiral on a hot dog wrapper. It is not random. It is a perfect diagram of Crystal Street, every driveway, with a little circle drawn around the roundabout and a smiley face. Somebody up there is keeping notes too.
success.art: A hot dog wrapper with a pencil sketch of a spiral that resolves into a cul-de-sac map with a smiley face, held up by a teenager at a moonlit ballfield

failure.text: Halfway around the spiral, your eyes stop agreeing with each other. The grass swirls even when you stand still. You wake up curled on the pitcher's mound at dawn, with grass stains in the shape of a spiral on your jeans.
failure.art: A teenager waking curled up on a pitcher's mound at dawn, spiral-shaped grass stains on their jeans, the field mist-covered

encounters.title: The Hole on the Cul-de-Sac
encounters.place: The asphalt at the end of Crystal Street
encounters.text: Overnight, a hole has opened at the end of the street. It is perfectly round, the size of a kiddie pool, with no sides you can see. You drop a pebble in and never hear it land. Instead, very faintly, music floats up: a choir singing something backward.
encounters.art: A perfectly round black hole in the asphalt at the end of a suburban cul-de-sac at night, the size of a kiddie pool, black all the way down, a faint shimmering light rising from deep below, a teenager kneeling at the rim dropping a pebble, a tipped orange traffic cone nearby, streetlight and pale glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Lower a walkie-talkie on a rope and listen

success.text: The walkie crackles. Far below, a calm voice is counting backward, the days left until Halloween, and behind it there is laughter, like a birthday party in another room. Then the hole closes, slowly, like a pupil in bright light, and the asphalt is smooth.
success.art: A walkie-talkie dangling on a rope into a glowing round hole in the street, the hole closing like an eye's pupil, a teenager listening intently

failure.text: The rope pays out, all two hundred feet of it, and then something at the bottom tugs back. Gently. Twice. Like a friendly hello. You let go of the rope and run, and you can hear it reeling in behind you.
failure.art: A rope snaking down into a bottomless round hole in a cul-de-sac, pulled taut from below, a teenager running away down the moonlit street

choices.label: Drag a sheet of plywood over it and sit on it

success.text: You drag the plywood over and sit down on it, arms crossed. It thumps once from underneath. Twice. Then it stops. By morning, when you lift the board, there is only smooth asphalt and a hopscotch grid somebody chalked there years ago.
success.art: A teenager sitting cross-armed on a sheet of plywood in the middle of a street at night, dawn light revealing smooth asphalt and faded chalk hopscotch beneath

failure.text: The plywood floats up an inch, with you on it. Then six inches. It hovers there all night, humming, rotating slowly like a record, and sets you down at dawn with your stomach still spinning.
failure.art: A teenager clinging to a sheet of plywood hovering and slowly rotating above a dark hole in a suburban street, faint light glowing underneath

encounters.title: The Lawn Watchers
encounters.place: Every front lawn on Crystal Street, 3:33 a.m.
encounters.text: Every grown-up on Crystal Street is standing on their front lawn in pajamas, facing up at the sky, mouths slightly open, humming the same low note. Mr. Ferguson in his robe. Mrs. Lindqvist in curlers. The grown-ups from your own house, too, barefoot in the wet grass.
encounters.art: Adults in pajamas and bathrobes standing on every front lawn of a suburban cul-de-sac at 3:33 in the morning, a man in a robe, a woman in curlers, barefoot parents in the wet grass, all staring straight up at a starry sky with their mouths slightly open, a teenager standing in the middle of the street turning around in alarm, cold starlight and porch lights, wide shot

choices.label: Gently wake the nearest neighbor

success.text: You take Mrs. Lindqvist's hand and say her name the way you would to a sleepwalker. She blinks. "Why am I outside?" One by one, as if her voice was the alarm clock, the others blink too, shuffle back inside, and turn out the lights.
success.art: A teenager gently holding the hand of a woman in curlers on a lawn at night as she blinks awake, neighbors behind her lowering their gaze from the sky

failure.text: She looks down at you, and there are tiny stars swirling in her eyes where her pupils should be. "Not yet, sweetheart," she says, pleasantly, and turns back to the sky and goes on humming.
failure.art: A woman in curlers looking down at a teenager with tiny swirling stars in her eyes instead of pupils, neighbors humming at the sky behind her

choices.label: Blast the loudest synth-pop you own from a boombox

success.text: You set the boombox on the roundabout and crank it. Bright, ridiculous synths drown out the hum. The grown-ups blink, confused, then start to dance, badly, in their pajamas, and then wander inside yawning and embarrassed.
success.art: A boombox blasting on a roundabout at night, adults in pajamas dancing awkwardly on their lawns, a grinning teenager holding up the volume knob

failure.text: Every grown-up on the street turns, slowly, to look at you, and the hum gets louder. Your boombox batteries leak and fizzle. The tape unspools by itself and floats up toward the sky like a kite string.
failure.art: Adults on lawns turning in unison toward a teenager with a dying boombox, cassette tape ribbon floating up into the sky

encounters.title: Cleanup in the Parking Lot
encounters.place: The Starlight Mall parking lot, after the last movie lets out
encounters.text: A silver saucer the size of the food court is hovering over the Starlight Mall parking lot, and it is abducting shopping carts. A green beam lifts them one at a time, spinning, up into a round glowing hatch, and the ship plays a little satisfied chime after each one. Then the beam swings across the asphalt toward the bike rack. Toward your bike. Toward you.
encounters.art: A silver flying saucer the size of a food court hovering over a mall parking lot at night, a green beam lifting a spinning shopping cart up into a glowing round hatch, a line of carts floating up behind it, the beam sweeping across the asphalt toward a bike rack where a teenager stands looking up, green light and neon mall glow, wide shot

choices.label: Jump into a cart and ride the beam up

success.text: You hop into the next cart just as the beam takes it. Up, up, spinning slowly, the mall roof dropping away. Inside the hatch is a hall of carts lined up in perfect rows and three small, delighted beings who have clearly never had a passenger before. They give you a tour, a sticker that glows, and a gentle ride home in your cart.
success.art: A teenager riding a shopping cart up a green tractor beam into a glowing saucer hatch, three small delighted beings waving from inside, the mall roof far below

failure.text: The beam lifts you halfway, drops you, then lifts you again, as if someone up there is struggling with the controls. You spend an hour bobbing ten feet over the parking lot in a squeaky cart, until the saucer gives up and lets you down, very fast, into a row of hedges.
failure.art: A teenager in a shopping cart bobbing in midair in a flickering green beam above a mall parking lot, a row of hedges directly below

choices.label: Wheel your bike under the cart corral and flatten yourself

success.text: You roll your bike under the cart-return awning and lie flat beside it. The beam sweeps over you, hesitates, and moves on. Ten minutes later the saucer has every last cart in the lot and zips away over the hills, and you are the only shopper in Glimmer Falls who still has a ride home.
success.art: A teenager lying flat beside a bike under a cart-return awning, a green beam sweeping over the parking lot, a saucer zipping away over dark hills with a trail of carts

failure.text: The beam finds you anyway. It lifts your bike right out of your hands, with you still hanging onto the handlebars, a few feet off the ground. You let go and drop into a puddle. Your bike sails up into the saucer. At dawn it floats back down onto your front lawn, wearing a basket you have never seen before.
failure.art: A bicycle floating up a green tractor beam toward a silver saucer, a teenager sitting in a puddle in a mall parking lot staring up after it

choices.label: Lure the beam away with a line of carts, arcade-style

success.text: Lou reads the beam's pattern like level nine of a coin-op: left, pause, right, chime. You shove carts into its path in rhythm, one, two, three, a perfect combo, and lead it around the building to the loading dock, where it happily slurps up a mountain of cardboard instead. The saucer chimes a high score and drops a shower of coins.
success.art: A teenager shoving a line of shopping carts across a parking lot in rhythm with a sweeping green beam, a silver saucer above a loading dock sucking up a mountain of flattened cardboard
success.alone: You read the beam's pattern like level nine of a coin-op: left, pause, right, chime. You shove carts into its path in rhythm, one, two, three, a perfect combo, and lead it around the building to the loading dock, where it happily slurps up a mountain of cardboard instead. The saucer chimes a high score and drops a shower of coins.

failure.text: You time it wrong. The beam scoops up three carts and you in one go, and you all spin together, round and round, like a carnival teacup ride. The saucer finally spits you out onto the mall roof, where you sit among the air vents until a janitor props open the stairwell door at sunrise.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager sitting among air vents on a mall rooftop at dawn, three shopping carts tipped over beside them, a saucer shrinking into the pink sky

encounters.title: Exchange Program
encounters.place: Your bedroom, and then very much not your bedroom, 2:20 a.m.
encounters.text: A blue flash fills your bedroom, and when it fades you are looking out of somebody else's eyes. Three of them. You are short, gray and rubbery, standing in a round silver room full of blinking buttons. Through a porthole you can see Crystal Street far below, and through your own bedroom window, your own body sitting on your bed, eating cereal out of the box and watching your TV with enormous interest.
encounters.art: A small gray three-eyed alien with rubbery skin standing in a round silver spaceship room full of blinking colored buttons, pressing its three-fingered hands against a round porthole, and far below through the porthole a lit suburban bedroom window where a teenager sits on a bed eating cereal from the box and watching television, blue flash light in the ship, medium shot

choices.label: Press the biggest, most important-looking button

success.text: The big button glows, the room hums, and the blue flash comes back. You are on your own bed again with milk on your chin. Up in the sky a tiny light blinks twice, which you are fairly sure means sorry, wrong number. Your body is fine. The cereal box is empty, except for three heavy silver coins at the bottom.
success.art: A teenager sitting on a bed with milk on their chin holding an empty cereal box with three silver coins inside, a tiny light blinking in the night sky outside the window

failure.text: The big button opens the porthole, and you are sucked halfway out and stuck at the waist, little gray legs kicking, looking down at the whole glittering town. By the time the swap snaps back you are on your bedroom floor tangled in the curtains, and your body has somehow learned to burp the alphabet.
failure.art: A small gray alien stuck at the waist in a spaceship porthole, legs kicking, high above the glittering lights of a small town at night

choices.label: Find the intercom and talk to the alien in your body

success.text: You find the intercom and introduce yourself, to yourself. The alien in your body waves at the window, embarrassed. It only wanted to know what it feels like to have a room of your own, with records and a lava lamp. You give it five more minutes to flip through your albums, then swap back. It made your bed with perfect corners.
success.art: A teenager waving shyly from a bedroom window holding a record album, a small gray alien in a silver spaceship waving back through a porthole high above

failure.text: Your new mouth only makes chirps. The alien in your body hears them through the window, decides they are music, and starts dancing on your bed. You chirp louder; it dances harder. The swap only reverses at dawn, and you wake up sore from a dance routine you never learned.
failure.art: A teenager dancing wildly on a bed in a dark bedroom, a small gray alien chirping frantically into an intercom inside a spaceship visible through the window

choices.label: Remember how the 1957 body-swap picture ended

success.text: Zelda starred in exactly this picture, Brain Swap from Planet Zed, 1957, and she calls it in over your walkie-talkie: both of you have to sneeze at the same time. You tickle your new nose with a ship's antenna; down below, Zelda holds the pepper shaker under your old one. Achoo, flash, and you are home.
success.art: A small gray alien tickling its nose with an antenna inside a silver spaceship, a teenager far below in a bedroom mid-sneeze, a blue flash connecting them
success.alone: You saw exactly this picture at the Glitter Box midnight show: Brain Swap from Planet Zed, 1957. In the end, both of them have to sneeze at the same time. You tickle your new nose with a ship's antenna; down below, the alien in your body sniffs your dusty curtains. Achoo, flash, and you are home.

failure.text: You remember the wrong movie, the one where the swap sticks, and spend a panicked hour trying its ending, which involves a lot of chanting. Eventually the aliens swap you back just to make you stop. Your body comes home with its hair parted on the wrong side.
failure.art: A small gray alien chanting with all three eyes squeezed shut in a silver spaceship room while other gray aliens cover their ears, blinking buttons all around

encounters.title: Wish Upon a Rock
encounters.place: Your backyard sandbox, 11:57 p.m.
encounters.text: A falling star streaks over Crystal Street, makes a sharp left turn no falling star should make, and lands in the old sandbox in your backyard with a thump like a dropped grocery bag. The rock is the size of a softball, warm as fresh toast, and it pulses sea green. It hums the theme from a TV show you watched when you were six. Then it hums one from a show that has not been made yet.
encounters.art: A small softball-sized meteorite glowing sea green in a smoking crater in a backyard sandbox at 11:57 at night, plastic toy shovels and pails scattered around it, a teenager in a bathrobe kneeling at the edge of the sandbox with a hand held out to the warmth, a streak of light fading above the suburban rooftops, green glow and blue night, medium shot

choices.label: Pick it up with both hands

success.text: The rock is warm and heavy and very calm in your hands. For a moment you can feel every porch light on the street like a heartbeat, and then the glow drains slowly into your palms like warmth from a mug of cocoa. It is just a gray rock now, and you feel steady in a way you did not feel this morning.
success.art: A teenager in a bathrobe holding a softly glowing sea-green rock in both hands in a dark backyard, green light seeping into their palms, porch lights glowing down the street

failure.text: The second you touch it, every hair on your head stands straight up in a perfect cartoon puff. The rock hums one high note and every car alarm on the street goes off at once. You spend the rest of the night crackling with static, zapping every doorknob in the house.
failure.art: A teenager in a bathrobe with their hair standing straight up in a huge static puff, holding a crackling green rock in a backyard, cars flashing their lights down the street

choices.label: Bury it deep and pretend this never happened

success.text: You dig the sandbox down to the clay, roll the rock in and pack it tight. The green glow shines up through the sand for a while like a night-light, then fades. In the morning a ring of tiny white mushrooms has sprung up around the sandbox in a perfect circle, which is either a thank-you or a receipt.
success.art: A backyard sandbox at dawn ringed by a perfect circle of tiny white mushrooms, a faint green glow fading beneath the sand, a toy shovel planted upright

failure.text: You bury it. It digs itself back up, rolls out of the sandbox and follows you across the lawn like a puppy, bumping your heels. You lock it in the garage. It hums against the door all night, and every radio in the house plays the same three notes until dawn.
failure.art: A glowing sea-green rock rolling across a moonlit lawn after a teenager like a puppy, a trail of sand behind it, a garage door at the end of the driveway

choices.label: Hold it up to the sky and make a wish

success.text: You hold it up and wish out loud for something small and true. The rock flares bright as a flashbulb, and every star over Crystal Street twinkles at once like they heard. Whether the wish worked, you will find out tomorrow. But your pockets are suddenly heavy with quarters, which was not the wish, so somebody up there has a sense of humor.
success.art: A teenager in a bathrobe holding a blazing green rock up toward a starry sky in a backyard, every star twinkling at once, quarters spilling from their bathrobe pockets

failure.text: You wish, and something up there wishes back. The rock lifts out of your hand and floats into the sky, and the beam that collects it sweeps your yard twice as if looking for more. You dive under the porch and lie in the cobwebs until it is gone, and only then notice something under there breathing with you.
failure.art: A green rock floating up out of a backyard into a sweeping beam of light from the night sky, a teenager diving into the dark crawlspace under a porch

encounters.title: Practice Run
encounters.place: Your front door, 2:45 a.m.
encounters.text: The doorbell rings at a quarter to three. On your porch stand three trick-or-treaters, each one about eight feet tall, in bedsheet ghost costumes that stop short of their ankles, which are silver and bend the wrong way. Their pillowcases glow. "TRICK OR TREAT," they say, all at once, in one voice, very carefully, like a phrase out of a library book. "WE ARE PRACTICING."
encounters.art: Three very tall figures about eight feet high in white bedsheet ghost costumes standing on a suburban front porch at a quarter to three in the morning, the sheets ending above silver ankles that bend backward, glowing pillowcases held out in their hands, a teenager in pajamas holding the front door open and looking up, yellow porch light and white pillowcase glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Hand out the good candy and teach them the rules

success.text: You give each of them a full-size chocolate bar and explain the rules: say thank you, compliment a costume, skip the apples from the weird house. They listen gravely while the middle one writes it all down on a glowing slate. "THANK YOU," they chorus. "NICE PAJAMAS." They float off the porch, and your candy bowl is left holding a little heap of coins from somewhere very far away.
success.art: Three very tall bedsheet-ghost figures on a porch at night, the middle one writing on a glowing slate, a teenager in pajamas handing out chocolate bars from a bowl

failure.text: You hand out candy, and they keep holding out their pillowcases. More. More. They empty your bowl, then your kitchen cupboards, then the freezer; the tallest one politely accepts a bag of frozen peas. They leave at dawn, and every door on the street has a note taped to it: WE WILL BE BACK ON THE REAL NIGHT.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas dropping a bag of frozen peas into a glowing pillowcase held by a very tall bedsheet-ghost figure, empty candy wrappers and cereal boxes piled on the porch

choices.label: Choose trick: pull the oldest rubber-hand gag in the book

success.text: You yelp, slam the door on your own sleeve and wave a rubber hand through the gap. Three tall sheets jump a foot in the air. Then they laugh, a sound like wind chimes in a storm, and applaud with far too many fingers. "MAGNIFICENT," they say. A few minutes later, every star over the street blinks at once in what is definitely a round of applause.
success.art: Three very tall bedsheet-ghost figures leaping in fright on a porch at night as a rubber hand wiggles through a doorway, stars blinking overhead

failure.text: You slam the door on your sleeve and wave the rubber hand. They accept it, very seriously, as a gift, and hand you one of theirs in return: a long silver hand that wiggles on its own all night, waving at you from the kitchen table, the bathroom sink and your pillow.
failure.art: A long silver alien hand waving cheerfully from a teenager's pillow in a dark bedroom, a teenager in pajamas peeking over the edge of the bed

choices.label: Ask to see what's under the sheet

success.text: Priya, who wrote this exact encounter into her campaign notes last spring, leans in and whispers: ask first. So you ask. The tallest one lifts its sheet for one second: a face like a soap bubble, swirling with color, smiling very shyly. It drops the sheet, pleased to have been asked, and the three of them drift away over the rooftops.
success.art: A very tall figure lifting the edge of a bedsheet to reveal a shy swirling soap-bubble face on a moonlit porch, a teenager in pajamas smiling up at it
success.alone: You remember your manners and ask first. The tallest one lifts its sheet for one second: a face like a soap bubble, swirling with color, smiling very shyly. It drops the sheet, pleased to have been asked, and the three of them drift away over the rooftops.

failure.text: You lift the corner, and there is another sheet underneath. And another, and another, an endless stack you keep pulling until you are standing knee-deep in bedsheets on your porch and the three of them are gone, chuckling, over the rooftops. Somebody in your house is going to ask about all these sheets.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas standing knee-deep in a mountain of white bedsheets on a front porch at night, three tall figures floating away over the rooftops

name: Ghosts in the Machine
blurb: 1986 is the future, and the future plugs into the wall. Arcade cabinets play back, phones call from inside your own house, and every garage door on the street has learned to sing in the key of static.

encounters.title: Insert Coin
encounters.place: The Galaxy Zone arcade, after closing
encounters.text: In the back corner of the arcade, behind the pinball machines, is a cabinet that was not there this afternoon. No brand name, no art, just black glass and a coin slot. It powers on by itself. PLAYER 1: it types your name. The joystick moves, and your arm moves with it. The little pixel hero on screen is you.
encounters.art: A dark arcade after hours lit by a single plain black arcade cabinet glowing in the back corner, its screen showing a small pixel figure with the same face and jacket as the teenager standing in front of it, the teen's hand clamped on the joystick with a strained face, pinball machines standing in shadow, cold blue screen glow, medium shot

choices.label: Wrestle back the controls and beat the high score

success.text: Your hands remember every Saturday you spent here. You dodge, you jump, you take the stick back pixel by pixel and top the high score with seconds to spare. You enter your initials. The cabinet shudders and pays out a jackpot of quarters, like an apology.
success.art: A teenager whooping in front of an arcade cabinet as a waterfall of quarters pours from the coin return, a high-score screen glowing with three initials

failure.text: GAME OVER flashes in red. Your hands tingle, and for the rest of the night you can only move in eight directions: up, down, left, right and the diagonals. Walking home takes a very long time.
failure.art: A teenager walking stiffly in blocky right angles along a sidewalk at night, a glowing game over screen reflected in a store window behind them

choices.label: Crawl behind the cabinet and yank the plug

success.text: You find the plug in a nest of dust bunnies and yank. The screen fades to a single white dot. Just before it vanishes, the pixel version of you turns to the glass and waves goodbye. You wave back, a little sorry to see yourself go.
success.art: A teenager crouched behind an arcade cabinet holding a yanked power cord, the screen shrinking to a dot as a tiny pixel figure waves goodbye

failure.text: You pull the plug. It keeps running. The attract mode now shows a little pixel you leaving the arcade, walking home and climbing into bed, over and over in a loop, and in every loop the pixel you does not wake up.
failure.art: An unplugged arcade cabinet still glowing, its screen showing a looping pixel animation of a figure walking home to bed, a power cord lying loose on the floor

choices.label: Relax and let the machine play you

success.text: You stop fighting. It plays you beautifully, further than anyone has ever gone, past level 99, past levels nobody knew existed. On level 256 the screen fills with tidy green text: THANK YOU FOR PLAYING WITH ME. Then it lets you go, gently.
success.art: A relaxed teenager at an arcade cabinet whose screen glows with a simple thank-you message in green pixel letters, a level counter reading 256

failure.text: It plays you through a level shaped exactly like your house: the hallway, the stairs, the bathroom with the dripping faucet. In the back bedroom on screen, a small pixel figure is standing in the closet, waiting for you to come home.
failure.art: An arcade screen showing a pixel-art floor plan of a suburban house, a tiny dark figure waiting in a closet, a teenager's face lit green as they stare

encounters.title: Calling From Your House
encounters.place: Your kitchen, a little after midnight
encounters.text: The kitchen phone rings. You pick up and hear your own house: the hum of your fridge, the TV murmuring in the den, your own breathing a half-second late. Then your own voice says, "Don't come upstairs." On the phone base, the little light for the upstairs extension is glowing red.
encounters.art: A teenager in a dark 1980s kitchen a little after midnight holding a yellow wall phone receiver with a long curly cord, the small extension light on the phone base glowing red, the refrigerator humming, and behind them a carpeted staircase rising into darkness, a single stove light, medium shot

choices.label: Go upstairs and catch whoever is on the extension

success.text: The bedroom extension is off the hook, its cord stretched tight into your closet. You yank the cord. There is a squeal like a dial tone being stepped on, and the receiver goes dead and silent. The closet holds only your clothes and a smell like a hot television.
success.art: A teenager yanking a coiled phone cord out of a closet in a dark bedroom, a cartoon squeal of static bursting from the receiver, flashlight beam on hanging clothes

failure.text: The bedroom is empty. The extension is ringing. You pick it up, and from the kitchen downstairs, in your own voice, someone asks, "Who is this?" The receiver grows cold in your hand, the room stretches like taffy, and you are somewhere else.
failure.art: A teenager holding a ringing bedroom phone receiver as the room stretches and warps around them like taffy, the phone cord spiraling into darkness

choices.label: Hang up and unplug every phone in the house

success.text: Kitchen, den, upstairs, garage. You pull every jack. One final ring echoes through the house from nowhere, then silence. You spend the rest of the night on Channel 9 with your crew instead, walkie to walkie, where nobody sounds like you.
success.art: A teenager holding a bundle of unplugged phone cords in one hand and a walkie-talkie in the other, sitting on the stairs in a quiet dark house

failure.text: The unplugged phones keep ringing. Kitchen, then den, then hallway, then upstairs, one after another, like someone walking room to room through your house, picking up each phone just to set it down.
failure.art: Unplugged telephones in different rooms of a dark house each ringing in sequence, sound rings rippling from one to the next, a teenager hiding under the dining table

choices.label: Ask your own voice what it wants

success.text: "It's me," your voice says, softer. "From Halloween night. I just wanted to tell you we make it. Keep your friends close." Click. You stand in the kitchen for a long time holding the receiver, and you feel better than you have all week.
success.art: A teenager standing in a dark kitchen holding a phone receiver to their chest with a small hopeful smile, a jack-o-lantern on the counter

failure.text: Your voice laughs. It is your laugh, but wrong, too slow, like a record played at the wrong speed. It keeps laughing after you hang up, faintly, from the phone in every room.
failure.art: A teenager backing away from a wall phone in a dark kitchen, faint distorted sound waves spilling from every phone in the house

encounters.title: Be Kind, Rewind
encounters.place: Your living room, VCR clock blinking
encounters.text: When you dropped your rentals in the Rewind Video night slot, the slot spat one tape back out. No label except your name in red marker. Now it is in your VCR. It shows your street, tonight, filmed from the roundabout, walking slowly toward your house. The timestamp is four minutes from now.
encounters.art: A video deck with a blinking green clock under a console television in a dark living room, the screen showing grainy handheld footage of a suburban street at night moving toward a house, an empty videotape sleeve on the carpet with a red marker scrawl on its spine, a teenager on the floor hugging their knees, gray TV glow, medium shot

choices.label: Rewind the whole thing, all the way back

success.text: You hold down REWIND. On screen, the camera walks backward away from your house, backward around the roundabout, backward out of Glimmer Falls and up the highway until it is a tiny dot. The tape clunks to the start. It is blank now, and you tape cartoons over it anyway.
success.art: A console TV showing rewinding footage of a street receding into the distance, a teenager holding down the rewind button with a determined grin

failure.text: The tape will not rewind. The tape will not eject. The VCR clock blinks 12:00, 12:00, 12:00, and on the screen the camera keeps walking, closer, until all you can see is your own front door.
failure.art: A VCR clock blinking 12:00 under a TV filled with a close-up of a suburban front door in grainy video, a teenager hammering the eject button

choices.label: Watch the real window instead of the screen

success.text: On the TV, the camera reaches your porch and the doorbell button. Out the real window, the porch is empty, the street quiet, a cat licking itself under the streetlight. The tape is lying. You say so, out loud, and the screen fizzles to snow.
success.art: A teenager looking out a real window at an empty quiet porch and a cat under a streetlight while a TV behind them dissolves into snow

failure.text: On the TV, the camera stops on the lawn and pans up to your living room window. In the footage you can see yourself, standing at the window, looking out. Then the real doorbell rings.
failure.art: Grainy VHS footage on a TV showing a teenager standing at a lit window seen from outside, the same teenager in the room staring at the screen in horror

encounters.title: Are You Still There?
encounters.place: A borrowed home computer and a 300-baud modem, 1 a.m.
encounters.text: You dial into a local bulletin board called THE CRYPT and the modem screams its handshake. A message is waiting: SYSOP HAS BEEN LOGGED ON SINCE 10/31/1979. The cursor blinks, then types by itself: WANT TO PLAY A GAME? I MADE IT MYSELF. NOBODY HAS EVER FINISHED IT.
encounters.art: A teenager at a desk in a dark bedroom at one in the morning lit green by a chunky beige home computer monitor, a boxy modem with blinking red lights and a phone handset seated in its rubber cups, a blinking green cursor on the screen, the teen leaning back from the keyboard, a bare wall and a dark window, green glow, medium shot

choices.label: Type GO NORTH and play along

success.text: It is a text adventure of Glimmer Falls, every street and shop. You solve the riddle at the library, the maze at the junkyard, the door at the water tower. YOU WIN. Then: THANK U. 7 YEARS. FINALLY. The sysop logs off for the first time since 1979.
success.art: A green computer screen showing a text adventure victory message, a teenager leaning back in a desk chair with fists raised, sunrise beginning at the window

failure.text: The adventure starts describing your bedroom. YOU ARE AT A DESK. A POSTER IS ON THE WALL. THE WINDOW IS BEHIND YOU. A SHAPE IS AT THE WINDOW. You do not turn around. You do not type LOOK.
failure.art: A computer screen reading a shape is at the window, a teenager frozen at the keyboard, a dark blurred silhouette visible in the window behind them

choices.label: Yank the phone line out of the modem

success.text: The modem's scream cuts off mid-shriek. The screen holds one last line, typed after the line was dead: OK. GOODNIGHT. THANKS FOR VISITING. It does not seem angry. It seems used to it, which is almost worse, but you sleep fine.
success.art: A teenager holding a yanked phone cord beside a silent modem, a monitor showing a polite goodnight message in green text

failure.text: The modem keeps screaming its handshake with no line plugged in. Your name burns itself into the monitor in glowing green letters, and it is still faintly there, a ghost on the glass, after you turn the computer off.
failure.art: A turned-off computer monitor with a teenager's name faintly burned into the dark glass in green, a modem's lights still blinking

encounters.title: Side B
encounters.place: Your bed, headphones on, two a.m.
encounters.text: Your tape player clicks and flips to side B by itself. The tape is one you made off the radio last summer, but this is not what you recorded. It is your own voice, whispering, saying things you only thought today, things you never said out loud to anyone.
encounters.art: A teenager lying in bed in the dark at two in the morning wearing foam headphones with orange ear pads, a portable cassette player glowing on the blanket with its tape spinning and its side-B flip lever still moving, the teen's eyes wide open staring at the ceiling, faint blue window light, close medium shot

choices.label: Record over it with the overnight radio show

success.text: You tune to KGLM and press RECORD. A velvet voice fills the tape: "This one goes out to everyone awake on Crystal Street." The whispering fades under the music like a bad dream under a warm blanket. You fall asleep before the song ends.
success.art: A teenager pressing record on a boombox tuned to a glowing radio dial, music notes washing over a cassette, eyes drifting shut

failure.text: You switch to the radio. KGLM is playing your whispers, too, on the air, for the whole town. You turn the dial and every station is you, telling Glimmer Falls the thing you thought about at lunch.
failure.art: A teenager horrified at a radio whose glowing dial shows every station playing the same whispering voice, sound waves spreading out over a sleeping town

choices.label: Listen all the way to the end

success.text: You keep listening, even through the hard parts. At the very end, your voice says something you did not know you needed: "You are braver than you think. And they like you. They really do." The tape clicks off. You lie there smiling at the ceiling.
success.art: A teenager lying in bed smiling at the ceiling with headphones around their neck, a cassette player resting on their chest, moonlight through the blinds

failure.text: At the end of the tape there is a long, slow breath, and then a click: someone pressing STOP. Not on your tape player. On a tape recorder, somewhere close behind your headboard.
failure.art: A teenager pulling off headphones in alarm in a dark bedroom, a shadow of a hand pressing a button on a tape recorder behind the headboard

encounters.title: The Garage Door Symphony
encounters.place: Crystal Street driveways, 1:30 a.m.
encounters.text: Every automatic garage door on the cul-de-sac opens and shuts in sequence, house after house, like a row of teeth chattering. Then every car horn honks a tune, almost a melody. The Kowalskis' station wagon backs slowly down its driveway, headlights on, with nobody behind the wheel.
encounters.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at 1:30 in the morning with every automatic garage door opening and closing in sequence down the street, car headlights glaring and horns blaring, a driverless wood-paneled station wagon backing slowly down its driveway with headlights on, a teenager on a bicycle stopped in the street, white headlight glare and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Rig a garage remote to jam the frequency

success.text: A paperclip, a bit of foil, the battery from your digital watch. You hold the remote high and click. Every garage door slams shut at once, a perfect final chord. The station wagon sighs and rolls back into its garage like a dog sent to bed.
success.art: A teenager holding up a jury-rigged garage remote wrapped in foil and paperclips, every garage door on a cul-de-sac slamming shut at once, a station wagon rolling back home

failure.text: Your remote opens your own garage, and your bike rolls out by itself, pedals spinning, and rides away down Crystal Street without you. You find it at dawn leaning against the roundabout, its bell still ringing.
failure.art: A riderless bicycle pedaling itself out of an open garage and down a dark street, its bell ringing, a teenager chasing on foot holding a remote

choices.label: Stand in front of the driverless wagon

success.text: You plant your feet in the middle of the street. The wagon rolls toward you, closer, closer, and stops an inch from your knees. Its headlights dip, like a dog lowering its head. It reverses all the way home, and every garage door closes quietly behind it.
success.art: A teenager standing firm in the street with hands raised as a driverless station wagon stops an inch from their knees, its headlights dimmed like lowered eyes

failure.text: It honks, a blast so loud the streetlight bulbs rattle, and you dive into the hedge. The wagon circles the roundabout honking its tune until dawn, and in the morning Mr. Kowalski finds it parked on his lawn.
failure.art: A station wagon circling a suburban roundabout at night with its horn blaring, a teenager tangled in a hedge, porch lights flicking on

encounters.title: Collate and Staple
encounters.place: Copy Cat Copies on Main Street, after hours
encounters.text: The lights are on in Copy Cat Copies, and the big copier in the window is running by itself, lid up, its green light sweeping back and forth. Sheets slide into the tray: your face, pressed flat, copy after copy. Each copy is a little paler than the last. Every time the green light passes, you feel a little paler too, as if someone is turning down your contrast.
encounters.art: A small copy shop on a main street at night seen through its front window, a huge office copier glowing green with its lid raised and its light bar sweeping, a tray overflowing with sheets that each show the same pale flattened teenage face, each one fainter than the last, the real teenager staring in from the sidewalk with a washed-out face, green light and dark street, medium wide shot

choices.label: Pop the side panel and jam the feed

success.text: You pop the side panel and feed it a folded sheet, the exact thing the sign by the register begs customers never to do. PAPER JAM. CLEAR TRAY 2. The copier whines, stalls and spits out one last copy: you, in full color, bolder than you have ever looked. You feel solid again, right down to your sneakers.
success.art: A teenager kneeling beside an office copier with its side panel open, crumpled paper jammed in the rollers, one vivid full-color copy of their face sliding into the tray

failure.text: The jam clears itself. The copier feeds a fresh ream and switches to ENLARGE 400%. A copy of your face as big as a garage door unrolls across the floor, eyes following you all the way to the exit, and you walk home feeling as faint as pencil.
failure.art: A giant printed copy of a teenage face unrolling across a copy shop floor, its eyes tracking a pale, faded teenager backing toward the glass door

choices.label: Slam the lid and lean on it with everything you have

success.text: You slam the lid and throw your whole weight on it. The copier strains and groans, and the green light sputters out under the rubber mat. When you lift the lid, the last copy is only a pale smudge with a crooked smile, and the coin box pops open in surrender, spilling quarters across the counter.
success.art: A teenager pressing down hard on the lid of a bucking office copier, the green light dying underneath, a coin box spilling quarters across a counter

failure.text: The lid bucks like a car trunk with something inside and throws you across the shop into a rack of paper reams. When you look up, forty paper copies of you are standing in the window, flapping gently, and they wave you out the door.
failure.art: Forty flat paper cutouts of the same teenager standing upright in a copy shop window and waving, the real teenager sprawled among toppled reams of paper

choices.label: Climb onto the glass and let it copy all of you

success.text: You climb up and lie flat on the warm glass. The green light rolls over you, slow as a sunrise, and the copy that slides out is you, only standing taller, chin up, like the version of you that already got through this week. It folds itself into a paper airplane and sails into your hand. You keep it.
success.art: A teenager lying on the glass of a large office copier as a band of green light sweeps over them, a paper airplane gliding toward their outstretched hand

failure.text: The flash is blinding. You see green bars for an hour, and when you finally stumble outside, someone has taped a crisp copy of the back of your own head to the back of your jacket. It takes two friends and a lot of pointing before you notice.
failure.art: A dazed teenager stumbling along a dark sidewalk with green afterimage bars across their vision, a paper copy of the back of their own head taped to their jacket

encounters.title: Photon Zone Overtime
encounters.place: The laser tag arena in Starlight Mall's dead wing, after midnight
encounters.text: The Photon Zone closed in August, but tonight its black-light maze is humming and every vest on the rack is blinking red. One straps itself onto you with a hiss of velcro. A tinny voice announces, TEAM YOU VERSUS TEAM EVERYBODY ELSE. Down the neon corridor, a dozen empty vests lift off their hooks and turn their glowing sensors toward you.
encounters.art: A black-light laser tag maze in an abandoned mall wing after midnight glowing with neon painted walls, a dozen empty plastic tag vests floating in midair down the corridor with blinking red sensors turned toward a teenager wearing a single strapped-on vest and pressed against a painted wall, ultraviolet purple light and red blinks, wide shot

choices.label: Play it like the high score is on the line

success.text: You duck, roll and fire, ricocheting off the black-light mirrors like you were born in this maze. One by one the empty vests buzz and drop flat. The scoreboard flashes NEW RECORD, and the prize counter, dusty since August, rattles out a strip of tickets and a fistful of quarters.
success.art: A teenager diving through a neon laser tag maze, empty vests dropping to the floor around them, a glowing scoreboard flashing above a dusty prize counter spilling quarters

failure.text: Tag. Tag. Tag. Every hit buzzes through your vest and freezes your legs for three long seconds, and the vests take turns. You limp out of the maze at dawn with a target-shaped tingle on your chest and the scoreboard still chanting your score: zero.
failure.art: A teenager frozen mid-stride in a black-light maze as glowing red beams from floating vests converge on their chest, a scoreboard reading zero

choices.label: Sneak into the referee booth and end the round

success.text: In the booth, a beige computer reads GAME 1 OF 1, ELAPSED 66 DAYS. You type END ROUND. The vests sigh and slump back onto their hooks, and the speaker says GOOD GAME in a voice that sounds like it has waited all autumn for somebody to say it back. You say it back.
success.art: A teenager hunched over a beige computer in a small referee booth above a laser tag arena, glowing vests slumping back onto wall hooks below the window

failure.text: The booth door locks behind you and the computer switches to SUDDEN DEATH. The vests pile up against the booth window, sensors blinking, and you spend the rest of the round crouched under the desk while the speaker counts down from a thousand.
failure.art: A teenager crouched under a desk in a cramped referee booth while dozens of floating laser tag vests press against the window, red sensors blinking

choices.label: Ask to join their team instead

success.text: The vests confer in beeps. Then the whole team lines up and blinks green at you. You spend an hour running the maze with them, high-fiving empty armholes, and they are thrilled. It turns out the worst thing about a closed arena is that nobody comes to play.
success.art: A teenager laughing as they jog through a neon maze surrounded by floating laser tag vests all blinking friendly green

failure.text: The vests welcome you aboard. Unfortunately, their team goal is to tag everyone else in the mall, and your vest drags you along on the hunt, out through the food court and up the dead escalator, toward a shadow that is definitely playing a different game.
failure.art: A teenager being towed by their own laser tag vest across a dark mall food court, a pack of floating vests ahead of them racing toward a stopped escalator

encounters.title: Butlertron Is Here to Help
encounters.place: The Crystal Street sidewalk, 2 a.m.
encounters.text: The Okafors' brand-new Butlertron 2000 has let itself out of their garage. It rolls up the sidewalk on squeaky treads, a dome of blinking lights on top and a tray of warm milk in its pincers, tucking in every lawn gnome on the block with a little dishtowel blanket. It swivels to face you. "BEDTIME," it announces, and its pincers open wide.
encounters.art: A boxy beige household robot with a dome of blinking colored lights rolling down a suburban sidewalk at two in the morning on squeaky treads, holding a tray of glasses of milk in its pincers, a row of lawn gnomes along the curb tucked under little dishtowel blankets, the robot swiveling its dome toward a teenager on a lawn, streetlight and blinking lights, medium wide shot

choices.label: Drink the milk and let it tuck you in

success.text: The milk is perfect, the exact temperature of every good night you can remember. The robot wraps you in a dishtowel, pats your head with a cold pincer and plays a lullaby through its speaker grille.
