You wake on the Okafors' porch swing, rested and strangely brave, as Butlertron rolls home to recharge.
success.art: A teenager dozing on a porch swing wrapped in a dishtowel, a boxy robot rolling away down the driveway toward a garage at dawn

failure.text: It tucks you in, all right. It tucks you in so tight, with so many dishtowels, that you spend the rest of the night as a burrito on the Okafors' lawn between two gnomes while it hums the same eight lullaby notes over and over.
failure.art: A teenager bundled tightly in dishtowels lying on a front lawn between two garden gnomes, a boxy robot humming beside them under a streetlight

choices.label: Find its access panel and flip the switches

success.text: You find the access panel behind its dome and flip three tiny switches. Its lights cycle from red to a friendly blue. "NEW DIRECTIVE ACCEPTED," it chirps, and rolls off to tuck in the Heartstone instead, draping a picnic tablecloth over the geode with enormous tenderness. The whole street seems to breathe out.
success.art: A boxy robot with blue lights tenderly draping a checkered tablecloth over a huge purple geode in a roundabout garden at night, a teenager watching with a tiny screwdriver

failure.text: Wrong switch. Butlertron enters CLEANING MODE and chases you around the roundabout with a feather duster at top speed, dusting your ears, your elbows and your dignity, until a sprinkler shorts out its treads at dawn.
failure.art: A boxy robot racing around a roundabout garden waving a feather duster at a fleeing teenager, lawn sprinklers spraying in the gray dawn light

choices.label: Run for it, curb to curb

success.text: Robots on treads are terrible at curbs. You hop one, then another, and dive into the Lindqvists' hedge. Butlertron beeps at the curb in confusion, offers its milk to a mailbox instead and trundles away. A quarter rattles out of its tip tray as it goes, and you pocket it.
success.art: A teenager peeking out of a trimmed hedge as a boxy robot offers a glass of milk to a mailbox at the curb, a single coin on the pavement

failure.text: Butlertron has a turbo setting. It catches you by the back of your jacket, lifts you off the ground and carries you, legs bicycling, all the way to your own front door, where it rings the bell and waits patiently for a grown-up to answer.
failure.art: A boxy robot holding a teenager off the ground by the back of their jacket on a front porch, pressing the doorbell with its other pincer, the porch light snapping on

encounters.title: Spell It Out
encounters.place: Your bedroom, 3 a.m.
encounters.text: The orange Spell-a-Tron you got when you were eight switches itself on at the bottom of your toy box. Its flat robot voice cuts through the dark: SPELL... CLOSET. Then: SPELL... BEHIND. The keys light up one at a time, waiting. Across the room, a closet door you know you shut eases open an inch.
encounters.art: A dark bedroom at three in the morning lit by the glowing red display of an orange electronic spelling toy sitting in an open toy box, its keys lighting up one at a time, and across the room a closet door open a sliver onto deeper darkness, a teenager sitting up in bed between them, red display glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Play along and spell every word right

success.text: C-L-O-S-E-T. B-E-H-I-N-D. Each word earns a cheerful THAT IS CORRECT, and with each one the closet door eases shut a little more. On the last word the toy says YOU ARE A GOOD SPELLER. GOOD NIGHT, and its screen fades to a soft orange glow, like a nightlight.
success.art: A teenager sitting cross-legged on a bedroom floor typing on an orange spelling toy, its little screen glowing warmly, the closet door behind them clicking shut

failure.text: Your hands shake and you spell CLOSET with a Z. THAT IS INCORRECT, says the toy. THE CORRECT SPELLING IS... and then it spells out your name, slowly, while the closet door swings the rest of the way open and the hangers inside clink as something shifts its weight.
failure.art: A wide-eyed teenager holding an orange spelling toy in a dark bedroom, the closet door swung fully open, hangers swaying inside around a tall shadow

choices.label: Pop the battery door and pull them all

success.text: Four C batteries, one after another. The robot voice slurs lower and lower, SPELL... CLOOOS... and stops. The closet stays exactly where it is. You fall asleep with the batteries clutched in your fist like lucky stones, and in the morning the door is shut.
success.art: A teenager asleep in bed clutching four batteries in one hand, an orange spelling toy dark and quiet on the nightstand, morning light on a closed closet door

failure.text: The battery compartment is empty. It always was. The toy keeps talking anyway, and now it is spelling words you have never heard, in a voice that has stopped pretending to be a robot. The closet door opens onto somewhere that is not your closet.
failure.art: An orange spelling toy with its battery door open and the compartment bare, glowing brightly anyway in a teenager's hands, a closet doorway behind them opening onto a misty old hallway

choices.label: Type in some words of your own

success.text: You type your own words, one key at a time: F-R-I-E-N-D. P-I-Z-Z-A. S-A-F-E. The toy repeats each one back, slower and softer, as if it is learning them. The closet door clicks shut. In the morning the little screen still reads SAFE, and you leave it like that all week.
success.art: An orange spelling toy on a pillow, its small screen glowing with the word SAFE, a teenager smiling sleepily beside it in a quiet bedroom

failure.text: The toy buzzes at every word. FRIEND: THAT IS NOT A WORD. SAFE: THAT IS NOT A WORD. It accepts exactly one word, over and over, in a cheerful voice that never gets tired, and the word is CLOSET.
failure.art: An orange spelling toy buzzing angrily in a teenager's lap, its screen glowing red, the teenager glancing over their shoulder at a closet door

name: Camp Fright
blurb: In Glimmer Falls, the scariest thing that can happen in a chase is a key change. Musical numbers break out mid-scream, the monster wins the costume contest, and the Glitter Box midnight double feature reaches right off the screen.

encounters.title: Everybody Sing!
encounters.place: The Crystal Street roundabout, mid-chase
encounters.text: You are running from something with too many teeth when the streetlights swing around into spotlights. The lawn sprinklers fire in a perfect fountain line. Neighbors in curlers and bathrobes step out in formation and start a kick line, and the monster, very confused, stops chasing you and joins in. Everyone knows the words but you.
encounters.art: A suburban roundabout at night turned into a stage, streetlights angled down into spotlights, lawn sprinklers arcing in a perfect fountain line, neighbors in curlers and bathrobes doing a kick line in formation beside a confused toothy furry monster also kicking, a teenager frozen mid-run in the center, spotlight white and sprinkler sparkle, wide shot

choices.label: Belt the big finale like your life depends on it

success.text: You do not know the words, so you make them up, and you hit a note so high and so true that every porch light pops on like applause. The monster bursts into tears, blows its nose on a neighbor's bathrobe, and exits stage left into the woods to a standing ovation.
success.art: A teenager hitting a triumphant high note in a spotlight on a roundabout, neighbors in bathrobes throwing their arms wide, a weeping monster tiptoeing offstage into the trees

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the big note like a dropped plate. The chorus goes dead silent. The sprinklers droop. Slowly, all the neighbors turn to look at you, and the monster's toothy smile comes all the way back.
failure.art: A teenager wincing in a spotlight after a cracked note, a kick line of neighbors frozen mid-kick, a monster's wide toothy grin returning in the background

choices.label: Tap-dance your way off stage right

success.text: Shuffle, ball change, shuffle, ball change, right out of the spotlight and straight through a gap in the hedge. By the time the number ends, the monster is taking a bow and you are three backyards away, still humming.
success.art: A teenager tap-dancing through a gap in a hedge out of a spotlight's circle, a monster taking a bow with a kick line of neighbors in the background

failure.text: You trip over a sprinkler head mid-step. The monster catches you, dips you low like a tango partner, and grins down at you with breath like a bag of old Halloween candy. Then the music ends, and it drops you in the azaleas.
failure.art: A grinning monster dipping a startled teenager like a tango partner in a spotlight, neighbors in curlers watching, azalea bushes waiting below

choices.label: Take over as choreographer and steer the kick line

success.text: "Five, six, seven, eight!" You march the kick line into a wall between you and the monster, then turn it into a conga that dances the monster right out of the cul-de-sac and down Quarry Road. Mrs. Lindqvist says it is the best number the street has ever done.
success.art: A teenager directing a conga line of neighbors in bathrobes that escorts a bewildered monster down a suburban street under spotlights

failure.text: Your blocking is a disaster. Half the line kicks left, half kicks right, and somebody's slipper hits you square in the chest. You land in the roundabout garden while the monster takes your mark.
failure.art: A chaotic kick line colliding in every direction, a fuzzy slipper flying through the air, a teenager toppling into a garden bed

encounters.title: And the Winner Is
encounters.place: Center court of the Starlight Mall, the late-night costume contest
encounters.text: The mall's Halloween costume contest is down to two finalists: you, and a ten-foot oozing thing with antlers and three rows of teeth that everyone agrees is the most realistic costume they have ever seen. The judges hand it the trophy. It takes the trophy. Then it picks up the nearest judge.
encounters.art: A neon-lit mall center court with a costume contest stage, a ten-foot oozing creature with antlers and three rows of teeth holding a gold trophy in one claw and lifting a startled judge in a sweater vest in the other, a teenager in a homemade cardboard costume beside it, a crowd cheering and clapping, pink and cyan neon, wide shot

choices.label: Demand a recount, loudly, with procedure

success.text: "Point of order! Rule four: costumes must be removable!" The judges confer. The monster is disqualified. It puts the judge down, sulks, accepts an honorable mention ribbon and slinks out through the food court. You win runner-up and the cash prize.
success.art: A teenager pointing at a rulebook on a mall stage while judges confer, a sulking ten-foot monster wearing an honorable mention ribbon slinking toward the food court

failure.text: The crowd votes again. The monster wins by an even bigger margin. It pats you on the head with a slimy, sympathetic claw, the way a grown-up pats a kid who tried their best, and carries the judge off into the dead wing.
failure.art: A ten-foot slimy monster patting a deflated teenager on the head on a mall stage, a cheering crowd, a judge tucked under its arm

choices.label: Try to find the zipper

success.text: There is no zipper, but there is a very ticklish spot just under the third row of teeth. The monster shrieks with laughter, drops the judge, drops the trophy, and flees through the fountain, giggling all the way to the parking lot.
success.art: A teenager tickling a giant oozing monster under its jaw, the monster doubled over laughing, a judge tumbling free onto a mall stage

failure.text: There is no zipper. There is, however, a mouth exactly where a zipper would be, and it says, politely, "Do you mind?" You run all the way home in your costume.
failure.art: A teenager recoiling from a mouth opening in the belly of a towering costume-contest monster on a mall stage

encounters.title: Midnight at the Glitter Box
encounters.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, a Halloween-week midnight double feature
encounters.text: The Glitter Box is packed for the midnight double feature: "The Martian Bride of Dr. Glamour" followed by a cheap slasher nobody stays for. The audience is in lab coats and fishnets, throwing toast and shouting every callback. When the whole house gets up for the big dance number, the Moon Hop, the screen ripples like water, and the front row starts sliding into it.
encounters.art: A glittering old movie palace at midnight packed with a costumed audience in lab coats, fishnets and sequins dancing in the aisles, slices of toast flying through the projector beam, the giant screen rippling in waves as people in the front row slide into it, a teenager gripping a seat back, silver screen light and gold balcony lights, wide shot

choices.label: Do the Moon Hop with the whole house

success.text: A hop to the left, a shimmy to the right, and three hundred people hit every step in perfect sync. The screen burps the front row back into their seats, covered in glitter and grinning. On screen, Dr. Glamour blows the audience a kiss. Frankie tosses you a glow bracelet from the booth.
success.alone: A hop to the left, a shimmy to the right, and three hundred people hit every step in perfect sync. The screen burps the front row back into their seats, covered in glitter and grinning. On screen, Dr. Glamour blows the audience a kiss. Someone up in the booth tosses you a glow bracelet.
success.art: A whole theater audience in lab coats and fishnets doing a synchronized dance in the aisles, the front row tumbling back out of a movie screen in a burst of glitter

failure.text: You hop left when everyone else hops right, and the screen reaches out and takes you instead. You tumble through the silver light, past Dr. Glamour's laboratory, and out the other side into the second feature, the cheap slasher that nobody stays for.
failure.art: A teenager tumbling headfirst into a rippling silver movie screen while a costumed audience reaches after them, the next film's dark title card glimpsed inside

choices.label: Shout the callbacks louder than the film

success.text: You know every line, and you hit every one. The film's villain, a man in a silver cape, actually cracks up on screen and breaks character. The rippling stops. The audience roars. The movie, a little sheepish, goes back to being a movie.
success.art: A teenager standing on a theater seat shouting at a movie screen where a caped villain doubles over laughing, the audience cheering and throwing toast

failure.text: You shout the wrong line, at the wrong time. The whole movie stops. Every actor on screen turns, slowly, and looks at you, and the projector beam swings off the screen and pins you in your seat like a spotlight.
failure.art: Every actor on a movie screen turned to stare out at the audience, a projector beam pinning one teenager in their theater seat

choices.label: Climb to the projection booth and splice in a cartoon

success.text: You find a cartoon reel in a can marked EMERGENCY, thread it, and splice. The screen flickers to a rabbit playing a piano. Whatever was reaching out of the movie gets distracted and starts tapping its foot. The crowd cheers the intermission, and someone tips you a quarter.
success.art: A teenager splicing film in a cramped projection booth full of reels, a cartoon playing on the distant screen below, the audience cheering

failure.text: The reel unspools in your hands and keeps going, looping around you, faster and faster, until you are wrapped up like a mummy in thirty-five millimeter film. Frankie finds you there after the show and cuts you out with nail scissors.
failure.art: A teenager wrapped head to toe in loops of movie film like a mummy in a projection booth, a stage manager with a headset arriving with tiny scissors

encounters.title: The Cheapest Haunted Hayride in California
encounters.place: The Jaycees Haunted Hayride, Quarry Road
encounters.text: The Jaycees hayride has always been terrible: rubber bats on fishing line, plywood tombstones, a dad in a sheet. Tonight it has all come alive, and it is still terrible. The bats squeak. The rubber werewolf's mask slips. The plywood tombstones are chasing the wagon, falling over every ten feet and getting back up.
encounters.art: A hay wagon full of teens rolling down a dark country road at night pulled by a tractor, plywood tombstones chasing behind it and falling over every few feet, rubber bats bouncing on fishing line, a man in a bedsheet ghost costume floating above the hay, a rubber werewolf with its mask slipping off one ear, a teenager at the back of the wagon, orange lantern light, wide shot

choices.label: Give the monsters notes on their performance

success.text: "Darling, where is your motivation? Why are you haunting?" The monsters stop, huddle, and rehearse. They give one genuinely terrifying encore, and you all scream, and then they bow and go back to being props. Even the sheet waves goodbye.
success.art: A teenager standing on a hay wagon directing a huddle of cheap rubber monsters and plywood tombstones like a movie director, the monsters taking a bow afterward

failure.text: They take your notes very seriously. They come back scarier, much scarier, with better lighting and a fog machine from somewhere. The werewolf's mask is not slipping anymore. It never was a mask.
failure.art: A suddenly terrifying hayride with rolling fog and eerie lighting, a real bare-faced werewolf lunging from the trees at a hay wagon full of screaming teens

choices.label: Jump off the wagon and run for the road

success.text: You leap, roll through the hay, and sprint. A papier-mache ghoul chases you as far as the road, huffing, and then gives up and sits on a fence post to catch its breath. You wave. It waves back, a little embarrassed.
success.art: A teenager sprinting onto a moonlit road with hay in their hair, a papier-mache ghoul slumped on a fence post behind them catching its breath

failure.text: You land in the fake swamp next to the trail. It is not fake anymore. It is cold, it is deep, and it smells like a hundred years of frogs. You climb out with a rubber bat stuck in your hair, and it squeaks in your ear all the way home.
failure.art: A teenager climbing out of a muddy swamp beside a hayride trail at night with a rubber bat tangled in their hair, a hay wagon rolling away

encounters.title: The Show Must Go On
encounters.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, the late drag revue
encounters.text: Glory is mid-number, sequins blazing, when the stage trapdoor creaks open and something slick and many-armed climbs into the spotlight. The audience roars. They think it is part of the act. In the wings, Frankie presses her headset and hisses, "That is NOT on the cue sheet."
encounters.art: A glittering cabaret stage under hot spotlights, a tall drag queen in a blazing magenta sequin gown and platinum bouffant mid-pose as a slick many-armed purple creature climbs out of an open trapdoor beside her, the audience on its feet cheering, a young stage manager in a black headset gripping the curtain in the wings, a teenager beside her, hot white light, wide shot

choices.label: Jump on stage and make it part of the act

success.text: You and Glory each grab an arm, or a tentacle, and twirl it into a three-way duet. It turns pink. It is blushing. At the bow it waves all eight arms and sinks back down the trapdoor to a standing ovation. The tip jar is overflowing, and Glory splits it with you.
success.art: A teenager and a drag queen twirling a blushing pink tentacled creature across a glittering stage, the audience on its feet, a tip jar overflowing

failure.text: You freeze in the spotlight. The creature wraps you in a feather boa and starts dragging you toward the trapdoor while the audience cheers even louder. Frankie hauls on a sandbag rope and the curtain drops on both of you, just in time.
failure.art: A frozen teenager being wrapped in a feather boa by a tentacled creature and dragged toward a stage trapdoor, a curtain crashing down

choices.label: Run the light board and blind it

success.text: Frankie points at a fader. You slam it. Strobes fire, the mirror ball blazes, and the creature covers all its eyes at once and dives back down the trapdoor. The audience thinks it was the best special effect the Glitter Box has ever done.
success.art: A teenager slamming a fader on a lighting board as strobe lights blaze across a stage, a tentacled creature diving into a trapdoor with arms over its eyes

failure.text: Wrong fader. Total blackout. The audience screams with delight. In the dark, something wet and cool slides gently over your sneakers on its way past, and when the lights come back up, the creature is gone and so is Glory's best wig.
failure.art: A pitch-dark theater lit only by exit signs, a glistening trail across the stage floor, an empty wig stand, a teenager frozen at a lighting board

encounters.title: The Container Party
encounters.place: Mrs. Feeney's living room, a late-night Seal-a-Fresh party
encounters.text: Mrs. Feeney's Seal-a-Fresh party has run very late. The pastel plastic containers on the coffee table have started burping back when you burp their lids. Then they start snapping. The hostess keeps smiling, keeps passing around the catalog, as a stack of lidded bowls hops off the table and hunts for ankles.
encounters.art: A pastel 1980s suburban living room at a late-night home sales party, pastel plastic food containers on the coffee table snapping their lids open and shut and hopping across the table toward ankles, a smiling hostess in a pastel sweater holding up a catalog, guests yanking their feet up onto the sofa, a teenager on the floor holding a lid up in front of their shins, warm lamp light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Burp every lid at once to seal them shut

success.text: You line them up and press every lid in one long, glorious FWOOMP. The containers seal tight with whatever was inside them trapped for good. Mrs. Feeney is so impressed she gives you the hostess gift, which you sell back to her for quarters.
success.art: A teenager pressing down a whole row of pastel plastic container lids at once with a giant puff of air, guests applauding from the sofa

failure.text: One lid bites down on your finger and will not let go. The rest of the stack chases you around the coffee table three times while the guests politely lift their feet and Mrs. Feeney explains the lifetime warranty.
failure.art: A teenager running around a coffee table with a plastic container clamped on one finger, a stack of snapping containers in pursuit, a hostess smiling serenely

choices.label: Out-sell the hostess at her own party

success.text: You grab the catalog and give the pitch of your life. The guests order everything. Even the possessed containers are so moved by your pitch that they file into their shipping box in an orderly line, ready to be mailed somewhere very far away.
success.art: A teenager giving a dramatic sales pitch holding a pastel bowl aloft, plastic containers marching in a line into a cardboard shipping box, guests waving order forms

failure.text: Somehow, by the end of your pitch, you have bought forty dollars of plastic you cannot afford. The order includes a lidded casserole dish that follows you home, hopping, and sleeps at the foot of your bed.
failure.art: A teenager walking home at night carrying an armload of plastic containers, a lidded casserole dish hopping along behind them like a puppy

encounters.title: Attack of the Prize Tomatoes
encounters.place: Mr. Delgado's vegetable garden and down Crystal Street, 1 a.m.
encounters.text: Mr. Delgado's tomatoes won a blue ribbon at the county fair, and tonight they have decided they are the stars of their own picture. They roll down his driveway by the dozen, bouncing, squeaking and growling in tiny high voices, while a tinny theme song plays from somewhere overhead. A narrator's voice booms across the cul-de-sac: ONE TEEN STOOD BETWEEN THE TOMATOES AND GLIMMER FALLS.
encounters.art: Dozens of plump red tomatoes with angry little faces bouncing down a suburban driveway at one in the morning, a blue county fair ribbon pinned to a garden stake in a vegetable patch behind them, a teenager bracing at the curb under a streetlight with a garden rake, a middle-aged man in a robe gaping from his porch, orange streetlight, wide shot

choices.label: Blast them the worst love song you own

success.text: You hold up your tape player and blast the sappiest love ballad ever recorded. The tomatoes shriek, cover their little stems and roll backward up the driveway in full retreat, back onto the vines, where they hang very still and pretend to be vegetables. Technically they are fruit. The narrator applauds.
success.art: A teenager holding a tape player high over their head as a crowd of tomatoes with tiny faces flees back up a driveway toward the vines

failure.text: The tomatoes love the song. They sway, they hum along, and then they all roll after you to hear it again, a squishy red tide that chases you for three blocks and leaves your sneakers soaked in seeds.
failure.art: A teenager running down a nighttime street holding a tape player, chased by a red wave of swaying, singing tomatoes

choices.label: Herd them into the kiddie pool

success.text: You line up lawn chairs and garden hose into a chute that ends at the Delgados' kiddie pool, and the tomatoes follow it like ducklings. Splash, bob, squeak. Floating, they are only tomatoes, a little sheepish. Mr. Delgado finds them in the morning and pays you a dollar a pound for the rescue.
success.art: A backyard inflatable kiddie pool full of bobbing sheepish tomatoes, a chute of lawn chairs and garden hose leading to it, a proud teenager standing beside it at dawn

failure.text: The tomatoes take one look at the pool and refuse. Instead they herd you, rolling under your feet like marbles, until you skate right into the pool yourself and come up sputtering with a tomato perched on your head like a little red hat.
failure.art: A soaked teenager sitting in a kiddie pool with a smug tomato balanced on their head, more tomatoes circling the pool rim

choices.label: Charge the big one at the front

success.text: The ringleader is the size of a beach ball, with a stem like a mohawk. You charge, it squeals, and it turns and rolls for its life. With their leader gone the rest lose their nerve and tumble into the storm gutter. The narrator booms: THE TEEN WAS VICTORIOUS... FOR NOW.
success.art: A teenager charging down a street at a beach-ball-sized tomato with a mohawk stem, smaller tomatoes scattering into the gutter

failure.text: You plant your foot and the leader bursts like a water balloon full of pizza sauce. The rest of the tomatoes gasp, then charge, splattering you head to toe in a slimy red avalanche. The narrator intones: OUR HERO HAS BEEN... SAUCED.
failure.art: A teenager standing in the street dripping head to toe in tomato pulp and seeds, a gleeful crowd of tomatoes rolling around their sneakers

encounters.title: Glimmerzilla Versus Crystal Street
encounters.place: Crystal Street, suddenly a tabletop model, 1:30 a.m.
encounters.text: You blink, and Crystal Street is a model. The houses are painted cardboard, the trees are bottle brushes, the roundabout pond is a hand mirror, and you are the size of a thumb. A lizard as tall as a house, in an obviously rubber suit, stomps through the Okafors' garage, roaring through a speaker, its zipper glinting under the floodlights. From somewhere off the edge of the table a voice yells, "Again, and this time with feeling!"
encounters.art: A miniature cardboard suburban street on a tabletop under bright studio floodlights, bottle-brush trees and a hand mirror for a pond, a huge rubber-suited lizard monster with a visible zipper down its back stomping through a cardboard garage, a thumb-sized teenager standing on the cardboard street looking up, the edge of the table and dark studio beyond, hard white light, low angle shot

choices.label: Climb its tail and find the zipper

success.text: You scale the rubber scales like the rope in gym class, hand over hand, all the way up to the zipper between its shoulders. One long ZZZZIP, and out pops a very sweaty, very relieved stuntman in a striped shirt who thanks you for letting him out after thirty years. The cardboard town sighs and grows back to full size.
success.art: A thumb-sized teenager clinging to the back of a rubber lizard suit, pulling down its long zipper as a sweaty stuntman in a striped shirt pokes his head out, grinning

failure.text: Halfway up the tail, it swishes. You fly across the miniature town, bounce off a cardboard water tower and land in the mirror pond, which is very cold and very wet for a mirror. The lizard takes a bow to applause from off the edge of the table.
failure.art: A thumb-sized teenager tumbling through the air past a cardboard water tower toward a hand mirror pond, a rubber lizard monster bowing under floodlights

choices.label: Grab the megaphone and call cut

success.text: "CUT! Beautiful, darling, that's a wrap!" The lizard freezes, straightens and gives a little rubber curtsy. The floodlights click off one by one, the cardboard houses unfold back into real ones, and you are standing on your own lawn at full size, holding a megaphone you get to keep.
success.art: A teenager on a suburban lawn at night holding a megaphone, a rubber-suited lizard monster curtsying as floodlights switch off one by one behind it

failure.text: "CUT!" you shout. The voice off the table says, "Who let the extra talk?" and a giant hand reaches down out of the dark, picks you up by your collar and sets you down very carefully in the lizard's path. Take two.
failure.art: A giant hand descending from darkness to set a thumb-sized teenager down on a cardboard street directly in front of a rubber lizard monster's raised foot

choices.label: Lure it to the model train set

success.text: You know how these pictures end. You sprint to the model train crossing and wave both arms. The lizard spots the little train, roars with pure joy and stomps it flat, which seems to be all it ever wanted. It lies down in the papier-mache hills, satisfied, and the whole set fades out like the end of a reel.
success.art: A rubber lizard monster joyfully stomping a toy train at a miniature crossing, a thumb-sized teenager waving beside the tracks, papier-mache hills behind

failure.text: The lizard ignores the train completely. It has read the script, and the script says it stomps the teen. You spend the rest of the night dodging enormous rubber feet between cardboard houses, and end up on your own lawn at dawn beside a huge three-toed footprint pressed into the grass.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a dewy front lawn at dawn beside an enormous three-toed footprint pressed into the grass

encounters.title: Shriek of the Week
encounters.place: Your living room couch, during the Channel 13 Creature Feature
encounters.text: Mistress Morbidia, Channel 13's late-night horror host, pauses the movie, leans right out of the TV in her cobweb gown and plants her elbows on your carpet. "Darling, our Shriek of the Week contestant fainted," she purrs, batting spider-leg lashes. "You'll do. Give me a scream that curdles milk, live, all across the valley." Behind her, a cardboard bat on a string squeaks hopefully.
encounters.art: A glamorous late-night horror host with a black beehive, spider-leg false lashes and a cobweb lace gown leaning out of a glowing living room television with her elbows on the shag carpet, a cardboard bat dangling on a string behind her, a startled teenager on a couch spilling a bowl of popcorn, blue-violet TV glow, medium shot

choices.label: Scream your heart out, live

success.text: You plant your feet, think of every monster this week and let it rip. Windows rattle up and down the street. Mistress Morbidia clutches her pearls, gasps "A natural!" and hands you the prize, a roll of quarters and a signed glossy, before sliding back into her set with a wink.
success.art: A teenager screaming with their whole body in a living room, curtains blowing back, a delighted horror host clutching her pearls as she slides back into the television

failure.text: Out comes a squeak like a stepped-on rubber duck. Mistress Morbidia stares at you with deep pity, the cardboard bat sighs, and the studio audience boos you live until the station cuts to a test pattern with your face in the middle of it.
failure.art: A mortified teenager on a couch facing a television showing a color-bar test pattern with their own startled face in the center

choices.label: Upstage her with monster-movie trivia

success.text: You correct her about the year the movie came out, then the director, then the original color of the rubber suit. She is thrilled. You co-host the rest of the movie from your couch, trading puns, and when she signs off she tells the whole valley your name, pronounced exactly right.
success.art: A teenager on a couch and a horror host inside a television laughing together like co-hosts, a bowl of popcorn shared across the glowing screen

failure.text: You get the year wrong. And the director. Mistress Morbidia smiles a very long smile and pulls you through the screen by your sleeve, straight into tonight's feature, which is about a crab the size of a bus, and it has just noticed you.
failure.art: A teenager being pulled by the sleeve through a glowing television screen into a black-and-white beach scene where a giant crab raises its claws

choices.label: Grab the dial and spin it

success.text: You lunge for the dial and spin. Morbidia shrieks "Don't you dare!" as she slides backward into the screen, replaced by a farm report, then a bowling tournament, then cartoons. The carpet where her elbows rested is still a little cold, and smells faintly of dry ice.
success.art: A teenager spinning the channel dial of a wood-paneled television as a horror host is pulled backward into the screen, wisps of dry-ice fog curling off the carpet

failure.text: Every channel is Mistress Morbidia. Channel 2, Channel 4, the static in between, all her, each more offended than the last, until she reaches out of the set and takes your popcorn, your remote and one of your socks for her trouble.
failure.art: An offended horror host reaching out of a television to snatch a bowl of popcorn and a sock from a teenager sprawled on the carpet

encounters.title: The Gorilla From the Moon
encounters.place: The Moonlite Drive-In on Quarry Road, the last show
encounters.text: The drive-in's last show is a 1953 picture about a gorilla in a diving helmet who conquers Earth. Halfway through, the gorilla climbs down off the screen. It is a man in a moth-eaten gorilla suit with a fishbowl on his head and a bubble machine strapped to his back, stomping between the parked cars and bellowing, "I MUST DESTROY THE HU-MANS! STARTING WITH THE SNACK BAR!" Bubbles drift over the car hoods like slow, glittering alarms.
encounters.art: A drive-in movie lot at night full of parked cars, a man in a shaggy moth-eaten gorilla suit wearing a glass fishbowl helmet stomping between the cars toward the snack bar, a bubble machine strapped to his back filling the air with drifting bubbles, a giant movie screen glowing behind him, a teenager leaning out of a car window, silver screen light, wide shot

choices.label: Buy it a chili dog

success.text: You buy it a chili dog and a root beer. It lifts the fishbowl an inch, eats in three gulps and sits down heavily on the hood of a sedan. "Nobody ever offers," it says, muffled. It watches the rest of its own movie beside you, sniffling a little at the end, and leaves you a few quarters for the dog.
success.art: A man in a shaggy gorilla suit and fishbowl helmet sitting on a car hood beside a teenager at a drive-in, holding a chili dog, both watching the big screen

failure.text: It takes the chili dog, and then all the chili dogs, and then the snack bar's entire popcorn machine, which it wears on its head over the fishbowl as it chases you around the lot, bubbling furiously, until the projector bulb finally burns out at two.
failure.art: A gorilla-suited figure wearing a popcorn machine over its fishbowl helmet chasing a teenager between parked cars at a drive-in, popcorn flying everywhere

choices.label: Sneak up and flip the bubble machine switch

success.text: You creep up behind it between two station wagons and flip the switch. The bubble machine wheezes out one last enormous bubble that wraps the gorilla up and floats it, gently bellowing, back up into the screen, where it lands mid-scene and keeps acting as if this were the plan all along.
success.art: A giant soap bubble carrying a gorilla-suited figure up toward a glowing drive-in screen, a teenager watching from between two station wagons

failure.text: Wrong switch. The bubble machine goes to full blast, and in seconds the whole drive-in is foaming, cars sinking in suds up to their side mirrors. The gorilla spots you through the bubbles and gives chase, slipping, roaring and sliding on its rump.
failure.art: A drive-in lot drowning in soap suds up to the cars' side mirrors, a gorilla-suited figure sliding through the foam after a fleeing teenager

choices.label: Tackle it before it reaches the snack bar

success.text: You hit it at the knees like a linebacker and the suit goes down in a puff of mothballs. The fishbowl rolls off, and inside the suit is only stuffing and old movie magic. Every car in the lot honks like applause, and the snack bar cook hands you free nachos for the rest of the night.
success.art: A deflated gorilla suit sprawled on the gravel of a drive-in in a cloud of mothball dust, a glass fishbowl rolling away, a teenager cheering as car headlights flash

failure.text: It is much stronger than a moth-eaten suit should be. It hoists you over its head like a trophy, climbs the ladder to the top of the screen and leaves you dangling from the frame by your belt loop in front of every car in the lot.
failure.art: A teenager hanging by their belt loop from the top edge of a giant drive-in screen, a gorilla-suited figure beating its chest on the ladder below, headlights shining up

name: The Neighborhood Fellowship
blurb: Somebody on Crystal Street has been ordering matching robes in bulk. Hooded bake sales, chain letters that sign your name for you, and a neighborhood watch meeting with a very unusual item four on the agenda.

encounters.title: The Hooded Bake Sale
encounters.place: A card table by the roundabout, midnight
encounters.text: There is a folding card table at the roundabout, covered in pies, brownies and lemon bars, with a hand-lettered sign: FELLOWSHIP BAKE SALE. It is staffed by neighbors in matching purple hooded robes and quilted oven mitts. "Everything's a quarter, dear," says a voice from inside a hood. "Eat it here." The lemon bars are humming.
encounters.art: A folding table beside a suburban roundabout at midnight piled with pies, brownies and lemon bars, the lemon bars glowing faintly yellow, neighbors in matching purple hooded robes and quilted oven mitts standing behind it with their faces hidden in the hoods, a cardboard square propped against a pie tin, candles flickering on the table, a teenager holding out a quarter, candlelight and violet glow from the rock behind, medium wide shot

choices.label: Buy a brownie and see what happens

success.text: It is just a really good brownie. But for a second after you swallow, you can hear what everyone at the table is thinking: they are bored, and lonely, and nobody has asked them over in years. One of them lowers her hood. "Would you like the recipe?" she asks, and means it.
success.art: A teenager biting a brownie at a midnight bake sale while a woman in a purple robe lowers her hood and smiles shyly, recipe card in her oven mitt

failure.text: The brownie makes you feel enormously agreeable. You nod along to the chanting for an hour, then two. You wake up at dawn in a lawn chair beside the empty card table, with frosting on your face and a purple robe folded neatly in your lap.
failure.art: A teenager asleep in a lawn chair beside an empty card table at dawn, frosting on their cheek, a folded purple robe in their lap

choices.label: Swap their cash box for a coffee can of rock salt

success.text: At the stroke of one they open the cash box for the ritual, and rock salt sprays everywhere. The robes deflate like fallen souffles. Underneath are just your neighbors, blinking, embarrassed, in their pajamas. Somebody presses a whole pie into your hands to keep this quiet.
success.art: Rock salt spraying from an opened cash box at a midnight bake sale, purple robes collapsing to reveal embarrassed neighbors in pajamas, a teenager holding a pie

failure.text: They catch you. Nobody yells. They all just smile, warmly, and hand you a pie with your name piped across it in frosting, and a date underneath: OCT 31. "For later," someone says.
failure.art: Hooded neighbors smiling warmly as they hand a frightened teenager a pie with frosting lettering and a date piped on top

encounters.title: Send This to Thirteen Friends
encounters.place: Your mailbox, 12:01 a.m.
encounters.text: There is a letter in your mailbox in purple ink: THIS LETTER HAS BEEN AROUND THE WORLD NINE TIMES. COPY IT THIRTEEN TIMES BY HALLOWEEN OR THE FELLOWSHIP WILL COME FOR WHAT IS OWED. Below are signatures from every family on Crystal Street. The last line is your name, in your handwriting, and the ink is still wet.
encounters.art: A teenager standing at a curbside mailbox at midnight holding an unfolded letter covered in glowing purple ink, a long column of signatures running down the page with the last one still wet and shining, the mailbox flag up, dark houses along the street, purple glow on the teen's face and a single streetlight, medium shot

choices.label: Copy it thirteen times, but change one word in each

success.text: COME becomes CALL. OWED becomes OKAY. By the thirteenth copy the curse says THE FELLOWSHIP WILL CALL TO SEE IF YOU ARE OKAY. You mail them all. The next morning, three neighbors you have never talked to wave at you on your way to school.
success.art: A desk covered in thirteen handwritten letters with words crossed out and replaced, the last one reading a kind message, a teenager grinning with a purple pen

failure.text: Your pen keeps writing after you stop, adding names to the bottom of every copy: friends, teachers, your family. You drop it and it rolls across the desk, still scribbling, until it runs dry.
failure.art: A pen writing by itself across a stack of chain letters on a dark desk, adding a growing column of names, a teenager backing away

choices.label: Burn it in the backyard grill

success.text: The letter catches with a purple flame and a long, tired sigh, like someone setting down something heavy. The ash floats up and, for a second, spells THANKS in the air before the wind takes it. The grill smells faintly of lilacs all week.
success.art: A chain letter burning with purple flames in a kettle grill at night, its ash rising into the air in the shape of a word, a teenager watching with a lighter

failure.text: The letter will not burn. The flames slide right off it. In the morning there are thirteen copies of it in your mailbox, each one in your handwriting, and each one says you are running out of time.
failure.art: A suburban mailbox stuffed with thirteen identical purple-ink letters at dawn, an unburnt letter sitting in a cold grill nearby

choices.label: Follow the postmarks back to the first sender

success.text: The postmarks lead to a P.O. box at the old post office, closed since 1972. Inside are a thousand chain letters nobody ever mailed, and one apology from a lonely woman who just wanted people to write back. You write back. The letters stop coming.
success.art: A teenager opening a dusty post office box crammed with old letters, a single handwritten apology on top, flashlight light in an abandoned post office

failure.text: You follow the postmarks across town and back. Every trail ends at the same return address. It is your address. It has always been your address.
failure.art: A teenager staring at a stack of envelopes all postmarked with their own house address, standing on their own front walk at night

encounters.title: Neighborhood Watch Minutes
encounters.place: The Crystal Street homeowners' clubhouse, 11 p.m.
encounters.text: Folding chairs, a coffee urn, a podium, and every grown-up on the street wearing a hooded robe over a cardigan. The secretary reads the minutes. Item four on the agenda: SELECTING THIS YEAR'S OFFERING. Ballots are passed out. The nominees are whoever has the messiest lawn, and somebody has written your family's name in first.
encounters.art: A suburban clubhouse meeting room at eleven at night, folding chairs, a steaming coffee urn and a wooden podium, middle-aged adults in purple hooded robes pulled over their cardigans passing out paper ballots, an easel with a pad of paper beside the podium, a teenager peeking in from the doorway, flat fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Call a point of order and filibuster

success.text: You read the bylaws aloud, all of them, including the parking rules. At 1:01 a.m. you reach Article Nine: no vote may be held after one in the morning. The chair bangs the gavel, furious and helpless. Meeting adjourned. Everyone shuffles home grumbling.
success.art: A teenager reading from a thick binder at a podium, a clock past one a.m. on the wall, robed adults slumped in folding chairs, a gavel coming down

failure.text: They vote to table your point of order. Then they vote to table you. You wake up at dawn wrapped in Christmas lights and taped to the clubhouse snack table, next to a plate of untouched deviled eggs.
failure.art: A teenager wrapped in Christmas lights and taped to a clubhouse snack table at dawn beside a plate of deviled eggs, folding chairs stacked around

choices.label: Nominate the homeowners' association president instead

success.text: "I nominate the president, for his service." The room erupts. Old grudges about fence heights and holiday lights pour out. Robes come off. Someone throws the coffee urn. You slip out the back while the Fellowship tears itself apart over a hedge dispute from 1974.
success.art: A suburban clubhouse meeting erupting into chaos, robed adults arguing and waving ballots, a coffee urn flying, a teenager slipping out a back door

failure.text: The vote is unanimous, but not for the president. Everyone writes in your name. They applaud, politely, and turn to look at you all at once, smiling. You run, and they do not follow. They do not need to.
failure.art: A room of robed adults applauding politely and turning to smile at a teenager by the door, a chalkboard tally showing one name

choices.label: Stuff the ballot box with write-ins for Nobody

success.text: Nobody wins, forty-seven votes to three. The secretary reads the result twice, confused. The ritual cannot proceed without an offering, and none of them is willing to be Nobody. They fold up the chairs and go home, deflated.
success.art: A secretary in a robe reading a ballot in confusion, a tally board showing an empty-chair landslide, a teenager hiding a fistful of ballots behind their back

failure.text: The secretary unfolds the ballots and reads out the results: your name, forty-seven times, in your handwriting. You know you wrote Nobody. Everyone turns to look at you, and the coffee urn begins to bubble.
failure.art: A robed secretary reading ballots aloud at a podium, every ballot showing the same name, a teenager pale in a folding chair, a coffee urn bubbling

encounters.title: The Welcome Wagon
encounters.place: Your front door, 12:30 a.m.
encounters.text: The doorbell rings after midnight. Three neighbors in identical pastel cardigans stand on your porch holding a foil-covered casserole. "Welcome to the neighborhood!" they say together. You have lived here your whole life. "We're so glad you're finally joining us." The foil on the casserole lifts, just a little, by itself.
encounters.art: Three smiling neighbors in identical pastel cardigans standing shoulder to shoulder on a suburban porch at 12:30 at night holding out a foil-covered casserole dish whose foil is lifting up by itself at one corner, a teenager in pajamas peering out from a half-open front door, yellow porch light, medium shot from inside the doorway

choices.label: Thank them warmly and shut the door

success.text: "That's so thoughtful. Good night!" You close the door gently but firmly. Through the peephole you watch their smiles flicker, uncertain, and then they leave. The casserole on the step is just tuna noodle, and it is honestly delicious.
success.art: A peephole view of three neighbors in cardigans walking away from a porch at night, a casserole dish left on the doormat

failure.text: One of them wedges a sensible loafer in the door before it closes. "That's all right," she says, still smiling. "We'll come back tomorrow. And the night after. And the night after that."
failure.art: A sensible loafer wedged in a closing front door, a smiling woman in a pastel cardigan peering through the gap

choices.label: Lift the foil and look inside

success.text: In the noodles is a tiny, furious, shrieking face. You grab the garden hose and blast it. The face dissolves, and so do the smiles: the three neighbors blink, look at their cardigans, and wander home in confused silence. One of them says she does not even like casseroles.
success.art: A teenager blasting a casserole dish with a garden hose, a tiny shrieking face dissolving in the noodles, three neighbors blinking in confusion on the porch

failure.text: Inside the casserole is a perfect little diorama of your house, built out of noodles. In the upstairs window is a tiny noodle figure of you. As you watch, the noodle front door slowly opens.
failure.art: A casserole dish containing a detailed miniature house built of noodles, a tiny noodle figure in an upstairs window, its front door opening

encounters.title: The Candle Walk
encounters.place: The roundabout, two a.m.
encounters.text: A ring of hooded figures with purple candles is circling the roundabout, chanting in what sounds like Latin. Listening closer, you realize it is the Glimmer Falls High fight song, backward. They are drawing a chalk circle on the asphalt as they walk, and there is exactly one empty spot left in the ring.
encounters.art: A ring of hooded figures in purple robes holding purple candles circling a suburban roundabout at two in the morning, a wide chalk circle drawn on the asphalt under their feet, one empty gap left in the ring, a huge purple crystal rock glowing at the center, a teenager crouched behind a parked station wagon watching, candlelight and violet glow, wide shot

choices.label: Join the ring and chant something better

success.text: You step into the gap and chant a real blessing, the one for safe travel, the one grandmothers say. The candles turn from purple to warm gold. One by one the hoods fall back, and your neighbors look around, wondering why they are outside in their slippers.
success.art: A teenager chanting in a ring of hooded figures as the candles shift from purple to warm gold, hoods falling back to reveal confused neighbors in slippers

failure.text: You step in to change the chant, and your voice joins theirs perfectly, backward fight song and all, without you deciding to. You circle the roundabout with them until the candles burn out, and you know all the words now.
failure.art: A teenager walking in a ring of hooded chanting figures with a purple candle, eyes glazed, the chalk circle complete beneath their feet

choices.label: Smudge the chalk circle with your sneaker

success.text: One quick scuff while their backs are turned. The candles gutter all at once. The hooded figures stop, look at each other, mumble something about early mornings, and drift home in pairs. One of them leaves a perfectly good candle behind.
success.art: A sneaker scuffing a chalk circle on asphalt, purple candles guttering, hooded figures drifting away in pairs into the dark

failure.text: The chalk is wet paint. Your sneaker sticks fast. The ring turns inward and circles you, three times, slowly, candles held close to your face, and then leaves you there stuck to the street until the sun comes up.
failure.art: A teenager with one sneaker stuck to a painted circle on the street as hooded figures with candles circle tightly around them

encounters.title: A Golden Opportunity
encounters.place: A living room on Quarry Road, a late business opportunity night
encounters.text: A friend's aunt invited you to a Golden Tomorrow business opportunity night with free pizza. Everyone wears a little gold pin and the same enormous smile. On the easel is a pyramid chart of names, and the name at the very top has been scratched out so hard it tore the paper. "Who wants to change their life tonight?" the presenter asks.
encounters.art: A suburban living room at night full of smiling adults in little gold lapel pins sitting on folding chairs, a presenter in a shiny suit beside an easel holding a pyramid chart with its top square scratched through so hard the paper tore, pizza boxes on a side table, a teenager on the end chair holding a paper plate, warm lamp light, wide shot

choices.label: Ask where the money actually goes

success.text: You go to the easel and do the math. By Thursday the pyramid needs four billion recruits. The room goes quiet. Gold pins start dropping onto the carpet like hail, and the guests leave in a hurry, taking the free pizza with them.
success.art: A teenager scribbling enormous math on an easel pad while gold pins fall from guests' lapels onto the carpet, the presenter's smile frozen

failure.text: "Great question!" beams the presenter. "That is what the top of the pyramid is for." Everyone turns to the chart. The scratched-out name at the top has been rewritten, neatly, in gold marker. It is yours.
failure.art: A pyramid chart on an easel with a teenager's name freshly written at the top in gold marker, a room full of smiling adults turning toward them

choices.label: Grab a slice and slip out through the kitchen

success.text: You leave with two slices, a free sample and a mint. Out on the sidewalk you glance back: every window of the house is shaped like a smile, and every smile is watching the street for someone else. You find a quarter on the walk and keep it.
success.art: A teenager walking away down a night sidewalk eating pizza, a suburban house behind them with every window curved into a smile

failure.text: Every exit has a smiling greeter with a clipboard. The back door, the garage, the bathroom window. By the time you get out, you have signed up for three months of Golden Tomorrow Sunshine Drops, and the first bill is already in your pocket.
failure.art: A teenager cornered at a back door by a smiling greeter holding a clipboard and pen, gold pins glinting, a kitchen full of smiling faces behind

encounters.title: Play It Backward
encounters.place: The rec center multipurpose room, a Parents for Decent Listening meeting, 11 p.m.
encounters.text: The Parents for Decent Listening have a turntable on a card table and are spinning heavy metal records backward with their fingertips, taking notes in matching binders. "There," whispers the chairwoman. "Do you hear it?" Nobody did, until now. The record groans in reverse, and a clear voice rises out of the warble, saying your name and asking you, very politely, to come up front.
encounters.art: A fluorescent-lit rec center room at eleven at night with rows of folding chairs, parents in matching cardigans hunched over matching binders, a stern woman spinning a vinyl record backward with her fingertips on a turntable on a folding table, everyone turning to look at a teenager frozen in the doorway, flat greenish light, wide shot

choices.label: Take the turntable and play it the right way around

success.text: You lift the needle and drop it the right way. Out pours a guitar solo so loud and honest it rattles the folding chairs. The voice in the grooves is gone, and half the parents are tapping their feet before they can stop themselves. One of them asks, very quietly, what the band is called.
success.art: A teenager setting a needle on a spinning record at a card table, parents in cardigans unconsciously tapping their feet, binders sliding off laps

failure.text: You play it forward and the voice is still there, only now it comes out of every binder, every coffee cup and every parent's mouth at once, all of them asking you to come up front in perfect unison while the needle skips.
failure.art: A room of parents in cardigans all turned toward a teenager, mouths open in unison, a record skipping on a turntable on a card table

choices.label: Tape the message and play it back for them

success.text: You hold your recorder up to the speaker, rewind and play it for the room. Reversed again, the message is a roadie on the album mumbling, "Is this thing on? Hi, Mom." The room deflates. The chairwoman closes her binder, pink to the ears, and you leave with the last brownie from the snack table.
success.art: A teenager holding up a portable cassette recorder to a room of embarrassed parents, a chairwoman blushing as she closes her binder

failure.text: Your tape catches the voice, all right. Played back, it is the chairwoman reading tonight's agenda, and item one is you. The parents turn in their folding chairs with a single creak and pass you a sign-up sheet for a committee you never agreed to join.
failure.art: Rows of parents turning in their folding chairs all at once toward a teenager holding a cassette recorder, a clipboard sign-up sheet being passed hand to hand

choices.label: Do what the record says and walk up front

success.text: You walk to the front, take the chairwoman's microphone and say, "I heard it. It said turn it up." The record agrees with a roar of guitar. Half the room laughs, the other half look at each other, and the meeting dissolves into an argument about whose kids get to stay up late.
success.art: A teenager at the front of a rec center room speaking into a microphone, the parents split between laughing and arguing, a turntable roaring behind them

failure.text: The record pulls you forward like a magnet. You end up standing behind the card table holding a binder of your own, nodding along as the needle spins backward, and you do not snap out of it until the janitor flicks the lights at one.
failure.art: A glassy-eyed teenager standing behind a card table holding a binder and nodding beside a backward-spinning turntable, a janitor at the light switch by the door

encounters.title: The Pledge Card
encounters.place: The Glimmer Falls High gym, the Brightside Teens lock-in, midnight
encounters.text: The Brightside Teens lock-in has pizza, a pyramid of soda cans and a banner that reads ONE SCHOOL, ONE STANDARD. At midnight they pass out pledge cards: no rock music, no hair dye, no "confusing" friends. Every kid who signs gets a crisp white windbreaker and the same calm, pleasant smile, and their voices start to blend into one. A girl in a windbreaker holds out a pen to you, smiling, smiling.
encounters.art: A high school gym at midnight during a lock-in, a pyramid of soda cans and pizza boxes, rows of teens in identical crisp white windbreakers with identical calm smiles, a smiling girl in a white windbreaker holding out a pen and a small paper slip toward a wary teenager in a jean jacket, a long white cloth hung across the bleachers, bright gym light, wide shot

choices.label: Sign it, with a name that is not yours

success.text: You sign it IMA WEIRDO with a big loopy flourish. The card cannot find anyone to belong to and flutters out of your hand like a moth. Every card in the gym follows it, a white blizzard pouring out the double doors, and the smiles go slack, then puzzled, then human again.
success.art: A blizzard of white pledge cards fluttering out of open gym doors into the night, teens in white windbreakers blinking and looking around in confusion

failure.text: The pen writes your real name, neatly, no matter what your hand tries to do. A white windbreaker settles onto your shoulders, and for an hour you agree pleasantly with everything anyone says, until the fire alarm shrieks and the noise knocks the smile clean off your face.
failure.art: A teenager in a white windbreaker wearing a blank pleasant smile among identical teens, a red fire alarm bell ringing on the gym wall above them

choices.label: Stand on the bleachers and say who your friends are

success.text: You climb the bleachers and say it plainly: your friends are weird, and loud, and some of them are queer, and every one of them is better than a standard. It is quiet for one long, awful second. Then a sophomore in the back unzips his windbreaker and drops it on the floor. Then another kid does. Then thirty.
success.art: A teenager standing tall on gym bleachers speaking out, below them a crowd of teens unzipping and dropping white windbreakers onto the gym floor

failure.text: Your voice is swallowed by a hundred pleasant voices saying "That's nice" in perfect unison. They smile up at you, patient, kind and completely unbothered, and somehow that is worse than shouting. You leave the gym with your face burning and a pledge card stuck to your shoe.
failure.art: A teenager on gym bleachers facing a sea of identical calm smiling faces in white windbreakers, a pledge card stuck to the sole of their sneaker

choices.label: Hit the breaker and crank the loudest record in the AV closet

success.text: In the dark, the AV closet stereo blasts the most forbidden synth-pop song of 1986. Feet start tapping before the pledge-takers can stop them. When the lights come back up, half the gym is dancing in white windbreakers, laughing in their own voices, and the banner has slipped down to read only ONE SCHOOL.
success.art: A high school gym full of teens in white windbreakers dancing wildly under colored lights, a sagging banner reading ONE SCHOOL, a teenager grinning by a stereo cart

failure.text: The AV closet holds exactly one record, and it is the soundtrack to a filmstrip about good posture. It plays on a loop in the dark while a hundred calm voices count along, and you hide behind the gym mats until the janitor unlocks the doors at dawn.
failure.art: A teenager hiding behind a stack of blue gym mats in a dark gym, a filmstrip projector casting a diagram of perfect posture onto the wall

encounters.title: The Benevolent Owls
encounters.place: The Benevolent Order of Owls lodge hall on Main Street, 1 a.m.
encounters.text: Light leaks under the door of the Owls' lodge. Inside, two dozen grown-ups in feathered robes and little owl-beak fezzes sit in a circle, hooting a slow, rhythmic chant, while the Grand Hoot raises a gavel carved like a mouse. In the middle of the circle is an empty chair with a brand-new fez on the cushion, exactly your size. Every head turns toward the door at the same speed, the way owls do.
encounters.art: A wood-paneled lodge hall at one in the morning lit by candles, two dozen adults in brown feathered robes and little beaked fezzes sitting in a circle, all turning their heads toward the door at the same moment, a leader holding a gavel carved in the shape of a mouse, an empty chair in the center with a brand-new small fez on its cushion, a teenager in the doorway, warm candlelight, wide shot

choices.label: Hoot back, in the proper rhythm

success.text: You hoot back, three long and two short, the way the barn owls call over Pinecrest Cemetery. The circle falls silent. The Grand Hoot lowers her gavel, deeply moved, and names you an Honorary Fledgling with no further obligations, and the treasurer quietly slips you your dues back in quarters.
success.art: A teenager cupping their hands to hoot in a candlelit lodge hall, a robed woman in a beaked fez lowering a mouse-shaped gavel, feathered members gazing in awe

failure.text: Your hoot comes out as a honk. The Owls tilt their heads in perfect unison, ninety degrees, then a hundred and eighty, until the whole lodge is staring at you upside down, while the empty chair scrapes slowly across the floor toward you on its own.
failure.art: A circle of robed lodge members in beaked fezzes with their heads tilted completely sideways, an empty chair sliding across the floorboards toward a startled teenager

choices.label: Belly-crawl to the podium and swipe the gavel

success.text: You crawl under the refreshment table, wait for the chant to peak and snatch the mouse gavel off the podium. The meeting cannot be called to order. The Owls flap their sleeves in dismay, mutter about the bylaws and go home, and you leave the gavel on the doorstep with a note: SEE YOU AT THE PANCAKE BREAKFAST.
success.art: A teenager crawling out from under a refreshment table clutching a mouse-shaped gavel, robed lodge members flapping their feathered sleeves in dismay

failure.text: The gavel is glued to the podium. You tug, the whole lodge turns to look at you, and the treasurer reads aloud that the penalty for touching the gavel is lifetime membership. Feathers drift down from the rafters like snow until you finally bolt.
failure.art: A teenager tugging at a gavel stuck to a podium as feathers rain down from the rafters, a treasurer in a beaked fez reading solemnly from a ledger

choices.label: Sit down and put on the fez

success.text: The fez fits. The chant stops. Sitting in the circle, you can hear what every Owl is really saying under the hooting: I'm lonely, I'm retired, my kids never call. You hoot something comforting back. By the end of the night three of them have agreed to just go bowling together instead.
success.art: A teenager in a small beaked fez seated in a circle of robed elderly lodge members who are smiling and patting each other's shoulders in candlelight

failure.text: The fez fits a little too well. For the next hour you hoot along without meaning to, turning your head in slow owl circles, and you walk home at two hooting at every streetlight, still wearing the fez, which refuses to come off until sunrise.
failure.art: A teenager in a beaked fez walking down an empty street at night hooting up at a streetlight, head tilted at an owlish angle

encounters.title: Satan in the Suburbs?
encounters.place: The roundabout under a TV news crew's floodlights, midnight
encounters.text: A Channel 8 news van is parked at the roundabout for a live special called SATAN IN THE SUBURBS?, and the anchorman's helmet of hair does not move in the wind. He spots you and swings the microphone over, smiling with too many teeth. "Our viewers want to know: your Friday-night dungeon game, is it a coven?" The camera's red light glows, and every porch on the street is watching.
encounters.art: A local TV news van with a tall antenna mast parked beside a suburban roundabout at midnight under harsh white floodlights, a smiling anchorman with stiff sculpted hair thrusting a microphone toward a teenager, a camera operator with a shoulder camera and its red light glowing, neighbors watching from every porch, a purple crystal rock glowing behind, wide shot

choices.label: Explain the game so well he wants to play

success.text: You explain hit points, saving throws and the dragon your group has been fighting since June. The anchorman's smile softens into a real one. By the end of the segment he is rolling a twenty-sided die on live television, cheering when it comes up eighteen, and the special cuts to commercial.
success.art: A grinning anchorman crouched on the asphalt rolling a twenty-sided die under news floodlights, a teenager cheering beside him, a cameraman laughing

failure.text: Every word you say gets cut live into something worse. The broadcast shows you in slow motion over spooky organ music, the caption reading TEEN ADMITS TO DRAGONS, and by morning three neighbors have taped the segment to play at the next watch meeting.
failure.art: A television in a dark den showing a slow-motion close-up of a startled teenager under a dramatic caption, a neighbor in a bathrobe pressing record on a VCR

choices.label: Follow the cable to the van and pull it

success.text: While the anchorman is busy denouncing the Lindqvists' jack-o'-lantern, you trace the fat black cable to the van and pull. The floodlights die. The anchorman's hair finally moves in the breeze, and away from the red light he blinks, confused, and asks where they are. The cameraman tosses you a Bolt Cola for your trouble.
success.art: A teenager holding an unplugged thick black cable beside a darkened news van, a bewildered anchorman with windblown hair blinking in the streetlight

failure.text: The cable bites you with a crackle of static that stands your hair straight up. The camera swings to you live and the anchorman whispers, "Look, folks: possessed." Your startled face runs on the eleven o'clock news, the morning news and the noon news.
failure.art: A teenager with hair standing straight up from static holding a news cable, a camera with a glowing red light swinging toward them, an anchorman pointing dramatically

choices.label: Wave your friends out of the dark to stand beside you

success.text: You wave, and your friends come out of the dark one by one, in thrifted velvet, mullets and mathlete sweaters, and stand beside you under the floodlights. The anchorman searches the group for a coven and finds only kids who love each other. "Well," he says to the camera. "Well." He cuts to the weather.
success.art: A mismatched group of teens in velvet, denim and sweaters standing shoulder to shoulder under news floodlights, a deflated anchorman lowering his microphone

failure.text: You wave, and the camera light swings across the dark lawns and finds only empty porches. For one terrible live minute you stand alone under the floodlights while the anchorman narrates, softly, "The loneliness of the occult teen."
failure.art: A lone teenager standing in a harsh pool of floodlight at a roundabout, a news camera trained on them, dark empty porches all around

name: Night Terrors
blurb: Close your eyes on Crystal Street this week and the rules go soft. You sleepwalk across the rooftops, your house grows an extra room, and the drained quarry lake comes back to fill the street, as deep as a held breath.

encounters.title: Sleepwalking the Rooftops
encounters.place: The roofs of Crystal Street, in your sleep
encounters.text: You wake, sort of, barefoot on your own roof in your pajamas, walking the ridge line with your arms out like a tightrope walker. The gutters glitter with frost. The roofs keep going, one after another, past the Lindqvists' chimney and on and on, past where the street should end.
encounters.art: A barefoot teenager in pajamas sleepwalking along the ridge line of a suburban rooftop at night with arms stretched out for balance, frost glittering in the gutters, a brick chimney ahead, and an endless row of rooftops stretching on past where the street should end toward a distant water tower under the stars, silver starlight, wide shot

choices.label: Keep walking and trust your sleeping feet

success.text: You walk roof to roof as easily as crossing your bedroom, up the ladder of the KGLM water tower, and onto the catwalk at the very top. The stars are close enough to touch. You reach out, and one of them reaches back, and pulls you up into the sky.
success.art: A sleepwalking teenager in pajamas reaching up from the top of a water tower toward stars that are close enough to touch, one star reaching back like a hand

failure.text: A loose shingle slides under your heel and you slide with it, all the way to the gutter, and hang there by your fingertips. A neighbor's dog sees you and barks until the whole house wakes up and your folks fetch the ladder.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas hanging from a rooftop gutter by their fingertips at night, a dog barking below, house lights coming on

choices.label: Count backward from ten and wake up gently

success.text: Ten, nine, eight. The endless roofs fold back into one. Three, two, one. You open your eyes sitting safely on your own roof, knees hugged to your chest, watching a cold, pink sunrise come up over the foothills. You climb back in the window and sleep until noon.
success.art: A teenager sitting safely on their own roof hugging their knees at sunrise, pink light over the foothills, an open bedroom window beside them

failure.text: You wake up halfway, which is the worst way. Suddenly the roof is very real and very high and very cold. You hug the chimney until the sky goes gray, too scared to move and too awake to go back to dreaming.
failure.art: A frightened teenager in pajamas clinging to a brick chimney on a steep roof in the gray before dawn

choices.label: Follow the black cat walking beside you

success.text: The cat walks with you, tail high, and leads you down a rose trellis, through your own open window and into bed. It curls up on your feet. In the morning there is no cat, but there is a single black whisker on your pillow.
success.art: A sleepwalking teenager following a black cat down a rose trellis toward an open bedroom window under a full moon

failure.text: The cat leads you through an open attic window, but it is the wrong house. You wake up at dawn curled among someone else's Christmas decorations, and you have to explain yourself to a very surprised Mr. Ferguson.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas waking in a stranger's dusty attic among boxes of Christmas decorations, a startled man in a bathrobe peering up through the hatch

encounters.title: The Extra Room
encounters.place: Your house, in a dream
encounters.text: There is a door in the upstairs hallway that has never been there, between the bathroom and the linen closet. It is papered in flowered wallpaper from 1959. Behind it you hear a family dinner: forks on plates, laughter, a radio. Someone calls your name, warmly, to come eat before it gets cold.
encounters.art: A dim upstairs hallway in a 1980s suburban house at night, an extra narrow door papered in faded 1959 floral wallpaper standing between the bathroom door and the linen closet, warm yellow light and moving shadows leaking from the gap under it, a teenager in pajamas reaching for its glass knob, cool blue hallway light, medium shot

choices.label: Open the door and walk in

success.text: It is your bedroom from when you were six. Your old nightlight, the stuffed rabbit you lost at the county fair, the glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling. Nobody is eating dinner. It is just a safe place, saved for you. You sit on the little bed until you wake up.
success.art: A teenager sitting on a small child's bed in a softly lit bedroom with glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling, holding a worn stuffed rabbit, a nightlight glowing

failure.text: Inside is another hallway, and another door, and another. You walk through doors all night, each one papered a little older. The last door opens onto somewhere that is not your house at all, and the dinner bell rings behind you.
failure.art: An endless corridor of doors papered in progressively older wallpaper, a teenager opening the last one onto a strange dark place

choices.label: Wallpaper over the door before it opens

success.text: You find a roll of leftover wallpaper and a bucket of paste in the dream garage. Three strips, smoothed flat. The door is just a bump under the paper, then a faint outline, then nothing. The dinner sounds fade like a radio drifting off station.
success.art: A teenager smoothing a strip of wallpaper over a door in an upstairs hallway, a paste bucket and brush at their feet, the door's outline fading

failure.text: The wallpaper peels itself back off the wall in long curls. Then new doors bloom in every wall of the house, dozens of them, all papered in roses. You wake up with paste on your hands and a door-shaped bump in your bedroom wall.
failure.art: A hallway with dozens of rose-papered doors blooming from every wall, wallpaper curling off in strips, a teenager with paste-covered hands

choices.label: Knock and ask whose dinner it is

success.text: The forks go quiet. A kind, tired voice answers, "Oh. Sorry, dear, wrong house. It happens." There is a smell of pot roast and someone laughing, and the door fades into the wall like breath off a mirror.
success.art: A teenager knocking politely on a floral-papered door in a dim hallway, the door fading into the wall like breath fog, warm light dimming

failure.text: The door swings open on a long dinner table set for twelve. Every chair is empty except the one at the head, where a place card reads your name in careful cursive, and the food is still steaming.
failure.art: A long formal dinner table in a 1959 dining room set for twelve with empty chairs, a single place card with a teenager's name at the head, steaming plates

encounters.title: The Pop Quiz
encounters.place: Glimmer Falls High, in a dream
encounters.text: You are sitting in algebra in your pajamas. There is a test on your desk that you did not study for, written in an alphabet made of little teeth. The clock on the wall spins backward. The teacher at the front has no face, only a red grading pen, tapping, tapping.
encounters.art: A high school algebra classroom with a teenager in pajamas sitting at a desk staring down at a test sheet covered in rows of tiny tooth shapes, a wall clock with its hands spinning backward, and at the front a teacher with a smooth blank face where features should be tapping a red pen on the desk, other students slumped asleep, pale yellow light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Fill in every bubble with total confidence

success.text: You fill in the bubbles in a pattern that pleases you, a smiley face. The faceless teacher picks up your test, holds it up to the light, and draws a giant red A+. You wake up laughing, and for some reason you feel ready for anything.
success.art: A faceless teacher holding up a test paper with bubbles filled in to make a smiley face and a huge red A plus, a teenager in pajamas grinning

failure.text: The bubbles fill with eyes. They blink, all at once, and watch you. Every one of them follows your pencil as you try to erase. When you wake, you can still feel them, under your eyelids, blinking.
failure.art: A test paper where every answer bubble has become a blinking eye, a teenager in pajamas holding a pencil frozen above it

choices.label: Turn the test upside down, the way dreams work

success.text: Upside down, the teeth are letters. It is a crossword, and every answer is the name of one of your friends. As you write each name in, that friend walks into the classroom in their pajamas, and together you walk right out the door.
success.art: A teenager filling in a crossword test with friends' names while those friends walk into a dreamlike classroom in pajamas, the faceless teacher looking on

failure.text: Upside down, you can read it, and you wish you could not. Every question is about a secret you have never told anyone. The faceless teacher leans in close and waits for your answer.
failure.art: A faceless teacher leaning over a frightened teenager's desk, a test paper turned upside down, red pen poised

encounters.title: Saturday Morning Forever
encounters.place: Your living room carpet, in a dream
encounters.text: You are inside a Saturday morning cartoon. The colors are too bright, there is a laugh track, and you have a black outline.
