The Sugar Sergeant, the grinning bird from the cereal box, insists you stay for just one more episode. And one more. The episodes never end, and the bird's grin is getting wider.
encounters.art: A teenager with a thick black cartoon outline standing inside a brightly colored Saturday morning cartoon world of flat candy colors, a grinning cereal-box bird mascot in a military cap looming over them, cartoon anvils dangling from ropes and a red canyon in the background, a giant bowl of cereal at their feet, flat saturated colors, wide shot

choices.label: Run off a cliff and just don't look down

success.text: You sprint off the edge of the canyon and keep running on thin air, legs spinning, not looking down. You run right out of the cartoon, through the TV screen and into your own bed with a squeaky sound effect. You wake up giggling.
success.art: A cartoon-outlined teenager sprinting on thin air over a deep canyon with legs blurred in a wheel, a glowing TV screen ahead of them

failure.text: You look down. There is a long, descending whistle. You hit the canyon floor in a puff of dust shaped exactly like you, and wake up on your bedroom floor with little birds circling your head.
failure.art: A teenager-shaped puff of dust at the bottom of a cartoon canyon, a dazed figure with little birds circling their head

choices.label: Wait for the commercial break and slip out

success.text: Every cartoon has a station break. You wait for the jingle, and in the half-second of black between shows, you step sideways through the edge of the screen. The Sugar Sergeant shouts "Stay tuned!" to an empty set.
success.art: A teenager stepping sideways out through the dark edge of a TV screen during a station break, a grinning cartoon bird mascot left alone on a bright set

failure.text: There are no commercials. There are no breaks. The Sugar Sergeant's grin stretches past the edges of its face. "You're our new favorite character!" it says, and the laugh track will not stop laughing.
failure.art: A cartoon cereal mascot bird with a grin stretching beyond its face, leaning over a trapped teenager, a laugh-track applause sign flashing

encounters.title: The Escalator Down
encounters.place: Starlight Mall, in a dream
encounters.text: The mall is closed, and it goes on forever. Every escalator only goes down. The same soft song plays from every speaker. Every storefront is the same orange juice stand, staffed by nobody, and the fountain at the bottom of each level is full of pennies with your face on them.
encounters.art: An endless shopping mall in hazy pastel light with escalators descending level after level into the distance, identical orange juice stands on every level with empty counters, a fountain at the bottom of each level filled with copper pennies, a lone teenager riding an escalator down with one hand on the rail, soft pink haze, high wide shot

choices.label: Run up the down escalator

success.text: You take the steps three at a time against the current, lungs burning. Level by level you climb back up, until you burst through the food court skylight and find yourself crawling out of the ceiling of your own bedroom, onto your bed.
success.art: A teenager racing up a descending escalator in an endless pastel mall, a skylight above opening onto a bedroom ceiling

failure.text: The faster you run, the faster the escalator goes. You run all night and stay in exactly the same place, and you wake up with your legs aching as if you have run a marathon in your sleep.
failure.art: A teenager running in place on a speeding escalator in an endless mall, the steps blurring, the same storefronts sliding past again and again

choices.label: Toss a quarter in the fountain and wish to wake up

success.text: Your quarter hits the water and the whole fountain ripples outward like a bell. The pennies with your face all turn heads-up and smile. You wake with your wish granted and a handful of real coins under your pillow.
success.art: A quarter splashing into a mall fountain filled with pennies, ripples spreading like rings of light, a teenager waking with coins on their pillow

failure.text: The fountain takes your quarter, then your other quarters, then your sneakers, then pulls gently at your sleeve. You back away barefoot and wake up with your pockets empty and your feet cold.
failure.art: A mall fountain pulling at a teenager's sleeve with watery fingers, sneakers sinking among the pennies, the teen backing away barefoot

encounters.title: The Lake Comes Back
encounters.place: Crystal Street, underwater, in a dream
encounters.text: In your dream, the old Crystal Springs lake is back. Crystal Street is the bottom. Fish drift through the beams of the streetlights, your neighbor's station wagon floats past upside down, and your bike rolls slowly along the lake floor. You can breathe, somehow. Far above, moonlight wobbles on the surface.
encounters.art: A suburban cul-de-sac completely underwater at night, fish swimming through the beams of the streetlights, a station wagon floating upside down past the houses, a bicycle rolling slowly along the lake floor, a teenager in pajamas suspended in the water and gazing up at moonlight rippling on the surface far above, blue-green water light, wide shot

choices.label: Swim hard for the moonlight on the surface

success.text: You kick hard, past the rooftops, past the TV antennas, past the top of the water tower. You break the surface with a huge gasp and wake up sitting bolt upright in bed, gulping air, completely dry and completely alive.
success.art: A teenager bursting up through the surface of a moonlit lake, water spraying, the drowned rooftops of a suburban street visible far below

failure.text: The surface keeps moving up as you swim. The moonlight gets farther, not closer. You swim until your arms give out and you wake, exhausted, with your sheets soaked through and a strand of lake weed on your pillow.
failure.art: A teenager swimming upward toward moonlight that keeps receding, a drowned street far below, lake weed drifting

choices.label: Let yourself sink and look around

success.text: On the lake floor, under the street, you see the beach that was here before: a lifeguard tower, a jukebox, kids dancing in the sand in 1955. It is not frightening. It is sad, like a song from someone else's summer. You wake knowing the town a little better.
success.art: A teenager floating near the bottom of a dream lake looking at ghostly figures of 1950s kids dancing around a jukebox on a sandy beach beside a lifeguard tower

failure.text: The bottom is soft, softer than sand, and you sink into it up to your knees, then your waist. It is warm and it does not want to let go. You wake with a gasp and find fine gray silt between your sheets.
failure.art: A teenager sinking waist-deep into soft gray silt at the bottom of a dark dream lake, bubbles rising, a drowned streetlight overhead

encounters.title: Running in Taffy
encounters.place: Crystal Street, in a dream
encounters.text: Something is behind you on Crystal Street, breathing like a vacuum cleaner, and you run, but the sidewalk has turned to warm saltwater taffy. Every step stretches out pink and sticky behind you, and you are moving in slow motion while the thing back there moves at normal speed. The streetlights stretch like taffy too, bending low over you to watch.
encounters.art: A suburban street at night melting into glossy pink saltwater taffy, a teenager running in slow motion with long sticky pink strands stretching from their sneakers, the streetlights drooping overhead and bending down toward them, a large dark shape looming at the end of the street behind, pink glow and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Stop running and turn around

success.text: You stop and turn around. The thing behind you skids to a stop too, and it is only your own shadow, enormous and embarrassed, which has been trying to keep up all along. It shrinks back to its normal size and settles at your feet, and you walk home at a perfectly normal speed.
success.art: A teenager standing firm on a pink taffy street facing their own enormous shadow as it shrinks back down to normal size at their feet

failure.text: You turn around and the street behind you is bare. It is in front of you now, and you are running straight at it in slow motion, unable to stop, and you wake up with your legs kicking under the blankets and your sheets twisted into a rope.
failure.art: A teenager thrashing awake in bed with sheets twisted into a rope around their legs, pink light fading from the bedroom walls

choices.label: Haul up a strand of sidewalk and make a rope

success.text: You grab a long pink strand of sidewalk and fold it, pull it and fold it, the way they do on the boardwalk, until it is a glossy rope. You lasso a streetlight and swing clear over the Lindqvists' roof, whooping, and wake up with the taste of strawberry on your tongue.
success.art: A teenager swinging high over suburban rooftops on a glossy pink taffy rope lassoed around a drooping streetlight, the moon behind them

failure.text: The more you pull, the more you stick. In seconds you are wrapped in pink taffy like a fly in a web, and the thing behind you leans in close and takes one long, slow sniff by your ear before you jolt awake.
failure.art: A teenager wrapped in strands of pink taffy on a dream street at night, a vast shadow leaning down close beside their head

choices.label: Kick off your sneakers and glide in your socks

success.text: You leave your sneakers stuck in the taffy and run in your socks, which the sidewalk cannot quite grip. You glide like it is all-skate night at the rink, faster and faster, and leave the thing far behind, chewing thoughtfully on your shoes. You wake with both sneakers beside the bed, laces neatly tied together.
success.art: A teenager in socks gliding across a pink taffy street like a roller skater, a pair of sneakers stuck in the taffy behind them beside a hulking shadow

failure.text: Your socks stick too, and then your feet, and you sink into the warm pink sidewalk up to your ankles. You wake at dawn, and all morning every step you take makes a small, faint, sticky sound.
failure.art: A teenager sunk ankle-deep in a glossy pink taffy sidewalk under a drooping streetlight, socks stretched in long sticky strands

encounters.title: Opening Night
encounters.place: The Glitter Box stage, in a dream
encounters.text: The curtain is rising and you are center stage in a play you never rehearsed, dressed in a costume made of tinfoil and pillowcases. The seats are full of everyone you have ever known, sitting in the dark and eating popcorn very loudly. Your scene partner is a store mannequin. It turns its smooth blank head toward you and waits for your line, while a prompter in the wings hisses something in a language made of moths.
encounters.art: A theater stage under a hot white spotlight, a teenager in a costume made of tinfoil and pillowcases standing center stage facing a smooth-headed store mannequin with its blank head turned toward them, a packed dark audience eating popcorn, small gray moths fluttering out of the wings where a prompter crouches, hot white light and black house, wide shot

choices.label: Make it up as you go

success.text: You open your mouth and say the first thing that comes, and it is perfect. The mannequin answers, warm and wooden, and suddenly the two of you are playing the best scene of your life. The whole house is on its feet. You wake to the sound of applause that keeps going for a few seconds after your eyes open.
success.art: A teenager and a store mannequin bowing together hand in hand on a theater stage, the audience on its feet applauding, roses landing at their feet

failure.text: Your line comes out as a long string of soap bubbles. The audience laughs, then stops laughing, then leans forward in their seats all at once, and the mannequin begins saying your lines for you, in your voice, better than you ever could.
failure.art: Soap bubbles floating from a teenager's mouth on a theater stage, a mannequin stepping into the spotlight beside them, a dark audience leaning forward in unison

choices.label: Search your costume for a script

success.text: There is a script in your tinfoil pocket. It is your diary, the whole play is just your week, and the ending is happy. You read it aloud, the scene works, and when the curtain falls you know something warm and certain about how Friday turns out.
success.art: A teenager in a tinfoil costume reading aloud from a battered diary under a warm spotlight, a heavy red curtain beginning to fall

failure.text: The script is blank except for one line, repeated down every page: YOU FORGOT. You flip faster and faster while the lights get hotter and hotter, and you wake with a stiff neck and the sound of pages still rustling in your ears.
failure.art: A sweating teenager frantically flipping through a script under blazing stage lights, every page showing the same single repeated line

choices.label: Exit stage left, and keep exiting

success.text: You walk calmly off stage left, past the ropes and sandbags, and keep walking: through the scene shop, through a dressing room, through a door that opens onto your own bedroom. You climb into bed. Somewhere far away the audience is still waiting, and that is their problem.
success.art: A teenager in a tinfoil costume stepping through a backstage door that opens directly onto their own cozy moonlit bedroom

failure.text: Stage left is the stage again. And again. Every exit drops you back into the spotlight, a little more lost each time, and each time the applause is a little thinner. You wake tired, still hearing someone in the dark ask, "Is this part of it?"
failure.art: A teenager stepping out of the wings straight back onto the same spotlit stage, rows of dim faces watching, ropes and sandbags looping endlessly behind

encounters.title: Wake Up, Wake Up
encounters.place: Your bedroom, again and again
encounters.text: You wake up in your bed, relieved, and your clock radio reads 88:88. You wake up again and the posters on your wall are upside down. You wake up a third time and your window looks out on your own bedroom. Every time you wake, the house is a little more wrong, and somewhere inside it an alarm clock is ringing that you can never find.
encounters.art: A teenager sitting up in bed in a bedroom where the band pennants and wall calendar hang upside down, a clock radio on the nightstand glowing with eights in every digit, and through the window the same bedroom repeated beyond the glass with another figure sitting up in another bed, gray dawn light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Follow the ringing through the house

success.text: You follow the ringing down the stairs, into the den, under a couch cushion, into a shoebox inside a shoebox. You slap the snooze button and the real morning arrives all at once, bright and ordinary, with the smell of somebody burning toast downstairs.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas slapping the button of a ringing alarm clock nestled inside a shoebox inside another shoebox on a den floor, morning sunlight pouring in

failure.text: The ringing leads you downstairs, and downstairs, and downstairs. Your house has never had this many stairs. The ringing is always one floor below, and when you finally wake for real, the alarm clock is clutched in your hand and you cannot remember picking it up.
failure.art: An endless spiral of carpeted suburban stairs descending into shadow, a teenager in pajamas hurrying down, the faint glow of an alarm clock far below

choices.label: Do a reality check: read something twice

success.text: You read the poster on your wall, look away and read it again. The words change, so you know you are dreaming, and knowing is like finding the light switch. You tell the house, firmly, to put itself back, and it does, room by room, until you wake for real with a grin on your face.
success.art: A teenager standing in a bedroom pointing commandingly as upside-down band pennants flip right side up and furniture slides neatly back into place

failure.text: You read the poster twice. Both times it says STILL ASLEEP. You read it a third time and it says WHO ASKED. You wake up, and up, and up, all night long, and by morning you are too tired to trust the toaster.
failure.art: A bleary teenager at a breakfast table staring suspiciously at a chrome toaster, dark circles under their eyes, a hand-painted banner on the kitchen wall behind reading STILL ASLEEP

choices.label: Lie down in the wrong bed and fall asleep on purpose

success.text: You lie down in the dream bed, close your dream eyes and fall asleep on purpose. Down, down, through soft layers of sleep like stacked blankets, until you surface on the far side into a plain, quiet, perfectly real morning, rested for the first time all week.
success.art: A teenager sinking peacefully through layer upon layer of soft quilts like clouds, a pale real morning glowing at the bottom

failure.text: You fall asleep inside the dream, and dream that you are falling asleep inside the dream, and somewhere in the stack you lose track of which one is you. You surface into a different dream entirely and count your fingers twice to make sure.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas counting their fingers while standing in a strange dreamlike landscape, layers of beds stacked like a tower behind them

encounters.title: Inside the Snow Globe
encounters.place: Crystal Street under glass, in a dream
encounters.text: In your dream, the sky over Crystal Street is curved glass, and past it is a giant mantelpiece in a giant living room. Somebody enormous picks up the whole street and shakes it. Purple glitter from the Heartstone swirls down like snow, the houses tilt, and you tumble across your lawn as the world turns upside down and back again.
encounters.art: A whole suburban cul-de-sac sealed inside a giant glass snow globe on a mantelpiece in an enormous living room, purple glitter swirling down over the split-level houses and a glowing purple crystal rock, the houses tilting, a tiny teenager tumbling across a lawn, a huge hand reaching for the globe, warm lamp light outside the glass, wide shot

choices.label: Climb the Heartstone and knock on the sky

success.text: You climb to the top of the Heartstone and knock three times on the sky. The giant face beyond the glass leans close: a kid, younger than you, lonely on a rainy afternoon. You wave. The kid waves back and sets the globe down gently on the windowsill where the light is good, and the glitter settles like a blessing.
success.art: A tiny teenager standing on top of a purple geode inside a snow globe, waving up at a huge gentle child's face peering through the curved glass, rain on a window behind

failure.text: The giant hears you knock and, delighted, shakes the globe harder, so hard you lose your sneakers, your hat and your sense of direction. You wake on your bedroom floor, dizzy, with purple glitter in your hair that will take a week to wash out.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager sprawled on a bedroom floor at dawn with purple glitter all through their hair and bare socked feet

choices.label: Grab a lamppost and ride out the shaking

success.text: You wrap both arms around a lamppost and hold on while the whole world flips. Up is down, down is up, station wagons drift past like leaves. When the shaking stops, you are the one thing on Crystal Street still exactly where it started, and you feel rooted, heavy and unshakable.
success.art: A teenager clinging to a lamppost while station wagons and mailboxes float sideways through swirling purple glitter inside a tilted snow globe

failure.text: The lamppost bends like a licorice whip. You lose your grip on the third shake and roll across the curved glass ground with the mailboxes and lawn flamingos, and wake up tangled in your sheets with the room still spinning.
failure.art: A teenager tumbling head over heels along the curved glass floor of a snow globe among mailboxes and pink lawn flamingos, a lamppost bent like licorice

choices.label: Search the glass for the hairline crack

success.text: Every snow globe has a hairline crack somewhere; you know it like you know the end of a scary story. You find it near the base, behind the Feeneys' garage, glinting. You squeeze through into cool, ordinary air and wake on top of your covers, one fleck of purple glitter on your fingertip, warm as a heartbeat.
success.art: A tiny teenager squeezing through a glinting hairline crack at the base of a giant snow globe into cool night air, purple glitter trailing behind

failure.text: You find the crack and press your eye to it. On the other side, a giant eye presses back. You leap away, and the globe is set down hard on the mantel with a thud that rings through every house on the street, and you wake to your own heart pounding.
failure.art: A huge curious eye pressed against the outside of a snow globe, peering in at a tiny startled teenager leaping back from the glass

name: Something in the Water
blurb: Something has been trickling out of the plant on Quarry Road since before anyone on Crystal Street was born, and this week it finally came to visit. The creek glows, the rain tastes like lime soda, and every kid in town has heard the one about the radioactive candy bar.

encounters.title: Glow Creek
encounters.place: The concrete drainage creek behind Crystal Street, midnight
encounters.text: The concrete creek behind the backyards is glowing the soft green of a nightlight, and it smells like a chemistry set left out in the sun. A big outflow pipe from the plant up on Quarry Road gurgles into it. On the bank, a chorus of two-headed frogs is singing in perfect four-part harmony. The green slick is creeping up the slope toward the backyard fences, one slow inch at a time.
encounters.art: A concrete drainage creek glowing soft nightlight green at midnight behind suburban backyard fences, a large outflow pipe trickling luminous water, a row of two-headed frogs singing on the concrete bank, a green slick creeping up the slope toward the fences, a teenager leaning over a back fence with a flashlight, green glow and dark sky, wide shot

choices.label: Scoop a sample in a pickle jar and work out what it is

success.text: You fill the jar without getting a drop on you. Under your desk lamp it fizzes like an acid, so you try a pinch of baking soda, and the goo in the jar goes clear and calm. By dawn you have dusted the whole creek from a coffee can, and the frogs are singing a little quieter, a little happier.
success.art: A pickle jar of glowing green creek water turning clear on a desk under a lamp, an open box of baking soda and a coffee can beside it

failure.text: The jar fizzes, gets warm, and the lid pops off like a champagne cork. A geyser of green foam shoots up and coats you from the eyebrows down, and the frog chorus switches to a slow, mournful ballad in your honor. You glow faintly for the rest of the night.
failure.art: A teenager coated head to toe in glowing green foam beside an erupting pickle jar on a creek bank, two-headed frogs singing mournfully

choices.label: Shove a curbside mattress into the outflow pipe

success.text: You drag a striped mattress off somebody's curb, down the bank, and jam it into the pipe with your whole body. The gurgle chokes, sputters and stops. Up the hill at the plant, an alarm starts whooping and a row of windows lights up that has been dark for years. Somebody up there is finally awake.
success.art: A teenager wedging a striped mattress into a dripping outflow pipe on a concrete creek bank, warning lights flicking on at a distant hilltop plant

failure.text: The pipe burps the mattress back at you like a spitball. You go down in the creek on your backside, and the current carries you off, mattress and all, through a culvert under three streets, toward something down there that is splashing back.
failure.art: A soaked teenager riding a mattress like a raft down a glowing green concrete culvert at night, arms flailing

choices.label: Join the frog chorus and lead it upstream

success.text: You find the harmony on the second try. The frogs swivel both their heads toward you, delighted, and follow your voice up the bank and away from the yards in a hopping, croaking conga line. They settle in the cattails by the plant fence and sing you a farewell encore.
success.art: A teenager walking up a moonlit creek bank singing, followed by a conga line of two-headed frogs hopping toward cattails by a chain-link fence

failure.text: Your note goes flat. Every frog stops singing at once and two hundred eyes turn to look at you. Then they all hop, together, straight at you, and you sprint for the fence with a dozen sticky little feet riding on your back.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting up a creek bank toward a backyard fence, a swarm of two-headed frogs leaping after them, several clinging to their back

encounters.title: The Glowing Full-Size Bar
encounters.place: Your bedroom floor, sorting candy after midnight
encounters.text: Everybody at school swears a van in the Starlight Mall lot was handing out free full-size Nougat Nova bars, and you got one. Now, sorting your stash on the carpet with the lights off, you notice it is glowing right through the wrapper. It is warm. It is ticking, faintly, like a wristwatch. Every rumor about radioactive Halloween candy you ever heard is suddenly front and center.
encounters.art: A teenager sitting cross-legged on a bedroom carpet after midnight with the lights off, surrounded by sorted piles of Halloween candy, holding one full-size candy bar glowing green through its wrapper, its light spilling across their face and the candy piles, a pillowcase at their side, green glow and dark room, close medium shot

choices.label: Build a Geiger counter from a coffee can and test it

success.text: Your coffee-can counter clicks like popcorn when it gets close, then settles down. The glow is only paint, a cheap phosphor some prankster brushed on the wrapper to scare kids. Underneath, the chocolate is perfectly ordinary. You eat it in four bites and sleep like a baby.
success.art: A homemade coffee-can radiation counter with dangling wires beside a peeled candy bar on a bedroom desk, glowing paint smudged on the wrapper

failure.text: The counter clicks faster, faster, then shrieks and pops a puff of smoke. Every dog on Crystal Street starts howling at once. The bar keeps ticking. You hide it in a coffee can in the garage and lie awake listening to the garage tick.
failure.art: A smoking homemade coffee-can counter on a bedroom floor beside a glowing candy bar, a teenager covering their ears

choices.label: Eat it. You only live once.

success.text: It tastes like caramel and thunderstorms. For one glorious hour you can see in the dark, hear the moths gossiping, and hop from your lawn onto the garage roof in a single bound. Then it wears off with a burp that lights the whole yard green. Worth it.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas leaping from a moonlit lawn onto a garage roof in one bound, their eyes faintly glowing green, moths circling

failure.text: Your tongue turns neon green and glows when you talk. Then the hiccups start, and every hiccup blows a slimy bubble the size of a beach ball that floats out the window and pops over a neighbor's car with a little green splat. It goes on until sunrise.
failure.art: A teenager with a glowing green tongue hiccuping giant slimy green bubbles out a bedroom window, one bursting over a parked car below

choices.label: Bury it by the back fence, the old way you bury bad luck

success.text: You dig by the back fence, drop the bar in, and cover it with salt, dirt and an upside-down flowerpot, the way the old stories say. The ticking fades to nothing. Your trowel clinks on a rusty coffee can somebody buried long ago, full of old quarters and a note that says FOR LUCK.
success.art: A teenager kneeling by a backyard fence at night with a trowel, an upside-down flowerpot over fresh dirt, a rusty coffee can of old coins unearthed beside them

failure.text: Every time you pat the dirt flat, the ground glows a little brighter, until your whole backyard is lit up like a ball field. A neighbor's porch light flicks on. You spend the rest of the night raking leaves over the glow and explaining nothing to anyone.
failure.art: A suburban backyard at night with the ground glowing bright green from below like a stadium, a teenager frantically raking leaves over the light

encounters.title: The Tanker on Quarry Road
encounters.place: The bend on Quarry Road, 1:20 a.m.
encounters.text: A truck with blank white sides has jackknifed across Quarry Road. The cab door hangs open, the CB radio crackling to an empty seat, and the driver is gone. Steel drums have tumbled off the trailer behind it, leaking something that glows the color of grape soda. One drum is rolling, slowly and very deliberately, downhill toward Crystal Street.
encounters.art: A jackknifed white tanker truck with blank sides lying across a dark country road at 1:20 in the morning, its cab door hanging open and the CB handset dangling, steel drums spilled across the asphalt leaking glowing purple liquid, one drum rolling downhill toward the distant streetlights of a suburb, a teenager on a bike stopped at the bend, purple glow, wide shot

choices.label: Sprint ahead of the rolling drum and stop it

success.text: You sprint downhill, get ahead of it and plant your sneakers. The drum hits you like a linebacker and stops. It hums against your palms, almost grateful. You roll it into the ditch, wedge it with rocks, and it settles down like a dog that has been told to stay.
success.art: A teenager bracing against a rolling steel drum on a dark downhill road, glowing purple goo dripping from its seams, a rocky ditch beside them

failure.text: The drum bowls you over like a pin and keeps going. You chase it all the way down to the cul-de-sac, where it circles the Heartstone twice, glowing brighter, and wanders off between the houses. It seemed very pleased to be home.
failure.art: A glowing steel drum rolling in a circle around a huge purple geode in a suburban roundabout at night, a breathless teenager chasing behind

choices.label: Grab the CB handset and call it in

success.text: You key the CB and call it in, crisp as a long-haul trucker. Minutes later Mix breaks into the KGLM overnight show: Quarry Road is closed, stay inside, lock your doors. Orange flashers come over the hill, and a tired woman in a hard hat hands you a reflective vest and a Bolt Cola.
success.alone: You key the CB and call it in, crisp as a long-haul trucker. Minutes later the KGLM overnight show breaks in: Quarry Road is closed, stay inside, lock your doors. Orange flashers come over the hill, and a tired woman in a hard hat hands you a reflective vest and a Bolt Cola.
success.art: A teenager in a reflective vest beside a jackknifed truck at night, holding a soda can, orange flashing work lights cresting a hill behind them

failure.text: A voice answers on the CB, low and slow: Breaker, breaker, we see you. It is coming from the cab speaker, and also, faintly, from inside the nearest leaking drum. You drop the handset and walk away very fast. Then you run, and every radio you pass is still talking.
failure.art: A dangling CB radio handset swinging inside an empty truck cab at night, its speaker glowing, a leaking purple drum on the road outside

choices.label: Creep along the trailer and find out what it was carrying

success.text: Clipped inside the cab door is the manifest. The cargo is listed as SURPLUS, 1959, RETURN TO SENDER, and the sender is the company that built Glimmer Falls. Taped beside it is a jar of change with a note in shaky marker: FOR WHOEVER CLEANS THIS UP. You figure that counts.
success.art: A flashlight beam on a clipboard manifest inside an open truck cab door, a jar of coins taped beside it, glowing purple puddles on the road below

failure.text: The drum by your foot sloshes, and a little wave of purple goo splashes over your sneaker. The shoe fizzes, foams and dissolves into a puddle of bubbles, laces last. You hop home on one foot in a sock that will glow for a week.
failure.art: A sneaker dissolving into purple foaming bubbles on a dark road beside a leaking steel drum, a teenager hopping away on one foot

encounters.title: Quarantine
encounters.place: The mouth of the cul-de-sac, two a.m.
encounters.text: People in white suits and fishbowl helmets are stringing yellow tape across the entrance to Crystal Street. A striped tent with a shower inside has gone up on the Heartstone lawn, and a woman with a clipboard is knocking on doors, calm and polite: everyone through decontamination, please. The neighbors who come out the far side are pink-cheeked, foamy and cheerful, and none of them can remember their own phone number.
encounters.art: Figures in white hazmat suits and round fishbowl helmets stringing yellow tape across the entrance to a suburban cul-de-sac at two in the morning, a striped decontamination tent glowing on a lawn beside a giant purple crystal rock, neighbors in bathrobes lined up at the tent, pink-cheeked foamy neighbors coming out the far side smiling, a woman with a clipboard knocking on a door, white floodlight, wide shot

choices.label: Politely ask the woman in charge for some identification

success.text: She hands over a laminated badge: Civil Defense, Glimmer Falls. The photo is from 1962. She stares at it as if she has not looked at it in years, then unscrews her helmet and admits the drill was scheduled a very long time ago. The whole crew packs up the tent and trudges off to bed.
success.art: A woman in a white hazmat suit holding her round helmet under one arm and squinting at an old laminated badge, a teenager beside her, a striped tent being folded behind them

failure.text: She checks her clipboard, nods, and two suits lift you under the arms and carry you, feet dangling, through the tent. You get hosed with warm pink foam that smells like bubble gum and floor wax, and you come out squeaky clean and unable to remember your locker combination for two days.
failure.art: Two figures in white hazmat suits carrying a teenager by the arms through a striped tent full of pink foam spray, the teenager's sneakers dangling

choices.label: Slip through a hedge and get behind the tent

success.text: Kev knows the gap in the Lindqvists' hedge from his paper route. You cut across three backyards and reach the tent from behind. The shower heads are fed by a tank stenciled with a skull. You twist its valve shut, and the next neighbor through gets plain cold water, yelps, and remembers their phone number just fine.
success.alone: You know the gap in the Lindqvists' hedge from a hundred games of hide-and-seek. You cut across three backyards and reach the tent from behind. The shower heads are fed by a tank stenciled with a skull. You twist its valve shut, and the next neighbor through gets plain cold water, yelps, and remembers their phone number just fine.
success.art: A teenager crouched behind a striped tent at night twisting a valve on a metal tank stenciled with a skull, hoses running into the tent, a hedge gap behind them

failure.text: You are halfway under the tape when a gloved hand catches your ankle. A suit shines a penlight in your eyes, says Contaminated in a voice like a vending machine, and stamps your forehead with a rubber stamp that will not wash off until Thursday.
failure.art: A figure in a white hazmat suit pressing a rubber stamp onto a startled teenager's forehead beside yellow caution tape at night, a penlight beam in their eyes

choices.label: Volunteer to go through first so the little kids can watch

success.text: You step up and go first, so the little kids in line can see it is safe. Inside, you hold your breath through the pink foam and walk out the far side still entirely yourself. You tell the line it tickles. The kids cheer, and the suits, outvoted by giggling, take the tent down.
success.art: A foam-covered teenager stepping out of a striped decontamination tent with arms raised, a line of small children in pajamas cheering on a lawn

failure.text: The foam is cold and it gets in your ears. You stumble out the far side wearing a big, pleasant smile you did not decide on, and it takes until breakfast for your face to feel like yours again.
failure.art: A dripping teenager stumbling out of a striped tent with a wide frozen smile, pink foam in their hair and ears, porch lights glowing behind

encounters.title: Instant Pets
encounters.place: The youngest Pell kid's bedroom, two doors down, 12:45 a.m.
encounters.text: The youngest Pell kid calls your house in tears. His mail-order Brine Buddies, the tiny brine shrimp from the back of a comic book, got a cup of creek water in their tank after the rain. Now there are three of them, each the size of a cocker spaniel, crammed in the fish tank with their long feathery legs, tapping on the glass in rhythm, wanting out.
encounters.art: A bedroom at 12:45 at night, three pink brine shrimp each the size of a cocker spaniel crammed into a bubbling fish tank on a dresser, their long feathery legs tapping on the glass, a small boy in pajamas peeking out from behind a bunk bed in tears, a teenager in the doorway holding a phone receiver, blue aquarium light, medium shot

choices.label: Haul them down to the creek in a red wagon

success.text: You fill a red wagon with bathwater and haul them down to the creek one at a time. Each one waves its feathery legs at the little Pell kid before it slips into the water. He waves back with both hands. Every morning that week, he finds a shiny pebble on his windowsill.
success.art: A teenager pulling a red wagon sloshing with water down a dark suburban street, a giant pink brine shrimp riding in it, a small boy in pajamas waving from a window

failure.text: Halfway down the block, the biggest one climbs out of the wagon and gallops off between the houses on all of its legs at once, chirping happily. You spend the rest of the night following wet footprints and finding it in a different neighbor's birdbath.
failure.art: A giant pink brine shrimp splashing in a backyard birdbath at night, wet footprints across the lawn, a tired teenager with an empty wagon behind it

choices.label: Read the packet's fine print and fix the water

success.text: By flashlight you read the packet: exactly one spoonful of Water Purifier per gallon, and never creek water, ever. You do the math, drain and refill, and the tank fizzes. The three giants shrink like sweaters in a hot dryer, back into tiny pink commas, wiggling happily. The kid names all three after you.
success.art: A bubbling bedroom fish tank full of tiny pink brine shrimp wiggling happily, a teenager with a measuring spoon and a seed packet, a grinning boy in pajamas

failure.text: You add too much. The water foams up like a root-beer float, the three of them grow another foot, and the tank cracks. Twenty gallons of salty creek water and three delighted shrimp spill across the bedroom carpet and right onto your socks.
failure.art: A cracked fish tank gushing foamy water across a bedroom carpet, three giant pink brine shrimp sliding out happily, a teenager hopping back with soaked socks

encounters.title: Suds City
encounters.place: Suds City 24-Hour Laundromat on Quarry Road, 1 a.m.
encounters.text: You came to dry a load of towels and found every washer in Suds City foaming over at once. The foam is pale green and warm, and it is gathering in the middle of the floor into one big, wobbling heap. It has eaten the lint from every dryer trap. It has eaten every orphan sock in the lost-and-found basket. Now it is rolling, slowly, toward your laundry basket.
encounters.art: A late-night laundromat at one in the morning under fluorescent lights, every washing machine overflowing with warm pale green foam that gathers into one big wobbling heap on the tile floor, mismatched socks and lint stuck in the foam, the heap rolling toward a plastic basket of towels, a teenager backing up against the dryers, white light, wide shot

choices.label: Heave a whole jug of fabric softener on it

success.text: You glug a jug of Cuddle-Soft over the heap. It sighs, goes fluffy and settles down like a cat in a sunbeam, purring and smelling like a springtime meadow. By two a.m. it has folded itself neatly into the empty washers and gone to sleep. Your towels have never been softer.
success.art: A fluffy pale green foam heap curled contentedly inside a row of open washing machines in a quiet laundromat, a teenager holding an empty softener jug and a stack of folded towels

failure.text: The softener makes it bigger and much, much friendlier. It hugs you. It keeps hugging you. You squelch out the door an hour later smelling like a springtime meadow and leaving green bubbles on every step all the way home.
failure.art: A huge pale green foam heap hugging a teenager in a laundromat, only their sneakers and one hand poking out, an empty softener jug on the floor

choices.label: Belly-slide across the floor and grab your basket

success.text: You belly-slide across the wet tile, snag the basket and ride a wave of suds right back out the door. Behind you the heap shivers with disappointment. Tangled in your towels are a dozen quarters the machines must have coughed up years ago.
success.art: A teenager belly-sliding across a sudsy laundromat floor clutching a laundry basket, quarters spilling from the towels, a wobbling green foam heap behind them

failure.text: The heap swallows the basket, and then you. It is warm in there and quiet, and it smells like a hundred years of laundry. It burps you out into the parking lot without your left shoe and with somebody's argyle sock stuck to your ear.
failure.art: A foam-covered teenager sprawled in an empty laundromat parking lot at night with one shoe missing and an argyle sock stuck to their ear, green suds drifting from the door

choices.label: Wade to the back room and throw the main breaker

success.text: You wade through foam up to your knees and haul down the big rusted lever. Every machine dies, the lights go out, and in the dark the heap settles with a long wet sigh, like a balloon running out of air. When the lights come back it is just a sudsy floor waiting for a mop.
success.art: A teenager knee-deep in green foam pulling down a big rusted breaker lever in a dim laundromat back room, the foam heap sagging behind them

failure.text: The breaker sparks, every dryer starts spinning backward and the foam rises to the ceiling tiles. You run for the door. Behind you, through the big front window, the whole laundromat glows green all night, like a fish tank somebody forgot to clean.
failure.art: A laundromat at night seen from the parking lot, its big front window packed with glowing green foam up to the ceiling, a teenager running away across the lot

encounters.title: Green Rain
encounters.place: Your front lawn, a little after midnight
encounters.text: It starts raining out of a clear sky full of stars, and the rain is green. Warm drops patter on the cul-de-sac and smell like lime soda and old pennies. Where they land, the lawn gnomes start to giggle and the paint on the Fenwicks' mailbox bubbles into blisters. A drop lands on your arm and leaves a little glowing freckle that tingles.
encounters.art: Glowing green raindrops falling on a suburban cul-de-sac from a clear starry sky a little after midnight, a garden gnome giggling on a wet lawn, a mailbox with its paint bubbling into blisters, a teenager on the front walk holding out one arm with a small glowing green freckle on it, green droplets and blue night, medium wide shot

choices.label: Hold a newspaper over your head and dash for the porch

success.text: You sprint for the porch, dodging the fattest drops like dodgeballs, and make it with only three green freckles. From the steps you watch the gutters carry the glow away down the street, and the rain stops as suddenly as it started.
success.art: A teenager with a newspaper over their head leaping onto a porch as glowing green raindrops splash behind them, green water swirling down a gutter

failure.text: The newspaper dissolves into green mush halfway across the lawn. By the time you reach the porch, your hair has turned the color of a tennis ball and stands straight up, crackling, and it will refuse to lie flat until the weekend.
failure.art: A drenched teenager on a porch with bright tennis-ball green hair standing straight up and crackling, soggy green newspaper pulp in their hands

choices.label: Catch a jar of it and read the drops like tea leaves

success.text: You hold a jar out into the storm and read the drops the way fortune tellers read tea leaves. They swirl into a picture: the plant on Quarry Road, a cracked tank, a stuck valve. The rain thins, as if embarrassed to be understood, and by the time you look up it has stopped.
success.art: A glass jar of glowing green rainwater held up to a porch light, the swirling drops inside forming the shape of a factory tank and a valve

failure.text: The drops swirl into a picture of your own face. Then they climb out of the jar and up your arm like ivy. You shake them off on the porch, but they leave a trail of tiny glowing footprints that follows you all the way to bed.
failure.art: Glowing green droplets climbing out of a glass jar and up a teenager's arm like ivy, a trail of tiny luminous footprints across a porch

choices.label: Kick off your shoes and dance in it

success.text: You dance in the green rain like it is the last song at the roller rink. Every drop that hits you sparks, and your freckles light up in constellations. When it stops you are glowing faintly from head to toe, and something very high above the cul-de-sac seems to be waving back.
success.art: A barefoot teenager dancing joyfully in glowing green rain on a suburban lawn, freckles lit up like constellations, a faint light hovering high in the starry sky

failure.text: You slip on the wet grass mid-spin and land flat on your back in a glowing puddle. It soaks through your shirt and leaves a perfect green outline of you on the lawn that the sprinklers cannot wash off, which the whole street will talk about all week.
failure.art: A glowing green outline of a sprawled person printed on a wet suburban lawn at night, a soaked teenager sitting up beside it

encounters.title: Best in Show
encounters.place: The Glimmer Falls High gym, the night before the science fair
encounters.text: You came back for the display board you left under the bleachers. Every science fair project is set out on folding tables in the dark gym, and one of them is winning. A petri dish labeled MOLD THAT GROWS TO MUSIC has crept off its table, across three other projects and up the bleachers in a soft gray-green carpet. The band room radio next door is playing, and every time the bass hits, the mold grows another foot.
encounters.art: A dark high school gym lined with folding tables of science fair projects, a soft gray-green mold spreading from one petri dish across three tables and up the wooden bleachers in a fuzzy carpet, a baking soda volcano half swallowed, light and music spilling from a band room doorway, a teenager holding a folded display board, dim light, wide shot

choices.label: Tiptoe along the wall and switch off the radio

success.text: You tiptoe along the wall and through the band room door, and click off the radio mid-chorus. The mold stops dead. Without a beat it shrivels back across the bleachers and into its dish like a tape rewinding. On your way out you even straighten the volcano.
success.art: A teenager switching off a boombox in a dim band room doorway while gray-green mold shrinks back across gym bleachers toward a small petri dish

failure.text: Your sneaker squeaks on the gym floor, loud as a whistle, and the mold hears you. Every fuzzy inch of it turns and grows toward the squeak. You leave by the fire door with spores in your hair and an alarm wailing behind you.
failure.art: A teenager bursting out a gym fire door at night with fuzzy gray-green spores in their hair, mold reaching after them across the floor, a red alarm light flashing

choices.label: Swap the radio for the saddest power ballad you own

success.text: You pop in your slowest mixtape, the saddest power ballad of 1985. The mold sways. It droops. By the second chorus it is weeping little drops of dew, and it curls back into its dish to feel its feelings. You leave the tape playing and tiptoe out.
success.art: A drooping gray-green mold weeping dewdrops as it curls back into a petri dish on a science fair table, a cassette player glowing softly beside it in a dark gym

failure.text: You hit play on the wrong side and get the dance remix. The mold goes wild. It swallows the bleachers, the scoreboard and the mascot costume, and grooves along the rafters while you crawl for the exit under a table of potato batteries.
failure.art: Gray-green mold swarming up a gym scoreboard and rafters in rhythmic waves, a teenager crawling under a science fair table of potato batteries toward an exit

choices.label: Load the baking soda volcano and aim it at the mold

success.text: You mix a triple batch in the volcano's cone and aim. It erupts in a gorgeous pink foam that drenches the mold, which shrivels with a tiny squeak. The next morning the volcano wins first prize, and its owner, who heard the whole story from the janitor, splits the prize money with you.
success.art: A papier-mache volcano erupting pink foam over a shriveling gray-green mold on a science fair table, a teenager aiming it like a cannon in a dark gym

failure.text: The volcano erupts backward. Pink foam fills your shoes, your pockets and your ears, and the mold, delighted, eats the foam and grows a little pink mustache. You slosh home leaving pink footprints all the way down Crystal Street.
failure.art: A teenager drenched in pink foam beside a backfired papier-mache volcano, a gray-green mold sporting a fuzzy pink mustache on the table beside them

encounters.title: Tented
encounters.place: The Haverford house, under a fumigation tent, 1:30 a.m.
encounters.text: The Haverfords' house has been zipped inside a giant red-and-yellow striped fumigation tent all week. Tonight the tent is breathing, in and out, slow and deep, like a sleeping circus. Purple fog is seeping from the seams and rolling across the lawns, and everything it touches grows a soft coat of fuzz: the hedges, a tricycle, the Kowalskis' cat, who looks very annoyed about it.
encounters.art: A suburban house wrapped in a giant red-and-yellow striped fumigation tent at 1:30 in the morning, the tent swelling and sinking in slow breaths, purple fog seeping from the seams across the lawns, a tricycle and a hedge covered in soft fuzz, an annoyed fuzzy cat on the sidewalk, a teenager holding their sleeve over their nose, streetlight and purple fog, wide shot

choices.label: Grab a roll of duct tape and seal every seam

success.text: You circle the tent slapping duct tape over every leaking seam while fog swirls around your ankles. The tent takes one last enormous breath, holds it, and lets it out slowly through the roof vent, straight up into the night like a smoke signal. Your hands smell like grape for a week.
success.art: A teenager slapping strips of silver duct tape along the seams of a striped fumigation tent at night, a thin column of purple fog rising from the roof

failure.text: The tent exhales just as you reach the front door seam, and a puff of purple fog catches you full in the face. By morning every inch the fog touched is covered in soft lavender fuzz, like a peach. It brushes off by Tuesday.
failure.art: A teenager covered in soft lavender fuzz like a peach standing beside a striped fumigation tent at dawn, a roll of duct tape in hand

choices.label: Hold your breath, duck under the flap and shut off the fog

success.text: You suck in the biggest breath of your life and duck under the flap. In the purple dark of the Haverfords' living room, a ring of rusty canisters has been chugging out fog all week with nobody there to turn them off. You crank every valve shut on one breath and stagger out gasping. The tent stops breathing.
success.art: A teenager with puffed cheeks cranking the valve on a rusty canister in a dark living room thick with purple fog, a ring of canisters around them

failure.text: You run out of breath halfway down the hall and gulp a mouthful of purple. Everything goes soft and slow and lavender. You wake on the Haverfords' lawn at dawn wearing a fuzzy coat you did not have before, with the annoyed cat asleep on your chest.
failure.art: A fuzzy lavender-coated teenager asleep on a dewy lawn at dawn beside a striped fumigation tent, an annoyed fuzzy cat curled on their chest

choices.label: Daisy-chain every box fan on the street and blow it back

success.text: You run extension cords from three garages and line up every box fan on the street. The purple fog rolls backward over the roof and away into Crystal Woods. The fuzzy hedges shed like dogs in spring, and by morning clumps of lavender fluff are tumbling down the street like tumbleweeds.
success.art: A row of box fans on a suburban lawn at night blowing purple fog back over a striped fumigation tent, extension cords snaking across the grass, lavender fluff tumbling down the street

failure.text: One extension cord too many. Every porch light on the block blows at once, and in the dark the fans keep spinning backward, pulling the fog toward your open bedroom window. You spend the night with towels stuffed under the door, listening to the tent breathe.
failure.art: A dark suburban street with every porch light out, box fans spinning in reverse, purple fog drifting toward an open upstairs bedroom window

encounters.title: Glow in the Dark
encounters.place: Your bathroom mirror, 3 a.m.
encounters.text: You get up for a glass of water and the bathroom is already lit. It is you. Your fingernails are glowing a soft mint green, one streak of your hair shines like a nightlight, and when you sneeze, you sneeze a puff of glitter that hangs in the air and twinkles. Whatever has been leaking into Glimmer Falls this week, a little of it ended up in you.
encounters.art: A teenager in pajamas staring into a bathroom mirror at three in the morning, their fingernails glowing mint green and one streak of their hair shining bright green, a puff of glittering sneeze hanging in the air in front of them, the dark bathroom lit only by their own soft green glow, close medium shot into the mirror

choices.label: Hide it under a ski cap, gloves and sunglasses

success.text: Ski cap, gloves, a turtleneck and your darkest sunglasses. You look ready to rob a bank, but you also look like you. By sunrise the glow has faded to a shimmer that only shows under black light, and the kids at the bus stop are none the wiser.
success.art: A teenager bundled in a ski cap, gloves, turtleneck and dark sunglasses at a suburban bus stop at sunrise, a faint mint shimmer at their fingertips

failure.text: The glow shines right through the ski cap, so now you look like a lamp wearing a hat. By four in the morning every moth on Crystal Street has found your window, and they brought their friends.
failure.art: A teenager in a ski cap glowing mint green through the knit like a lampshade, a cloud of moths pressed against the bedroom window behind them

choices.label: Knock on the garage clinic and ask for a checkup

success.text: Dr. Haddad, in a bathrobe and slippers, peers at your glowing fingernails through a magnifying glass, hums, and hands you a bottle of chalky pink tummy medicine. One swig and the glow drains out of you like color from a sunset. He sends you home with a first-aid kit and keeps one glitter sneeze in a test tube.
success.alone: The garage clinic is dark, so you raid your own medicine cabinet instead. One swig of chalky pink tummy medicine and the glow drains out of you like color from a sunset. Under the sink, behind the drain cleaner, you find a first-aid kit you had forgotten, and you keep it close.
success.art: A bottle of chalky pink medicine beside a first-aid kit on a garage workbench at night, a teenager's fingernails fading from mint green under a magnifying glass

failure.text: The medicine fizzes in your stomach like a shaken soda. You burp, and the burp glows. Every burp for the rest of the night lights up the room green, which makes it very hard to sneak back into bed without waking up the whole house.
failure.art: A teenager tiptoeing down a dark hallway in pajamas, a burst of green light puffing from their mouth and lighting up the family photos on the wall

choices.label: If you're going to glow, glow on purpose

success.text: You paint the rest of your nails to match, gel the green streak into a spike and practice your best runway walk up and down the hallway. By dawn the glow has faded, but the look stays, and honestly, it is a look.
success.art: A teenager strutting a runway walk down a dark hallway with a gelled glowing green hair spike and matching glowing nails, striking a pose

failure.text: You lean into it and the glow leans back. It spreads, cheerful and unstoppable, until you are lit up like a jukebox from head to toe, and the family dog wakes and barks at the lamp that just walked down the hall.
failure.art: A teenager glowing bright green from head to toe like a jukebox in a dark hallway, a startled dog barking at them from a doorway

name: There Goes the Neighborhood
blurb: Crystal Street was built to be perfect, and perfect has rules: edged lawns, matching mailboxes, porch lights off by eleven. This week every ordinary thing on the cul-de-sac turns up one notch, from the grass that grows while you watch to the midnight yard sale with your name on a price tag.

encounters.title: The Lawn That Won't Quit
encounters.place: Your front yard, 12:30 a.m.
encounters.text: You can hear it growing. Your front lawn, mowed this afternoon, is up to your knees and rising, thick and green and whispering. It has swallowed the garden hose, the welcome mat and your bike. A runner of crabgrass is feeling its way up the drainpipe toward your window, and in the garage the lawnmower is revving all by itself, like it has waited its whole life for this.
encounters.art: A suburban front lawn at 12:30 at night grown waist high in thick whispering grass, a bicycle handlebar and a garden hose sticking out of it, a long runner of crabgrass climbing a drainpipe toward a lit upstairs window, a lawnmower revving by itself in the open garage with its headlight on, a teenager on the porch steps, porch light and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Fire up the mower and fight back

success.text: You yank the cord and the mower roars like a muscle car. You cut a path to your bike, then to the hose, then mow the whole yard in neat, furious stripes until the grass gives up and lies down. The neighbors will say your lawn has never looked better.
success.art: A teenager pushing a roaring lawnmower through towering grass at night, neat mowed stripes behind them, a rescued bicycle lying on the cut lawn

failure.text: The mower gets three feet into the lawn and the lawn takes it. Grass wraps the wheels and drags it under with a muffled sputter. You back away slowly. All night, from somewhere deep in the yard, you hear the mower still running, happy and very far away.
failure.art: A lawnmower being dragged down into thick tall grass by wrapping green blades, its handle sinking out of sight, a teenager backing away across a dark yard

choices.label: Round up the goats from the house on Quarry Road

success.text: Kev knows a family on his paper route who keeps four goats for exactly this kind of emergency, and they owe him a favor. Twenty minutes later the goats are in your yard, chewing in contented rows. By dawn the lawn is a putting green and the goats are asleep in a heap on your porch.
success.alone: You remember the family on Quarry Road who keeps four goats for exactly this kind of emergency, and you knock until they answer. Twenty minutes later the goats are in your yard, chewing in contented rows. By dawn the lawn is a putting green and the goats are asleep in a heap on your porch.
success.art: Four goats asleep in a heap on a suburban front porch at dawn, a freshly cropped lawn as smooth as a putting green in front of them

failure.text: The goats eat the lawn, then the hedge, then the Fenwicks' wreath, then the hem of your pajamas. When they finish, the grass grows straight back, and now the goats are shoulder high and peering in at your bedroom window, chewing thoughtfully.
failure.art: Enormous shoulder-high goats peering into a lit bedroom window at night, chewing, tall grass surging back around their hooves

choices.label: Pour a line of salt along the property line

success.text: You pour a line of salt along the curb, the front walk and the property line, the way old-timers salt a porch against bad things. The grass reaches the salt and stops dead, shivering, like a dog at a fence. By morning it has shrunk back to a regulation two inches, sulking.
success.art: A white line of salt along a suburban curb at night, towering grass on one side trembling and stopping at the line, a teenager pouring from a coffee can

failure.text: The grass drinks the salt like potato chips and grows faster, thirsty and greedy. It swallows the mailbox, the porch steps and one of your sneakers, and you have to climb in through your own bedroom window to get back inside.
failure.art: A teenager climbing in through their own bedroom window from a sea of towering grass that has swallowed the porch steps and mailbox

encounters.title: Notice of Violation
encounters.place: The curb in front of your house, 1:05 a.m.
encounters.text: A thin man in a beige windbreaker and a pith helmet is kneeling on your lawn, measuring blades of grass with a ruler by flashlight. He is the Crystal Street Homeowners Association compliance officer, he says, and you are in violation. He has already slapped orange stickers on your mailbox, your jack-o-lantern and your bike. Everything he stickers turns beige, slowly, from the sticker outward.
encounters.art: A thin man in a beige windbreaker and a pith helmet kneeling on a suburban lawn at one in the morning measuring blades of grass with a wooden ruler by flashlight, orange stickers on a mailbox, a jack-o'-lantern and a bicycle, each one fading to beige outward from its sticker, a teenager watching from the front door, flashlight beam and porch light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Out-quote him on the HOA bylaws

success.text: Article Six, Section B: no citation may be issued during Halloween week to any decoration with a face. His mouth opens and closes. He peels every sticker off with a tiny, defeated scrape, and the color floods back into your jack-o-lantern like a blush.
success.art: A deflated man in a beige windbreaker peeling an orange sticker off a jack-o-lantern as its bright orange color floods back, a teenager holding a thick bylaws binder

failure.text: You quote a bylaw. He quotes a better one, then an amendment, then a footnote from 1959. By the time he is done your whole porch has gone beige, and so has your left sneaker, and he has written you up for loitering on your own lawn.
failure.art: A suburban porch faded entirely to beige at night, a teenager with one beige sneaker, a man in a pith helmet scribbling on a citation pad

choices.label: Peel off a sticker and slap it on his back

success.text: While he measures the hedge, you peel a sticker off your bike and press it gently between his shoulder blades. He goes beige from the collar down, notices, gasps, and hurries off into the dark to file a complaint against himself. The stickers on your stuff curl up and drop like dead leaves.
success.art: A man in a pith helmet turning beige from the collar down and hurrying away down a dark sidewalk with a clipboard, an orange sticker on his back, a teenager grinning by a hedge

failure.text: He spins around before you can stick it and slaps a sticker on your forehead instead: UNSIGHTLY. You feel yourself going a little beige, a little quiet, a little like you should probably repaint the shutters. It takes until breakfast to scrub off.
failure.art: A teenager with an orange sticker on their forehead slowly fading to beige from the face outward, a man in a pith helmet holding a sticker pad

choices.label: Bring him a lemonade and ask about his own yard

success.text: You ask about his own yard, and his face crumples. He has not had one since 1971; he lives in the clubhouse and measures everybody else's. You talk until two. He leaves a note on your door, YOUR LAWN IS LOVELY, and the stickers fall off on their own.
success.art: A man in a beige windbreaker sitting on a porch step at night holding a glass of lemonade and wiping his eyes, a teenager listening beside him, orange stickers drifting to the ground

failure.text: He drinks the lemonade, smacks his lips and writes you up for serving a beverage without a permit. Then he writes up the glass. By dawn your porch railing is covered in orange stickers, and your welcome mat says, in faded letters, WELCOME, MOSTLY.
failure.art: A porch railing plastered with orange violation stickers at dawn, an empty lemonade glass with its own sticker, a faded welcome mat

encounters.title: Everything Must Go
encounters.place: A driveway on Quarry Road, a midnight yard sale
encounters.text: Somebody is holding a yard sale at midnight, with a string of bare bulbs and card tables down the driveway, and a sweet old lady in a cardigan is selling everything you remember. Your first bike, the one with the banana seat. The cassette of your seventh birthday party. A mason jar labeled THE TIME YOU WERE BRAVE, priced at a quarter. Two neighbors are already haggling over it.
encounters.art: A suburban driveway yard sale at midnight under a string of bare bulbs, folding tables holding a child's banana-seat bicycle, a cassette tape and a glowing mason jar priced on a small tag, two neighbors tugging at the jar, a sweet old woman in a cardigan holding a handheld price labeler and smiling, a teenager staring at the bicycle, warm bulb light and black night, wide shot

choices.label: Haggle her down like a pro

success.text: You point out the scratch on the bike, the warble on the tape and the dent in the jar's lid, and you talk her down to a nickel for the lot. She laughs, delighted, and throws in a shoebox of quarters that turns out to be your old allowance. Holding the jar, you remember exactly how brave you were.
success.art: A teenager walking away from a midnight yard sale hugging a glowing mason jar, a shoebox of quarters under one arm, a laughing old woman waving behind them

failure.text: You haggle. She haggles better. By the end, you have paid every quarter in your pocket for one cassette, and when you play it at home it is your birthday party with you cut out of every song.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a bedroom floor beside a tape player at night, staring at an old birthday cassette, empty pockets turned out

choices.label: Tell her why the jar matters

success.text: You skip the haggling and tell her about the day you stood up for a kid on the bus. She listens, nods slowly, and hands you the jar for free. When you unscrew the lid at home, the bravery pours back in like warm cocoa.
success.art: An old woman in a cardigan handing a glowing mason jar across a card table to a teenager under bare bulbs, both smiling

failure.text: One of the haggling neighbors outbids you with a crisp dollar bill and walks off with your jar, whistling. All night you can see it glowing on his kitchen windowsill across the street, and you cannot quite remember what was in it.
failure.art: A glowing mason jar on a kitchen windowsill across a dark suburban street, seen from a teenager's bedroom window

choices.label: Snatch her price gun and tag everything FREE

success.text: You grab the price gun and go table to table: FREE, FREE, FREE. Your memories hop off the tables and flutter home through the dark like startled birds, each to its own window. The old lady watches with her hands on her hips, then laughs, tags herself FREE too, and strolls off into the night humming.
success.art: Glowing memories shaped like a bicycle, a cassette and a jar fluttering off yard sale tables into the night like birds, a teenager holding a handheld price labeler, an old woman laughing

failure.text: The price gun bucks in your hands like a garden hose and tags you: 25 CENTS, AS IS. The old lady smiles and sets you on a table between a waffle iron and a lava lamp. You spend an hour sitting very still while neighbors pick you up and put you down.
failure.art: A teenager with a price sticker on their chest sitting stiffly on a yard sale table between a waffle iron and a lava lamp, neighbors browsing under bare bulbs

encounters.title: Just One More Demonstration
encounters.place: Mrs. Bramley's living room, a Glow-Rite candle party
encounters.text: Mrs. Bramley's candle party started at seven-thirty. It is well past midnight now, the mantel clock still says 9:45, and the hostess is lighting just one more candle. Each scent has a name: Fresh Linen, Sunday Pot Roast, Stay A While. The guests keep smiling and turning the pages of their catalogs, and some of their dresses look like 1974. One of them has cobwebs in her beehive.
encounters.art: A cozy suburban living room crowded with smiling guests holding catalogs, dozens of lit scented candles on every surface, a mantel clock stopped at a quarter to ten, some guests in 1974 polyester dresses, an older woman with cobwebs in her beehive, a hostess lighting one more candle, a teenager by the door checking their wristwatch, warm candlelight, wide shot

choices.label: Blow out every candle in the room

success.text: You take a breath and work down the coffee table like it is the world's biggest birthday cake. With each candle, a guest blinks, checks her watch and gasps. When the last flame dies, the mantel clock lurches to 1:12 a.m. and everyone grabs their coats at once, apologizing, thanking the hostess, finally going home.
success.art: A teenager blowing out a long row of candles on a coffee table, thin smoke trails rising, startled party guests checking their watches and reaching for coats

failure.text: The candles relight themselves the moment you turn away, every one, with a soft pop. The hostess pats your hand and says you must be tired, dear, sit. You sit. You smell Fresh Linen. You wake on the couch at dawn holding a catalog with your order already filled out.
failure.art: A teenager asleep on a floral couch at dawn clutching a candle catalog, every candle in the room still burning, smiling guests seated all around

choices.label: Announce you're hosting the next party, right now, at your place

success.text: You stand on the ottoman and announce the next party is at your house, starting now, and everyone has to walk. The guests applaud and file out behind you. Out on the sidewalk, in the cold night air, they blink, yawn and drift home one by one. You never have to host anything.
success.art: A teenager leading a line of party guests in dated dresses out a front door onto a cold suburban sidewalk at night, the guests yawning and drifting toward their own houses

failure.text: Everyone applauds. The hostess writes your name in her book, in pen, and smiles a candlelit smile. Then she hands you off to a beaming woman in a lilac robe, who says the regional meeting is starting right now, a few doors down, and you are expected.
failure.art: A smiling hostess writing in a ledger by candlelight while a woman in a lilac hooded robe takes a startled teenager by the elbow toward the door

choices.label: Slip down the hall and dig your jacket out of the coat pile

success.text: You dig through the coats on the guest bed until you find your jacket, then keep digging and pull out a car coat with a 1974 bus pass in the pocket. A guest gasps, That's mine! One by one they come down the hall for their coats, and the whole party follows you out the door. There are three quarters in your jacket you do not remember.
success.art: A teenager holding up an old car coat beside a mountain of coats on a guest bed, party guests crowding in the bedroom doorway reaching for their own

failure.text: The coat pile goes down and down. You dig past coats, then winter boots, then a rotary phone, then a Christmas tree still in its stand. When you finally climb out, the hostess is waiting at the top with a tray of cheese balls and a fresh candle called Stay A While.
failure.art: A teenager climbing out of an impossibly deep pile of coats on a bed, a rotary phone and a Christmas tree poking out of it, a smiling hostess holding a tray of cheese balls

encounters.title: The Carpool
encounters.place: The end of your driveway, 12:15 a.m.
encounters.text: A wood-paneled station wagon pulls up to your curb with its headlights off. Behind the wheel is a carpool driver in a quilted vest and a perfect smile, and the back seats are packed with kids in soccer uniforms, shin guards, sleeping bags and ballet buns. You're late, sweetie, she says. Practice. Hop in. You do not play soccer, and you are fairly sure none of these kids live in Glimmer Falls.
encounters.art: A wood-paneled station wagon idling at a suburban curb at 12:15 at night with its headlights dark, a smiling woman in a quilted vest at the wheel leaning toward the open passenger window, the back seats crowded with sleepy children in soccer uniforms, shin guards and ballet buns, a teenager in pajamas standing at the end of the driveway, dome light glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Get in and read the route on her map

success.text: You buckle up and unfold the map on the dashboard. The route is a loop: every stop is a house where a kid was ever left waiting for a ride, all the way back to 1962. You find the one stop that leads out, the rec center, and point. She sighs and turns, and every kid gets dropped at a lit gym where their families are waiting with orange slices.
success.art: A road map spread across a station wagon dashboard at night with a looping route traced in red, a teenager pointing at one stop, a lit gym ahead through the windshield

failure.text: The map folds itself back up in your hands and refuses to open. The wagon pulls away and the route goes on and on: soccer, piano, scouts, the dentist, around and around Glimmer Falls until dawn, and she drops you off at a house that only looks like yours.
failure.art: A station wagon driving through an endless loop of identical dark suburban streets at night, a teenager pressed to the back window among sleeping children

choices.label: Thank her and say your ride is already coming

success.text: You thank her, sweet as pie, and say your ride is on the way. She blinks. Nobody has ever turned down the carpool. She checks her clipboard, crosses you off, and the kids in the back wave as the wagon glides away. The littlest one tosses you a glow bracelet through the window.
success.art: A station wagon gliding away down a dark suburban street, children waving from the back window, a small hand tossing a glowing bracelet toward a teenager on the curb

failure.text: She keeps smiling. The back door swings open by itself. The kids all scoot over to make room at the same time, staring straight ahead. You back up the driveway step by step, and the wagon idles at the curb until sunrise, honking softly every ten minutes.
failure.art: A station wagon idling at a curb at night with its back door hanging open and a row of children scooted over staring straight ahead, a teenager backing up a driveway

choices.label: Yank the back door open and let the kids out

success.text: You haul the back door open and shout that practice is canceled. A dozen kids pile out onto your lawn like a clown car. Each one looks around, yawns, and walks home in a different direction, wide awake and themselves. The wagon drives off empty, very slowly, as if confused.
success.art: A dozen children in sports uniforms and ballet clothes tumbling out of a station wagon onto a moonlit lawn, a teenager holding the back door open

failure.text: The door is child-locked. Of course it is. The wagon lurches forward and you jog alongside it all the way around the roundabout, knocking on the glass, while the driver turns up the radio and the kids sing a camp song at you through the window.
failure.art: A teenager jogging beside a moving station wagon around a suburban roundabout at night, knocking on the window, children singing inside

encounters.title: You've Been Flocked
encounters.place: Your front lawn, 2 a.m.
encounters.text: Somebody flocked your yard. There are pink plastic flamingos everywhere, hundreds of them, staked so close together you cannot see the grass. A note taped to the door says the flock will leave when you pay to send it on to a friend. Then, all together, with a soft plastic creak, every flamingo turns its head to look up at your window.
encounters.art: Hundreds of pink plastic lawn flamingos staked so close together on a suburban front lawn at two in the morning that the grass is hidden, every one of them turning its head toward a lit upstairs window, a teenager looking down from that window, a folded paper taped to the front door below, yellow porch light, high wide shot from the window

choices.label: Start pulling stakes, two flamingos at a time

success.text: You yank stakes two at a time and stack the flamingos in the garage like firewood. The flock creaks in protest, but by four a.m. the lawn is clear. One last flamingo stands by the mailbox. It gives you a small, respectful nod and walks off down the street.
success.art: A garage stacked to the rafters with pink plastic flamingos like firewood, a single flamingo walking away down a dark street, a tired teenager watching from the lawn

failure.text: For every flamingo you pull, two more are standing in the hole. By dawn the flock has spread to the roof, the gutters and the hood of the car, and one is perched on your headboard when you finally fall asleep.
failure.art: A suburban house at dawn covered in pink plastic flamingos on the roof, gutters and car hood, one flamingo perched on a bedroom headboard visible through the window

choices.label: Pay the fee and send the flock to the jolliest house on the street

success.text: You tape three quarters to the note and write down the most cheerful house on the street. In the morning the flock is gone, and three doors down the neighbors are on their lawn in bathrobes, laughing and taking pictures. By noon your quarters are back, taped to a thank-you note.
success.art: Neighbors in bathrobes laughing and taking instant photos on a lawn crowded with pink flamingos in morning light, a thank-you note with coins taped to a door nearby

failure.text: You pay the fee, and the flock does leave, all at once, a pink stampede down the middle of Crystal Street. It does not go to your friend's house. It goes to the HOA president's, and he knows exactly whose lawn it came from.
failure.art: A stampede of pink plastic flamingos racing down the middle of a dark suburban street toward a tidy house where a man in a robe stands glaring on the porch

choices.label: Dress every flamingo as a classic movie monster

success.text: If you cannot beat them, costume them. You raid the dress-up box and give every flamingo a cape, a mummy wrap or a bolt through the neck.
