By morning your yard is the talk of Glimmer Falls, and the flock, thrilled with itself, wins the Yard of the Week ribbon and five dollars before it wanders off.
success.art: A suburban lawn full of pink plastic flamingos dressed as vampires, mummies and monsters with neck bolts, a blue ribbon pinned to the mailbox in morning light

failure.text: The flamingos hate their costumes. They shake off the capes, peck holes in the mummy wraps and follow you inside single file, creaking with offense, and stand in a pink ring around your bed all night.
failure.art: A ring of pink plastic flamingos with torn capes and unraveling mummy wraps standing around a bed in a dark bedroom, a teenager peeking over the blanket

encounters.title: Big Trash Night
encounters.place: Crystal Street curbs, bulk trash night
encounters.text: It is bulk trash night and every curb on the cul-de-sac is piled with old furniture: lamps, a waterbed frame, a box of macrame. As you walk home, a plaid recliner from the Fenwicks' curb is following you. Every time you turn around it is one driveway closer, footrest up, reclined just slightly, the way a dog rolls over to ask for a belly rub.
encounters.art: A suburban street on bulk trash night lined with curbside piles of old furniture, lamps, a wooden waterbed base and a box of macrame, a plaid recliner with its footrest raised sitting in the middle of the road one driveway behind a teenager walking home who is glancing back over their shoulder, streetlights, wide shot

choices.label: Sit down in it

success.text: You sit. It is the most comfortable chair in the history of chairs. It hums, it rocks, and then it carries you all the way home, up the porch steps, and parks you in front of the TV. Down in the cushions you find a dollar in quarters and the remote the Fenwicks lost in 1979.
success.art: A teenager lounging blissfully in a plaid recliner rolling up a porch step at night, a handful of quarters and an old TV remote in their lap

failure.text: You sit. The footrest snaps up, the back drops down, and the recliner folds you up like a taco and trundles off to the Fenwicks' garage, where it parks you between the lawnmower and a rack of bowling shoes until dawn.
failure.art: A teenager folded up inside a plaid recliner parked in a cluttered garage between a lawnmower and a rack of bowling shoes, dawn light under the door

choices.label: Drag it back to the curb where it belongs

success.text: You grab the armrests and drag it, protesting, back to the Fenwicks' curb, then set the box of macrame on its seat, which seems to soothe it. It settles in, footrest down, and stays. In the morning the trash truck takes it, and it waves its lever at you as it goes.
success.art: A teenager dragging a plaid recliner by its armrests back to a curbside furniture pile at night, a box of macrame plant hangers on the seat

failure.text: You get it as far as the roundabout before it digs in its little wooden feet. Then every other piece of curbside furniture on the street turns toward you: the lamps, the waterbed frame, a whole dinette set. You run home and refuse to look back at the clatter behind you.
failure.art: Curbside lamps, a dinette set and old furniture shuffling down a dark suburban street after a running teenager, a plaid recliner planted by a roundabout

choices.label: Walk it down the street to a porch that needs a good chair

success.text: You walk it like a puppy down to the one porch on the street that needs a good chair. Mrs. Washington looks at the recliner, the recliner looks at her, and something clicks. She sits, it purrs, and she declares it the best thing anybody ever found on a curb.
success.alone: You walk it like a puppy to a porch at the end of the street where a broken lawn chair sits by the door. You haul the old chair to the curb and set the recliner in its place. It purrs and settles in, and in the morning you hear somebody on that porch laugh with pure delight.
success.art: A plaid recliner settled happily on a cozy front porch under a yellow porch light, a broken lawn chair left at the curb, a teenager waving good night

failure.text: Every porch you try already has a chair, and every chair takes offense. By three a.m. you have been chased off two porches by a pair of furious lawn chairs, and the recliner is still following you, dejected, its footrest dragging on the asphalt.
failure.art: Two folding lawn chairs snapping angrily at a teenager fleeing down porch steps at night, a sad plaid recliner waiting on the sidewalk

encounters.title: The Vacation Slides
encounters.place: The Petersens' den, a little after midnight
encounters.text: The Petersens caught you on the sidewalk and insisted you come in for their vacation slides. The carousel projector clicks, slide after slide: the Grand Canyon, the world's biggest ball of twine, a motel pool. In every slide there is someone in the background, a little closer each time, and by the Hoover Dam you can see it is you, waving, in the clothes you have on right now.
encounters.art: A dim wood-paneled den a little after midnight, a carousel slide projector on a coffee table casting a bright snapshot of a big canyon onto a pull-down screen, a smiling middle-aged couple on the couch, a teenager squeezed between them, and in the background of the projected slide a small figure waving in the same clothes the teenager is wearing, projector beam and dark room, medium wide shot

choices.label: Walk right up to the screen and look closer

success.text: You walk up to the screen. The you in the slide stops waving, points at the projector and mouths: last slide. You pop it out of the carousel. It shows the roundabout on Halloween night, full of your friends, and somebody has written HAVE FUN along the edge. The Petersens yawn, say good night, and the den feels warm and ordinary.
success.art: A teenager holding a single slide up to a projector beam in a wood-paneled den, the tiny image showing friends gathered at a roundabout on Halloween night

failure.text: Up close, the you in the slide is not waving. It is knocking from the inside of the screen, and it looks worried. You step back into the dark of the den and realize the Petersens on the couch have not blinked in a very long time.
failure.art: A slide projected on a pull-down screen showing a worried teenager knocking from inside the image, the real teenager stepping back, a couple on the couch staring with wide unblinking eyes

choices.label: Fake a sneeze and bump the projector

success.text: You fake a sneeze, bump the table, and the carousel jams with a satisfying crunch. The bulb flares and dies. In the dark the Petersens chuckle, say, Well, that's the show, and switch on a lamp. On the blank screen, for one second, a tiny you gives a thumbs-up and fades.
success.art: A jammed carousel slide projector with a fading bulb in a dark den, a faint tiny thumbs-up figure on a pull-down screen, a teenager stifling a fake sneeze

failure.text: The carousel spins faster instead, slides flickering by like a flip book: the canyon, the twine, the motel, your house, your room, your bed, with someone standing over it. Then the bulb blinks out. You go home and sleep with the lamp on.
failure.art: A slide projector spinning wildly in a dark den, a blur of flickering slides on the screen ending on an image of a bed with a shadowy figure standing over it

choices.label: Ask real questions about their trip

success.text: You ask what the motel was like and whether the canyon was as big as it looks. The Petersens light up. They tell you about the flat tire, the lost suitcase and the best pie in Arizona. The stranger in the slides fades out of the background, and they send you home with leftover pie and two quarters for listening.
success.art: A beaming older couple on a den couch telling stories and gesturing wide while a teenager listens with a plate of pie, an ordinary sunny canyon snapshot on the screen

failure.text: Every question makes the show longer. A second carousel comes out of the closet, then a third. By three in the morning you have seen every rest stop between here and Albuquerque, and in all of them you are standing in the back, looking tired.
failure.art: A stack of slide carousels on a den coffee table at three in the morning, a weary teenager slumped on the couch, a rest-stop snapshot on the screen with the same teenager in the background

encounters.title: The Ice Cream Truck
encounters.place: The roundabout, 1:40 a.m.
encounters.text: An ice cream truck you have never seen before is parked at the roundabout, playing its jingle slow and a little warped, like a music box winding down. The menu on its side has a picture of every neighbor on Crystal Street, and under each one the name of a flavor: Mr. Fenwick's Secret, What Mrs. Delgado Really Puts in the Meatloaf, The Thing Under the Fergusons' Pool Cover. Exact change only.
encounters.art: A pastel ice cream truck parked at a dark suburban roundabout at 1:40 in the morning under one streetlight, its side panel lined with small painted portraits of the neighbors from the street, a shadowy driver behind the serving window, a purple crystal rock glowing behind it, a teenager on the sidewalk counting coins in their palm, pastel truck lights, medium wide shot

choices.label: Buy a Mr. Fenwick's Secret and taste it

success.text: It tastes like butterscotch, and you know the secret instantly: Mr. Fenwick cries at dog food commercials. That is all. You laugh, then decide it is sweet, and keep it forever. The jingle sours, because the secret was not scandalous at all, and the truck pulls away disappointed.
success.art: A teenager licking a butterscotch ice cream bar and laughing under a streetlight as a pastel ice cream truck pulls away from a roundabout

failure.text: It tastes like burnt toast, and you learn something that was not yours to know: who on the street is lonely, and how much. It sits in your stomach like a cold stone. All night you cannot look at a single porch light without feeling it.
failure.art: A teenager standing alone at a dark roundabout holding a half-eaten gray ice cream bar, looking at a row of lonely porch lights along the street

choices.label: Head off the little kids drifting toward the jingle

success.text: Kids in pajamas are drifting out of their houses toward the music. You get in front of them and announce, very seriously, that tonight's flavor is broccoli, extra chunky. The little ones groan and trudge back to bed. With nobody buying, the jingle runs down and stops, and the truck rolls away into the dark.
success.art: A teenager with arms spread wide turning back a group of small children in pajamas on a dark suburban sidewalk, a pastel ice cream truck waiting at the roundabout

failure.text: The kids walk right past you, humming the jingle. Each one buys a cone and comes back very quiet, knowing something about the grown-ups on the street they were never meant to know. You walk every one of them home, and none of them will say what it was.
failure.art: A line of small children in pajamas holding ice cream cones walking home silently along a dark sidewalk, a worried teenager walking beside them

choices.label: Chase the truck on your bike and see where it parks

success.text: When the truck pulls away you chase it on your bike, past the edge of town, to the old dairy lot on Quarry Road. Its freezer is packed with melting secrets dripping into a drain. You yank the freezer's plug, and every flavor on the menu fades to plain vanilla.
success.art: A teenager on a bike in an abandoned dairy lot at night pulling the plug on an ice cream truck freezer, colorful melting ice cream dripping into a drain

failure.text: The truck speeds up as you chase it, its jingle getting faster and faster, until it turns a corner and is simply gone. Then the jingle starts again right behind you, very close, and you pedal straight into the next nightmare to get away from it.
failure.art: A teenager pedaling hard down a dark suburban street at night, the glowing headlights of a pastel ice cream truck looming close behind them

encounters.title: Best Decorated House
encounters.place: The Merrill and Yoshida front yards, 11:55 p.m.
encounters.text: The Merrills and the Yoshidas have fought over Best Decorated House every October since 1971, and this year it has finally gone too far. Fog machines roar on both lawns. A Merrill inflatable ghost the size of a garage is wrestling a Yoshida animatronic witch. A plastic skeleton army is marching across the property line, and both sets of grown-ups are in lawn chairs on their porches, cheering.
encounters.art: Two rival suburban front yards at 11:55 at night overflowing with Halloween decorations, fog machines roaring on both lawns, a giant inflatable ghost the size of a garage wrestling an animatronic witch, an army of plastic skeletons marching across the property line through thick fog, two sets of grown-ups cheering from lawn chairs on their porches, a teenager in the middle of the fog, orange and green lights, wide shot

choices.label: Stand on the property line and judge it fair and square

success.text: You stand on the property line in the fog and declare a tie: both houses, Best Decorated in Glimmer Falls history. The ghost and the witch stop wrestling and shake hands. The skeletons bow. The Merrills and the Yoshidas, sheepish, carry thermoses of cocoa across the line to each other for the first time in fifteen years.
success.art: An inflatable ghost and an animatronic witch shaking hands in a foggy yard at night, plastic skeletons bowing, two families meeting at a property line with thermoses of cocoa

failure.text: Both families accuse you of taking bribes, and both yards turn on you. You flee down the sidewalk chased by a dozen plastic skeletons, a wobbling inflatable pumpkin and a foam tombstone that keeps falling over and getting back up, all the way into somebody else's B-movie.
failure.art: A teenager running down a foggy suburban sidewalk chased by plastic skeletons, a wobbling inflatable pumpkin and a foam tombstone tipping over

choices.label: Follow the tangle of cords and pull the plug

success.text: Every cord on both lawns runs to one overloaded outlet in the Yoshidas' garage. You yank it. With a long, sad whine, the ghost deflates, the witch freezes mid-cackle and the skeletons collapse in a heap. Both families, each blaming the other, pay you a quarter apiece to keep quiet about who blew the fuse.
success.art: A deflating inflatable ghost sagging over a heap of collapsed plastic skeletons in a foggy yard, a teenager holding a fistful of unplugged extension cords in a garage doorway

failure.text: You pull the plug and both yards keep going. They were never plugged in at all. The inflatable ghost turns its giant vinyl head toward you, the skeleton army changes course, rattling, and you spend the next hour hiding in the Merrills' hedge.
failure.art: A giant inflatable ghost turning its head toward a teenager crouched in a hedge, a rattling army of plastic skeletons marching toward them through fog, a dangling unplugged cord

choices.label: Build one decoration so good it ends the war

success.text: You raid both garages and build it in an hour: a twelve-foot jack-o-lantern made from every spare decoration on the street, lit from inside with a strobe. Both yards stop dead to stare. The war is over. Your monster wins Best Decorated, and both families want to know how you did it.
success.art: A towering twelve-foot jack-o-lantern built from mismatched Halloween decorations glowing with strobe light between two foggy yards, stunned families staring up at it

failure.text: Your creation stands up. It looks around, takes a lawn chair from each porch and declares itself the new Best Decorated House. Then it decides your house is next, and you spend the night pinning sheets over your windows while it strings lights all over your roof.
failure.art: A giant patchwork jack-o-lantern creature stringing orange lights across a suburban roof at night, a teenager pinning bedsheets over the windows below
